"PUT TO ROUT." (From the German of Pffarins by Baroness Swift.) Unto the forest I wander'd one day, But not one of my cares stay'a at home! Often I paus'd, though in vain, on my way, • For with me those companions would roam! Then when we unto the green wood drew nigh, What a stir and a rustling. I heard! "Forth from our kingdom, dull cares, quickly fly !" Loudly twitter'd and sang ev'ry bird.; Each tiny grass-blade essay'd to oppose Their approach to the wood, while the trees . Blew them asunder, and with cruel blows They were scourg'd by the branches of trees. : Hither and thither they ran to and fro, Hustled e'en by the rocks where they flew; Some quickly melted 'neath Sunshine's warm glow, While all others were drown'd by the dew! "You've had your deserts!" thus gladly I cried, "If with me in the woods ye will roan:, This is what ever to you will betide, So, another time, pray stop at home !"
"THE UNKNOWN MARTYR." It stood in the long gallery— ... A picture of a maid ‘"""-- Crowned with a simple wreath of flowers,

In quaint old dress arrayed. "The Unknown Martyr," it was called, For, so tradition told, The maiden died for Jesus' sake In the dark days of old. Holding the faith she knew was right, - Aye, even to the end. Her very name was blotted out By father, mother, friend. Yet still her portrait held its place In the old gallery, And lo! the lesson of her life Was there for all to see. . For centuries those true brave eyes Taught every passer-by. For the dear Christ who died for us How best to live or die. "The Unknown Martyr," called they her; Hers is undying fame As long as lasts this world of ours; And Jesus knows her name. •—" The Quiver," George Weatherly.

"What is the best uniform to fight in ?" asked George IV. of a gallant Life Guardsman after the Battle of Waterloo. "Shirt-sleeves, your Majesty," responded the man.

A short man became attached to a tall woman, and somebody said he had fallen in love with her. "Do you -call it falling in love?" said an old bachelor; "it is more like climbing up to it." Crusty says falling in the street is bad enough, without having the first idiot that passes try to thrust the addi- tional misfortune of his acquaintance upon you by ask- " Did you hurt yourself?" Two men were conversing the other day, and one of them asked the other when he intended to go back home, the person addressed having come from America. He replied—" If I live till I die—and heaven knows whether I will or not—l intend to visit my native land once more before I leave this country." Dr. Wolcot, better known as Peter Pindar, had for a time a most violent cough, and his physician persisted in recommending him to take ass's milk as a remedy. The bard, tired of the doctor's importunity, at length quieted him by sending him the following:—

Dear doctor. do you really think That ass's milk I ought to drink? It would quite remove my cough, you say, And drive my old complaint away It cured yourself—l grant it true— But it was mother's milk to you. _ _

The true foundation of a happy.' life—lt is not what life is to bring to a man, but what he is able to carry into it, that will determine his happiness. It he has been so influenced as to hold the former lightly, and to give to the latter his enthusiastic interest, the true foundation of a happy life has been laid. Then luxurious desires will be kept in check and small troubles will be borne patiently, not so much by a martyr-like effort of self-sacrifice as by a simple and real appreciation of their relative insignificance. Other things will appear of so much more consequence that the petty interest of life will sink to their true level.

RABBINICAL ABSURDITIES.—The Rabbinical schools, in their meddling, carnal, superficial spirit of word-weaving and letter-worship, had spun large accumulations of worthless subtlety all over the Mosaic system. Among other things, they had wasted their idleness in fantastic attempts to count, and classify, and weigh, and measure all the separate commandants of the ceremonial and moral law. They had come to the sapient conclusion that there were 248 affirmative precepts, being as many as the members in the human body, and 365 negative precepts, being as many as the arteries and veins, or the days of the year; the total being 613, which was also the number of letters in the Decalogue. They arrived at the same result from the fact that the Jews were commanded (Numb. xv. 38) to wear fringes (tsitsith) on the corners of their tallith, bound with a thread of blue; and as each fringe had eight threads and five knots, and the letters of the word ts-itsith make 600, the total number of command- ments was, as before, 613. Now, surely, out of such a large number of precepts and prohibitions, all could not be of quite the same value; some were "light" and some were "heavy." But which? and what was the greatest ; commandment of all? According to some Rabbis, the most important of all is that about the tephillin and the tlitsith, the phylacteries and fringes; and "he who diligently observes it is regarded in the same-light as if he had kept the whole Law." Some thought that the omission of ablutions as bad as homicide; some that the precepts of the Mishna were all "heavy ;" those of the Law were some heavy and some light. Others considered the third to be the greatest commandment. None of them had realised the great principle that the wilful violation of one commandment is the transgression of all (James ii. 10), because the object of the entire Law is the spirit of obedieace to God.—Froni " Farrar's Life of Christ" for August. WIFE SELLINCI.—in the course or some notes on the sale of wives, a correspondent says that on the sth of September, 1772, a Mr. Bott, of Langley Common, led his wife by a rope tied round her waist ieto Derby Market- place, and sold her for is. 6d. The following describes a similar sale in 1855 :—" I cannot give the exact date— but about 1855, I think—l saw from the windows of the 'Derbyshire Club,' at the King's Head, a crowd collected near the Town Hall; presently a man led a woman away by a rope round her neck; they were surrounded and followed by a concourse of people jeering and laughing. On inquiring the meaning of the stir, I was told that the lady had just been sold for is. 6d. and a quart of ale! This was on a market day." A Derby paper (we believe the Advertiser) of August 29th. 1873, thus refers to a similar sale at Belper :—" The sale of a wife by auction is a spectacle which (paee French writers) is of suffi- ciently infrequent occurrence in England to render it re- markable. Our Belper correspondent informs us that the Market-place of the classic town of Belper was the theatre of such a scene last Saturday, the circumstances causing some trifling departures from the prescribed rule. He writes :—‘ A young woman, the wife of a man named Thompson, who is said to have left her and his ,creditors and gone to America, was the interesting article submitted to competition. Her past conduct seems to have had a deal to do with Thompson's disappearance. On Saturday Thompson's goods, &c., were sold, and the wife claimed a portion of the proceeds, and told the auc- tioneer that he must either share the money with her or sell her. This seems to have called forth the sympathy —or something else—of a bystander, who volunteered to undertake the rOle of auctioneer. A halter was borrowed from a neighbour, and the woman led into the Market- place, accompanied by a crowd of persona. No bidders, however, seemed to be amongst them. This disgraceful scene was enacted on the Saturday afternoon, and was witnessed by large numbers of spectators, many of whore expressed their disgust and annoyance.' " • :NOTHING BRITISIL.StrictIy speaking, there is nothing really and truly British; everybody and everything is a naturalised alien. Viewed as Britons, we all of us, human and animal, differ from one another simply in the length of time we and our ancestors have continuously inhabited this favoured and foggy isle of Britain. Look, for example, at the men and women of us. Some of us, no doubt, are more or less remotely of Norman blood, and came over, like that noble family the Slys, with Richard the Conqueror. Others of us, perhaps, are in the main Scandinavian, and date back a couple of gene- rations earlier, to the bare-legged followers of Canute and Guthrum. Yet others, once more, are true Saxon Englishmen, descendants of Hengest, if there ever:was a Hengest, or of Horse, if a genuine Horsa ever actually existed. None of these, it is quite clear, have any just right or title to be considered in the last resort as true- born Britons; they are all of them just as much foreigners at bottom as the Spitalfields Huguenots or the Pembrokeshire Flemings, the Italian organ boy, and the Flindoo prince disguised as a crossing-sweeper. But surely the Welshman and the Highland Scot at least are undeniable Britishers, sprung from the soil and to thel manner born! Not a bit of it- inexorable modern science, diving back remorselessly into the remoter past, traces the Cvniry across the face of Germany, and fixes in shadowy hypothetical numbers the exact date, to a few centuries, of the first prehistoric Gaelic invasion. Even the still earlier brown Euskarians and yellow Mon- golians, who held the land before the advent of the ancient Britons, were themselves immigrants; the very Autochthones in person turn out, on close inspection, to be vagabonds and wanderers and foreign colonists. In short, man as a whole is not an indigenous animal at all in the British Isles. Be he who he may, when we push his pedigree back to its prime original, we find him always arriving in the end by the Dover steamer or the Harwich packet. Five years, in fact, are quite sufficient to ,eive him a legal title to letters of naturalisation, unless, , indeed, he be a German grand duke, in which case he can always become an Englishman off-hand by Act of Parliament.—Cornii Magazine.

At a crowded lecture, the other evening, a young lady standing at the door of the hall was addressed by a hon- est Hibernian, who was in attendence on the occasion. "Indade, miss, I should be glad to give you a sate, but the empty ones are all full. A teacher was illustrating the process of evaporation to a class of young scholars. "Suppose I should set a basin of water out in the school-yard in the morning and let it remain all, day, what would happen ?" It would get upset," was the practical reply. " What ! women overworked? Fudge! Think of the men!" "All, but you know the old saying, Woman's work is never done !" "I know it; and that's the rea- son she.oughtn't to complain; for a man has to do his work or lose his job !" One day, in the country, Sheridan Knowles said to Abbot, with whom he had been acting there—" My dear fellow, I'm off to-morrow. Can I take any letters for you ?" "You're very kind," answered Abbot; "but where are you going to ?" "I haven't made up my mind."

In reply to the question of a sportsman whether he had seen any rabbits, an Irish rustic answered, "Yes, your honour; whole funerals of them !"—the word "funerals" representing the greatest combination of length and numbers witlx which his experience had ren- dered him acquainted. AN UNNEXPECTRD COMMENT FROM His WIFT.,..—" It is a curious'custom the Japanese have, my dear," remarked a husband, "of taking their shoes off when entering the house." "The custom is curious," replied :the lady, "from the fact that it is practised at all hours instead of at night only" and the husband said "Yes" with a rising reflection, Which was about all he could say. Charles Lamb, who was somewhat troubled with an impediment in his speech—whose quips and quibbles have been relished by many of us—while one day sitting at a public table had odcasion to use a pepper-box. After shaking it with alt due vehemence, and turning it in various ways, he found that the crushed pepper-corns were not inclined to come forth. 'a " T-t-h-this p-p-pe- pepper-box," he exclaimed, ;with a facetious grin, "is something like myself." "Why so ?" asked a neighbour. "P-p-poor delivery," he replied. An anecdote is told of a gentleman in MOnmouthshire which, exhibits the pride of ancestry in a striking point of view. His house was in such a state of dilapidation that the proprietor was in danger of perishing under the ruins of the ancient mansion: which he venerated even in decay. A stranger whom he accidentally met at the foot of the Skyrrid, made various inquiries respecting the country, the prospects, and the neighbouring houses, and, among others, asked: "Whose is this antique man- sion before us ?" "That, sir, is I'Verndee, a very ancient house; for out of it came the Earls of Pembroke of the first line, the Earls of Pembroke of the second line, the Lords Herberts of Cherbury, the Herberts of Coldbrook,

Ramsey, Cardiff, and Yoik, the Morgans of Acton, the Earlr, of Hunsdon, the houses of Ircowm and Lanarth ; and all the Powells. Out of this house also, by the female line, came the Duke of Beaufort." "And pray, sir, who lives there now ?" "I do, sir." "Then pardon me, and accept a piece of advice : Come out of it yourself, or you'll soon be buried in the ruins of it." A NOBLE SACRIFICE.—During the last war in Afghani- stan a young officer, with a small body of soldiers, was sent uport some mission a short distance from the English Camp. As they were returning, riding gaily along a iihrrow mountain gorge, they suddenly perceived a troop of Afghans galloping headlong down after them. Being greatly outnumbered, the best chance of safety for the little band of English soldiers lay in flight, and

being well mounted, the' soon began to distatice "their pursuers. All at once a shot from •an Afghan trifle struck one of the soldier's horses, which staggered a few paces and then fell, crushing his rider beneath him. In an instant, while the others rode on, the young officer had drawn rein, flung himself from the saddle, and dragged the fallen man to his feet. " Quick !my horse will carry two," he cried. But, alas !!!the horse, finding himself free, and terrified, perhaps, by the shouts of the Afghans, had galloped after his retreating '.comrades, carrying with him the only hope of the two soldiers. One minute more, and the noble young' officer and the man he had vainly tried to save were dying; lifeless, pierced by the long knives of their merciless foes.— "Little Folks Magazine" A WORKING MAN ON THE SUNDAY QUESTION.—In my frequent journeys in all parts of the country, from the Orkneys to the Land's End, and from Lowestoft to Aberystwith, as well as through every county in Ireland, I have sought the company of workings men. Deeply sympathising with them, I have been anxious to get at their viaws on a question which so vitally affects their interest. Of course many contend for:the relaxation of all prohibiting laws in regard to the Sabbath. But I have never yet met with any thoughtful working man who has not admitted that he had no answer to the argu- ments which these men presented to Lord:Talmerston- Because they came from men of their own class, the effect produced was far deeper than by that which I had to say. 1 met, many years ago,with a singular illustration of this question, which is very pertinent. Coming out of our mission-house in Moorgate Street, I said to the man who was waiting to take us to the railway station, "Cabby, this is very serious,weather, isn't it?" For the rain had been falling in torrents, and in July, when dry weather was so much needed by the ripening corn. "What have you got to say agin the weather? Don't you think the Almighty can manage that matter better than we poor mortals ?" "Certainly. But good and gracious as God is, He sometimes sends judgments as well as shows mercy. But how do you get on at such times ?" "How do I get on, sir? Why;if I get down in the dumps I think of that passage—' All things work to- gether for good to them that love God." t"Cabby, do you really believe those words?" "Do I believe 'em? Why, I -live upon 'em every day." Having a few minutes to spare when we got to the station, I resumed my talk with cabby, and said, "How do you manage on Sundays? Do you work on that day?" "See my hoss, sir, and look at me—if I ain't handsome, I thank God I am strong and healthy. And do you think that either of us would be as well as we are, if I broke God's laws ?" "You interest me greatly. Tell me how you manage."---" Well sir, when I gets up on Sundays, I first looks after my hoss, gives him a good dressing, his corn and water, and says to un, 'There, now, you be quiet until I comes again.' And then I helps the wife to get the breakfast, and me and the children tidy up ourselves, have a chapter, and a bit of prayer, send the children off to Sunday-school and by-and-by we all go to church to worship and praise God. We come home and enjoy our dinner; children are off again to school, and I and my wife take a quiet stroll, and as many of us as can, go to service in the evening. After that I see to my hoss again, finish up with reading in the blessed Book, and off to bed to sleep as sound as a top. And we get up in the morning as fresh as a daisy!" It was impossible not to extend one's hand to this simple good man, in brotherly sympathy, and we bade each other "God-speed"---The Quiver for August. A PIG IN A CARPET BAG.—Since people have got to carrying dogs, bundles, chests ot tools, loaded market baskets, and such articles inside omnibuses, we presume no regular patron of any route would be much surprised to hear of a pig being transported in a carpet bag, and that carpet bag bundled into an omnibus besides. A pretty strong proof that such a thing could be done was witnessed in an omnibus not long ago. The day was rainy, and everybody out of doors in bad humour, of course—particjarly such as. after waiting under a dilapidated awning or in a dripping doorway for half an hour, rush out into the rain and mud, and run the risk of their lives to get a 'bus, and are told by twelve inside that it's "all full." As a general rule, persons thus bluffed off pick their way back to the pavement the best way they can, and wait for another chance; but there r are some who will not sta-nd it, and force their way into the vehicle, no matter how many object. One of these won't-be-refused persons paid liberally for his boorish- ness, as the story will show. An omnibus, filled with its complement of twelve, was hailed by a big man in a wet, shaggy coat,and carrying a large carpet bag. The driver stopped, of course. '*Who, ever heard of a driver fancying his 'bus full? "All full." "Go on, driver." "There's no room here, sir !" And a dozen other ex- clamations came from the insiders; but the driver sat still on his box, and the dripping stranger pulled away at the door, which a man was holding on to by a strap. The outsider was too strong for the insider, however, and pulling the door open, jammed in and passed roughly along over boots and gaiters to the front of the 'bus. Here he deposited his carpet bag upon the feet of a lady passenger, and crowded about one-third of his huge per- son upon the bit of spare space on the opposite seat, and " faced the audience." "A pretty idea tolkeep a man standing out in the rain and mud, wasn't it?" exclaimed the angry intruder. The ladies looked at each other and smiled, while the men laughed outright. "Maybe I've been amongst civilised people sorneltime in my life," said the now enranged stranger, "even if they didn't have painted omnibuses, and painted people in 'ern !" This drew a deprecating glance from the ladies, while the gentlemen looked as if they wouldn't mind pitching the fellow out. " Wee-e-e !" came from the carpet bag " Hello ! What's that ?" asked a little man with big hair: and thin voice. "A pig in at, carpet bag!" shouted another. 4' We-e-e-e-ooh-we-e-e-e !" from the carpet bag. 'Throw it out !" cried the man with a: thin voice. , "There aint any pig there !" roared the shaggy coat. " Them's my clothes, and noth'n else !" ".Wee-e-e-e !" "There ain't ?" from a dark-looking man. -"Pitch him , out, with his live pork !" "Let 'em try`fit !" roared the shaggy man. "Who's a-going to do it ?" " Wee-e-e-e-- ooh—ooh—wee-e-e !" " Gentlemen ! we can't stand this any longer !" "Go out with your hog, you brute !" cried the little man, assuming immense indignation. "Stop the omnibus, and let me out," cried one of the ladies. "I tell you I ain't got no pig in that bag !" growled the shage,9 man; "I'll bet £lO on that! The critter is some- where else—under some of the seats, maybe." "Wee-e-e-e !" Here the alarm of the ladies began to be intense. Several insisted on getting out, and one im- provised a very good feint at a faint. Here, guard! This nuisance is not to be borne any longer!" The vehicle was stopped and the dark-looking man got out, then walked straight into the Victoria Hotel, bestowing, as he entered the door, rather a quizzical look at the people in the omnibus. "'Who is that fellow?' growled the shaggy coat. "I've a mind to get out and thrash him! The idea of my having a pig in that carpet bag !" "That man," answered the person addressed. "that iS Mr. Love, the ventriloquist." CHEAPEST HOUSEhi the city for Glass, China, Oriental Wares, and Fancy Goods.-175, Oxford-street, laachester.- 4c/rt.

div.head: . THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
div.p: . THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
MINOR BREEDS OF FRENCH POULTRY.

In previous articles we have described the chief breeds of French poultry, by which we mean those best known outside France itself, and we now propose to deal with those that are not so well distributed, and are, in fact, almost entirely limited to the land of their birth. There are several of these which deserve, for one reason or other, to be better known and to be appreciated both in England and America. First, then, we shall place

LA BRESSE, Which, as may be known to some, is regarded as the best of all the French fowls for table purposes. Some few months ago we had the opportunity of tasting a very fine specimen of the La Bresse variety, and, for flavour of meat and tenderness, we never met with its equal. It was decidedly in advance of the Dorking which we had on the table at the same time. Some of thi4 might be due to the feeding, for the French fowl hal been fed according to the Gallic method, whilst the English fowl had been ptepared in the way which is usually the case for the home market. The fiE sh of the former really melted in the mouth, and it was a rare treat.

This breed is divided into two varieties, nameTy, the grey and the black. The former, which has really a pencilled marking, is chiefly bred in the department of the Bourg, and the latter in the Arrondisseme4 of Louhans. Lemoine gives the following description of the La Bresse:—The Bresse cock has an active and pleas- ing gait, its head is fine, its eyes bright, its crest simple, straight, strongly fixed, and much indented. The beard feathers are long and fine, the ear feathers white. The tail is ornamented with beautiful plumage, well arranged, forming an elegant curve. Its legs are slender and of a greyish blue colour. The Bresse hen is very agile. Its crest is bent towards the side. The ear feathers are white, the beard feathers of a medium size. In the grey variety the plumage of the head, the chest, and the back of the grey Bresse cock is white. The wings are white with some black feathers, the tail plumes are black with some speckled rays. The hen has its plumage more or less pencilled, forming a greyish tint. But one may see in certain places, hens in which the covering of the wings, the chest, and the under parts show white feathers; in addition the extremities of the feathers of the tail have more black than white. The other variety is completely black. Hens of both these varieties are good layers, and very rarely sit. The eggs of the blacks are much the larger, weighing nearly two-and-a-half ounces each, whilst the eggs of the greys only weigh about one-and-three-quarter ounces. Both varieties lay about 150 eggs every year.

div.head: COURTES PATTES.
div.p: COURTES PATTES.

• This quaint little variety has been known to a small extent in England for a few years, but it has never won any great amount of popularity. This' doubtless is due to the fact that their peculiar shape has led people to the opinion that they are more ornamental than useful. This is, however,kfar from being the case, as they are fairly good layers,t-apital table fowls, and reliable sitters and mothers_ The plumage is entirely black, and they are medium in size. The peculiarity consists in the short- ness of the legs, which causes them to walk with a strange gait. They are on this account very suitable in- deed for keeping in gardens, as' they do not scratch. They are very hardy, and grow at a rapid rate. M. Lemoine thus describes the Courtes Pattes :—" The Courtes Pattes cock, notwithstanding his lowness, holds his head upright, as though he had a desire to increase his stature. He is like all the fowls of the department of La Sarthe—the eye large and open. His plumage is entirely black, with greenish reflections. Each feather is very full, especially on the neck. The body is hori- zontal, wide, and long, the comb fleshy, straight, single, indented regularly with very high spikes, and very thick at the base. The beard feathers are long, the ear feathers white and long, the legs thick, of a dark gray, and very low, not very much more than an inch in length. The tail is fully furnished, and the plumes carried high. The hens have a less strange appearance, and if among the young any are found which by chance have longer legs it is noticeable that they much resemble the black variety of the La Bresse fowl. The Courtes Pattes hen has its body wide and long, but rounder than that of the cock. Its plumage is entirely black, its crest simple, but to a slight extent falling back and bent aside. The beard feathers are round, the ear feathers round and white, the feet very short, thick, and of a dark gray. These hens will lay about 110 eggs per annum, each weighing about two ounces.

div.head: MANS.
div.p: LE MANS.

This is another variety of fowls whose home is found in the Department of La Sarthe, whence come the La Fleche and the Courtes Pattes. It is a very large fowl, not neatly So pleasing in appearance as either La Fleche or the Creve Creeur, but withal of a very useful type. It is large, a non-sitter, and the flesh is excellent. From it is made one of those epicurean dishes for which France is so famous, namely, the savoury" Poule le Mans." The system of rearing adopted in the district where it is bred is one likely to bring out the best. qualities of a fowl, and there are those who think that many of the merits of this breed are due as much to the rearing and feeding as to the intrinsic merits of the fowl itself.

The description of this variety given by M. Lemoine is as follows :—The shape of the Mans male bird is less up- right than that of the La Fleche. It has, however, like that one a fine appearance, its plumage being completely black, the chest broad, and its tail plumes are well fi.-*d and fall back in an elegant manner. Instead of having two straight horns, as in the case of the La Fleche cock, the comb of the Mans is triple; the feathers are very pointed and terminate by a point in the form of a spear. The ear feathers of the Mans bird are white, the beard feathers white and long, the legs of a deep gray. The Mans hen has equally with the cock entirely black plumage, its crest is small and bent, terminating by a point, the ear feathers are round and white, the beard feathers are almost round and very little elongated, and the legs are of a deep gray. The hens of this breed are fairly good layera,

div.head: OTHER VARIETIES.
div.p: OTHER VARIETIES.

There are several other varieties of French fowls which it is not at all necessary that we should describe at any length. Some of these, though given entirely distinct names, are but variations of one or other of the standard breeds. In this country we endeavour to give all varieties of one breed the same name, tnerely defining their variations by the colour affixed; but in France it is not so, and the effect is misleading rather than helpful. We have noticed that this course is followed to some ex- tent in America, but it is to be deprecated, and we trust may not be encouraged, but discouraged. Thus, in France, the De Mantes is merely a variety of the Houilani There is, however, one breed which deserves especial mention. We mean the Barbezieu; this appears to be a coarser edition of the Minorca. It has the same type of body, and, we should imagine, owes its origin to the same source, but has not had the advantage of the care- ful breeding which has fallen to the lot of the English Minorca. The names of the other French varieties had better be mentioned. They are the Gournay, the Coucou de Rennes (from the Ardennes), the Cussades, from the Gascony district.

SEASONABLE HINTS. We mentioned some time ago that it was desirable to ' separate the sexes amongst the chickens, and it will now be found advantageous to divide the young pullets into flocks of twenty. They are found to thrive much better than when kept in larger numbers. If they can be scat- tered about in groups widely apart they will thrive all the more, and the advantages of putting the young stock out on to the fields after harvest will 'be found, in the extra size and stamina obtained by them. If kept in large numbers too-'ether they worry each other and do not thrive so well, retarding their growth and postponing the time when they will begin to lay,

I wheat and barley are especially'ato :bechosen4 as " - these have been found to be least affected by the fly. Likewise, all measures calculated to cause vigorous and strong growth counteract attacks of this pest, but where the attack has occurred on land which,- as in the case now under observation, has been treated with farm manure not well rotted but still long ' and strawy, which it is extremely likely may be of imported straw, it would be desirable to insect an ac- count of where the straw came from. The may have been brought in the chrysalis state in the straw, and also it is possible that it may remain in the seed. If the flax-seeds' are not thoroughly cleared from the wheat or barley with the chaff they are likely to set at- tack on foot again, therefore no. seed from infested fields should be sown. It is of serious importance to prevent this attack spreading, and for the present the measures to be used may be shortly recapitulated thus :-1. Where' the attack is found, cut the corn so high as to leave the chrysalids in the stubble, and then burn it. 2. Do not put corn in again for the next crop on infested ground. 3. Do not use seed corn from infested ground. 4. Use all measures to secure good growth, and likewise, where circumstances allow, use a plough with a skim-coulter, so that the upper soil may be turned over, and the lower being thrown on it, the insect will be so buried that if left in this condition till past the time of development in the following spring, there 'will be no fear of its re- appearance. All information as to the nature and means of prevention of attack will be at once given on applica- tion to me."

Several East Kent freehold fruit and hop farms were offered for sale by auction at Canterbury on Tuesday, but failed to find buyers, although the reserve prices fvere very moderate.__

A good, kind breeding sow, bearing ten or more pigs at a litter, will net more money proportionately to her owner than a horse or cow costing much more to buy and more expensive to keep. With two litters a year a sow should double her value once every six months. Mr. Handley, Greenhead, Westmorland, has purchased from Mr. John Law, New Keig„ Whitehouse, Aberdeen- shire, the three-year-old Shorthorn bull Reformer, which was second in the aged class at Dumfries, and was the cup winner at Alford this year. Reformer was bred by Mr. Duthie, Collynie, Tars-es, and is by the famous Earl of March.

As milk becomes scarce, or the calves become too old to need it, they generally have as hard a time as at any period of their lives. The grass at this time of the year often fails, and a little corn or cake given twice a day will tell in the value and appearance of the animal. Every chance of rearing a calf profitably is lost if it is not kept well the first twelve months of its life.

Mr. James A. Gordon, Arabella, Ross-shire, has sold to to an American buyer the yearling Shorthorn heifer Roan Princess, that was first prize winner at the High- land Society and also first at the Royal 'Northern and joint show at Forres. Roan Princess was bred by Mr. Inglis, Newmore, sired by Star of the Wee, and out of Vail Princess.

A report from Kentucky says that 20 or 30 cows have died of what is supposed to be hydrophobia there, and many more are dying. The diseased cattle suddenly be- come frantic, bellow with pain, and fight with each other. Men on horseback have been chased by them. The cattle die in spasms and frothing at the mouth within 24 hours after being taken sick. Two dogs supposed to have been mad were killed a few weeks ago, and it is thought that they may have spread the disease. SALTING HAY.—W. asks :—" Will you be good enough to give me information as to salting hay?" It is the opinion of many farmers that salt is of no benefit when applied to hay as it is being put into the mow in a green state. Some claim that it is a positive injury, as it ex- tracts a greater amount of the proper juices and pro- longs a lower fermentation, thereby causing more de- composition than would otherwise take place. Hay cured in this way will usually come out more or less discoloured or musty. The better way, where one has a small amount of such at one time, is to mix dry straw with the hay, in quantity sufficient to absorb the excess of moisture, first putting a layer of hay and a layer of straw until all is used. The straw will be benefited as well as the hay, and readily consumed by most kinds of stock. "FELON."—T. M. asks "What is a preventive for felon in heifers' bags. We are' very much troubled with it both in served and geld heifers. It. is high, dry gravelly land, but a good many trees. Also what effect has hard sweat hay on ewes in lamb in winter?" The best pre- ventive to "felon' in cows' bags is to give them an oc- casional dose of cooling medicine; do not giTe a suf- ficiently strong dose to violently purge them, but only to cause a relaxed condition of the bowels. The simplest and best medicines for this purpose are Epsom salts and saltpetre; combined with a little ground ginger. Ewes in lamb will do very well in winter with "hard- sweat" hay, if it be given in moderate quantities and combined with other suitable food; indeed, sheep are rather fond of dark hay, and thrive well upon it, when used with discretion. AGRICULTURAL RETI7RIt3.---A summary of the agricul- tural returns of Great Britain for 1886 was issued by the Agricultural Department of the Privy Council on Wednesday night. The following was the acreage of crops as compared with 1885 :—Wheat, 2,286,064, a de- crease of 192,254, or 7.8 per cent.; barley, 2,241,266, a decrease of 16,080, or 0.7 per cent.; oats, 3,081,701. an increase of 141,211, or 4.8 per cent.; potatoes, 553,990, an increase of 5,259, or 1 per cent.; hops, 69,967, a de- crease of 1.360, or 1.9 per cent. The total number of live stock in Great Britain in 1886, as compared with 1885, was as follows :—Cattle, 6,646,785, an increase of 4,821, or 01 per cent.; sheep, 16,176,410, a decrease of 361,197, or 22 per cent.; lambs, 9,344,924, a decrease of 652,104, or 6.5 per cent. The total number of sheep and lambs was 25,521,334, a decrease of 1,013,301, or 37 per cent.; pigs, 2,221,557, a decrease of 181,823, or 7 per cent. How TO KEEP A CELLAR COOL.—A great mistake is sometimes made in ventilating cellars or dairies. The purpose of ventilation is to keep the cellars cool and dry, but this object often fails of being accomplished by a common mistake, the cellar being made both warm and damp instead. A cool place should never be ventilated, unless the air admitted is cooler than the air within, or is at least as cool as the latter, or a very little warmer. The warmer the air, the more moisture it holds in suspension. Necessarily, the cooler the air the more this moisture is condensed and precipitated. When a cool cellar is aired on a warm day, the entering air, being in motion, appears cool; but as it fills the cellar the cooler air with which it becomes mixed chills it, the moisture is condensed, and dew is deposited on the cold walls, land may often be seen running down them in streams. Then the cellar is damp, and soon becomes mouldy. To avoid this, the windows should only be opened at night, and late—the last thing before retiring. There is no need to fear that the night air is unhealthful; it is as pure as the air of midday, and is really drier. The cool air enters the apartment during the night, and circulates through it. The windows should be closed before sun- rise in the morning, and kept closed and shaded through the day. If the air of the cellar is damp, it may be thoroughly dried by placing in it a peck of fresh lime in an open box. A peck of lime will absorb about 71b. or more than three quarts of water, and in this way a cellar or milk room may soon be dried, even in the hot- test weather.—lron. _ _

LABOURERS' HOLDUVIS.—The Manchester Examiner says : —" One year's trial of a modest commercial experiment in the way of providing labourers with small holdings has been reported at the first general meeting of the shareholders of the Small Farm and Labourers' Land Company. Hitherto they have dealt only with one small estate at Lambourne. About half of the estate had been sold, and a third of the money received had been spent in improving the remainder' with the result that the company received more rent from the remain- ing half than was formerly received for the whole; the second third had been spent in management, and the third was distributed as a 5 per cent. dividend for the shareholders. According to the testimony of Lord Wantage, the chairman, the tenants of the company are well satisfied with the amelioration in their condition brought to them by the occupancy of a little plot of land. They are prosperous and contented. One of them formerly a stone breaker on the road, was-paying sums under the purchasing clauses and gradually becoming owner of the land which he occupied. He had built a house, chiefly with his own hands, at a cost of £75, erected a cowshed, and fenced in the pri,perty. Yet the company was no loser by the transaction. The society proposed to acquire more capital and to extend its operations, in which case the cost of management will become relatively smaller. In order to carry on their operations no change in the law is needed. All that tho company wants is an Act simplifying and cheapening the cost of transferring land. There is plenty of land to be got; there are plenty of tenants to hire it and work it at a living profit; and there is still a margin to give the shareholders a substantial dividend. Agricultural prospects are dark indeed, but this is a ray of light to solace and encourage us. We have great faith in ex- periments not dependent on pecarious benevolence for their success."

div.head: INSECT ATTACK ON WHEAT.
div.p: INSECT ATTACK ON WHEAT.

Miss E. A. Ortnerod. consulting entomologist of the Royal Agricultural Society, writes :—" I should be obliged if you would permit me to draw the attention of agriculturists to the appearance of an attack to the straw of wheat and barley which has recently been brought under my notice, and which, if allowed to establish itself, will prove of very serious importance. The presence of the attack is shown by the corn stem falling down with a sharp bend, but with not quite a crack through it, just aboye the second joint from the ground, giving somewhat the appearance of the stalk being what is in some district called 'root-fallen.' The injury is caused by the presence of a maggot just above the second joint, and on examination (in the present stage of the attack) this maggot will be found turned to a smooth brown shining chrysalis, lying partly fixed in the stem inside the leaf just outside and above the second knot. This chrysalis is distinguishable by its flattened *shape, giving it much resemblance to a flax- seed, and the attack corresponds in every way with that of the very destructive corn-stem pest, commonly known as the Hessian fly, of which (for the above-mentioned reason) the chrysalids are commonly known as ' flax- seeds 'in the United States and in Canada. This insect has not hitherto been specially noticed, even if known at all, as one occurring in England; but as it is the cause of very serious damage in other countries it has been fully described, and that which has within the last fortnight been brought under my observation exactly coincides in every particular with the Hessian fly, known scientifically as the Cecidomyia destructor, Say. It is one of the same genus as the well-known wheat midge, the Cecid omyia tritici, which produces the "red maggot," but differs in habits in the matter of attacking the stalk instead of the ear; consequently on this the supply of sap to the stem is lessened, and the ear is stunted, while the stem bearing it being weakened falls, and the loss, where the attack is bad, is of the most serious nature. At present the crop which has been in- spected so completely confirms the reports of the extent of injury caused by " flax-seed " attack, that the atten- tion of all agriculturists is requested, firstly, to ascertain whether it is in their corn, and more particularly in stems of wheat and barley; and secondly, to the use of measures in such cases to stamp out the pest before it spreads. At present the measure most to be desired, where the doubled-down corn with the flax-seed above the joints is seen, is to arrange the cutters of the reapers to sever the corn above the second joint, so that thus no infested straw could be carried off the field, from which afterwards the flies might spread. The chrysalids which were not de- veloped would remain in the stubble, which should as soon as possible be collected and burnt. Corn crops should not be sown on land which has been infested this year, or the attack is very likely to be con= tinued—and strong and hearty-growing kinds of

div.head: SCTENTIFIC NOTES.
div.p: SCTENTIFIC NOTES.

The Athenepuna anncunces a new work, entitled "A Strange journey," from the pen of Commander V. Lovett Cameron, R.N., the well-known African traveller. The scene is laid in the unexplored country behind Marka, on the east coast of Africa. and the work incorporates Arab tales and native folk-lore.

A Pittsburgh genius has discovered a process for manufacturing coke from natural gas. From this coke, it is said, are manufactured carbon points for electric lights, and thus is the red flare of natural gas made to contribute to the white and blinding brilliancy of elec- tric jets. A PROCESS or PRESERVING EGGS has been patented by Mr. John W. M•Kee, of Stoutland, Mo. It consists in first subjecting them .to the fumes of sulphurous acid and bromine, and then immersing them in a solution of lime, salt, cream of tartar, citric acid, nitrate of potash, chlorate of potash, borax, alum, and water, whereby it is claimed the eggs will be kept sweet and fresh tor seve- ral years. But who would eat eggs after they have come in contact with so many different chemicals? CANADIAN SLEEPING CARS.—The newest improvement in sleeping cars is the addition of bathrooms. Some of these have been placed on the Canadian Pacific Railway, and tired and dusty travellers who cross the Continent will be able to take a thorough wash at any time during the journey. These cars also have buffets, smoking- rooms, and all the other latest sleeping car improvements which tend to make long-distance journeys comfortable and enjoyable. The Canadian Pacific owns and operates its own "sleepers." and they are built and furnished in a manner almost regardless of expense. A SIIIITTLELESS SEWING MACHINE is the latest dis- covery. A Welsh gentleman, named Jones, has for some years studied the working of a sewing machine, and although not engaged in the trade, he has been working for a long time to produce a machine which would sur- pass all others in speed. He claims now to have suc- ceeded in his invention. A certain mystery surrounds it, but is stated that the machine is of the ordinary size, is built without cog or spring, and has no shuttle. At each revolution :two stitches are made, the capacity of the machine being double that of many at present in the market.

SPREADING WEATHER REPORf s.—The Norwegian Me- teorological Institute of Christiana, says Nature, has adopted an ingenious plan for disseminating its weather reports among the farmers, fishermen, &c. Thus, on the brake of every train departing from the capital to any part of the country after 3 um., a signal is exhibited in- dicating the weather to be expected for the ensuing 24 hours. These signals are very simple, consisting of red and white triangles, squares, and balls, each of which, or several combined, have their meaning; a white ball, for instance, "fine weather," &c. These signals will also be displayed from the masts of several coasting steamers.. ahe arrangement is in force from July 1 to October 1.. AN INDIAN ADAPTATION OF AN ENGLISH NOVA:L.—The Bombay Gazette has received two numbers of a Gujemti adaptation by Mr. K. N. Kabrajee, of Mrs. Henry Wood's "East Lynne." "The scene is laid in a Parsee house, and the performers are all Parsees. The play appeared at first in a serial form in the pages of the Stri Bodh, a magazine of which Mr. Kabrajee is the editor, but which is chiefly written by Parsee ladies. It produced quite a sensation in the Gujerati reading public at the time. The thrilling incidents of the tale were reproduced in such a masterly manner that they touched the hearts of the readers in an unprecedented degree. In compliance with a generally expressed wish, the tale is now being republished in serial form." THE VOLTA PRIZE.—Le Progree Medical (August 7th) reports that the French Minister of Education has just fixed the date of competition for the Volta Prize. It is of the value of £2,0010, and was instituted by a decree dated June 11th, 1882, in favour of the author of a dis- covery which shall render electricity economically useful In one of the following applications :—As a source of heat, of light, of chemical action, of mechanical power, as a means of transmission of despatches, or in the treat- ment of disease. The competition will remain open to June 30th, 1887, and the prize will be awarded the follow- ing December. Scientists of all nations may compete. A commission, nominated by the Minister of Education, will be charged with the examination of the discovery specified by each competitor, with a view to determine if it fulfils the required conditions.—The Lancet.

AFRICAN TRA4RL.—Lieutenant. Greelup, a Swedish officer till lately in the service of the Congo Free State, has arrived in this country after a remarkable journey across Africa. Having been sent by his employers to Stanley Falls, the station of the Congo State furthest up the river, he grew tired of the monotony of the life there, and, taking advantage of the opportunities offered him, he made his way to Nyangwe, with which Mr. Stanley alone had previously familiarised himself. Thence he reached and crossed Lake Tanganyika to lajiji, whence he made his way to Zanzibar, arriving there six months after his departure from Stanley Falls. Lieutenant Greelup intends writing an account of his journey, which in some respects is without parallel in the history of African travel. It will be published in the first instance in English. A MURDERED MAN'S Mmarr.—M. Maspero has added an incident of a peculiarly horrible character to the story of the unwrapping of the Royal mummies of Deir-el- Bahari, which has already been told in the Academy. Among them was found the body of a 'young man be- tween 25 and 30 years of age, bearing neither name nor inscription of any kind, which is by itself an extraordi- nary circumstance. Instead of having been embalmed in the usual way, the body had merely been dried by some skilful process, without removing any of the in- ternal organs, and had been covered with a thick layer of some mixture at once fatty and caustic. Above all, the attitude of the corpse, its bent leas, its feet turned against each other, its clenched hands, the expression of its face—all combined to indicate that the unknown per- son had died in extreme agony. At first, M. Rlaspero was tempted to suspect that he had come across a case of the embalment of a living man—a form of murder which it is not difficult to reconcile with Egyptian usage. Medical men, however, who had been consulted, were disposed rather to recognise the symptoms of poisoning. In any case, we are brought face to face with a palace tragedy, for a body found among the Royal mummies of Deir-el-Bahari can hardly be other than that of a princely personage. WOOD WO6L.—For some time past attention has been directed to a very interesting product, consisting of ex- tremely thin and slender shavings of wood which are comparable to paper cut for packing. It is known by the name of "wood wool." This product was first intro- duced into France as a packing material. It weighs about 40 or 50 per cent, less than the materials used for such a purpose. Its beautiful appearance, its fineness, and its extreme cleanness at once brought it into favour with shippers. It was afterwards found that the material was well adapted for the manufacture of mattresses, for litter for cattle, for the filtration of liquids, and for stuff- inehorse collars, &c., the most suitable species of wood being selected for each of these fi urposes. Its elasticity- causes it to be considered as the best material for bed- ding after horsehair, and it is even preferable to any other substance when it is derived from resinous wood, since it does not then absorb moisture. In workshops wood wool is tending to replace cotton waste for clean- ing machinery, and it has likewise found an application on the rolling stock of railways for lubricating car axles. While it has the same property which cotton waste has of absorbing oil, it costs the tenth that material. Its use is said to be rapidly growing in Austria and Germany, and also in France.—lron._

MANUFACTURING CAR I.VILEELS.—A new machine and process for manufacturing car wheels, invented and patented by Mr. J. J. Carr, has been tested, it is stated, with satisfactory results at the works of the Dickson Manufacturing Company, Wilkesbarre, Pennsylvania. It is claimed for the new process of manufacture that, while by the old method of moulding, casting, dressing, and boring the wheels, the average product of three men per day of twelve hours is 18 wheels, with the new process the same number of men are able to turn out one perfect wheel every minute, or 720 wheels per day. The principal feature appears to be the subqtitution of a steel core for one of sand in casting the wheels. This has been tried before, but no one has hitherto hit upon a means of getting this core out of the wheel after it was cast. This is now accomplished by a centre key which falls out upon a single stroke of the hammer, and plets the steel core drop out, leaving the hole in the wheel ' perfectly true and ready to be put upon the axle with- out any dressing or boring. The sand is run into the moulding box by a hopper, and both matrices are moulded into the pattern drawn out by the single revo- lution of a shaft driven by steam power. The matrices are carried away upon movable platforms to the cupola, and then the piece is cast as under the old proces:s., The moulding is done as rapidly a 3 a revolving disc can carry the boxes under the pressers.—lron.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDEN I NU.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDEN I NU.

One of the chief labours infthe'tarden at present is to destroy the weeds, which have been thriving amazingly of late. In dry, hot weather it is an easy matter to rid the garden of weeds, if we only apply the hoe to the surface of the soil between the crops. But, with the weather of the past two or three weeks, that method of destroying them is useless, and we have no alternative but to pull them up with the hand, or, where space admits without injuring the roots of plants, the weeds may be buried by turning the ground over, which can be done in less time than it takes to pull up every weed. The ground so served will keep clean for a greater length of time, and moreover a great portion of the food that was taken up by them is restored to the soil for the use of more serviceable plants. Every effort should be made to prevent weeds flowering and maturing their seeds, as they will provide endless labour when they are dis- tributed by the wind all over the garden. The garden plots in the vicinity of Lancaster are models of cleanli- ness, and out of about seventy that we inspected, only in one did we see any weeds. Fortunately this was situated at the end of one of the groups, or it might have been a source of annoyance to a dozen owners of neighbouring plots. As it is, only the owners of plots adjoining are likely to suffer from the neglect or indif- ference of their neighbour, who allows the weeds in his holding to flower and scatter their seeds. Green Crops!: Where the system of planting these between potatoes is practised, it may be necessary to turn the tops of the latter on one side, giving them at the same time a slight twist, which wi4l be the means of preventing them re- turning to their former position. Scarlet-runner Beans: When these have reached three parts the height of their supports, they might with advantage have the points pinched, in order to dwarf them and induce them to throw out side shoots below. When the bulk of the growth is at the top of the supports there is greater danger of them giving way when acted upon by the wind.

THE FRONT GARDEN.—Geraniurns of various kinds that are usually planted out should have cuttings taken off in order to secure a stock for another year. Select those pieces that have an inch or two of moderately- firm wood at the base, and with a sharp knife cut just above a joint obliquely and prepare the base of the cut- ting by making an even horizontal cut just below the lowest pair of leaves, which must also be severed within a quarter of an inch of the shoot. It will be;found that if the growth is too young the cuttings will shrink, and very few, if any, of such will form roots. MostUardeners allow the cuttings to lay in their potting shed for a day or two before they are put in, in order that the bruised cells may heal up, and we venture to assert that no one ever lost a cutting in consequence. Half a dozen cut- tings round the inside of a five-inch pot is a good arrangement, and the dimensions of the:lpot is a con- venient one either for the window or greenhouse. TI (11 drainage should be good and the soil rather poor, a-;t I object should be to secure solid sturdy growth, such as is likely to withstand the vicissitudes of winter. If half an inch of sand is placed on the surface of the soil and worked into the holes as the cuttings are dibbled failures are reduced to a minimum. Sand is incapable of holding water between its particles as compared with ordinary soil, which is largely composed of decayed vegetable matter. In this the cutting attracts more water than' it can digest, consequently its fluids become putrid, and it is soon the victim of decay. If at the time the cuttings are inserted the soil is moderately dry a sprinkling may be given overhead, otherwise water might be withheld for a week even with daily sunshine. Such weather as we are having now is most disastrous to succulent cut- tings like Geraniums if exposed day after day when:first put in, and if it should continue we would urgelthat they should have the protection of a greenhouse frame or window for a week or ten days, then the base of the cut- tings will have formed what gardeners term a "callus," which has the appearance of small granules at first, round the inner bark, which ultimately increase aud form a continuous ring. This is the effect of the cellular horizontal system of the cutting repairing the injury made by the knife and preparing for the reception of the perpendicular system which is to pass through it in the form of roots. The scented leaf section of Geraniums are differently constituted, and must at no time be per- mitted to get dry, as their woody texture prevents the entrance of much water at a time, and they may safely be placed out of doors. The same remarks are applicable to single and double ivy leaved. THE GREENHOUSE.—Everyone having a greenhouse should grow Grassula Coccinea, flowering as it does when flowers in the greenhouse are scarce. After the flowering season is over cut down all the shoots that have borne flowers within an inch or two of the base, and stand the Wants in the open air for a few weeks, but lay the pots on their sides during wet weatheoAThis will mature the shoots that have not flowered this year, and prepare them for doing so next season. Cuttings made of these tops and inserted singly in the smallest sized pots root freely during the next two or three weeksLif not over watered; or if a specimen is desired quickly four or five may be inserted in pots as many inches in diameter. Un- like the majority of cuttings, they require no shade.

GRAPPENHALL PRIMIrSE LEAGUE. On Saturday afternoon the inaugural meeting of the Grappenhall Polling District Habitation of the Primrose League was held, by permission of Mr. J. Charlton Parr, in the grounds of Grappenhall Heyes. There were between 500 and 600 present, amongst the number being Mr. and Mrs. Parr, the Mayor and. Mayoress of Waxrington (Alderman and Mrs. Har- rison) and Miss Atkinson, Mr. and Mrs. E. Greenall, Mrs. T. Greenall, Mr. and Mrs. E. Greenall, junn, Mr. and Mrs. 11. Greenall, Mr. Wynne Jones (hon. sec.), Mr. 11. Lyon, Mrs. W. C. Jones, Mr. and Mrs. John White, Mrs. Robert Davies, Major and Mrs. Litton, Captain and Mrs. Reynolds and the Misses Reynolds, Captain and Mrs. Nicholson, Mr. Tinsley, and Mrs. lErnest Crosfield. An excellent tea, provided by Mr. ITaylor, of the Norton Arms, Latchford, was par- taken of in a large tent. After tea an open-air ,Imeeting was held at which tke charter of habita- tion was read by the Ruling Councillor (Mrs. Parr). —Mr. PARR having welcomed those present, Mr. R. I. WYNNE-JONES announced that the number of members of the league were as follows :—Wilders- pool, 200; Grappenhall, 182; Latchford, 86; Apple ton, 57; total, 525. In addition there were the dames to the number of .close upon 40.—Mr. JOHN WHITE said they were aware that the primrose movement had arisen from an act of the people. It was a spontaneous act of veneration for one of the greatest states- men England had ever possessed. He should like to say that they were not banded together merely for the sake of venerating the name of a great statesman, but more to maintain those prin- ciples which were so dear to him and which he strove so hard to carry out whilst he was alive. (Cheers.) The latest report was that their oppo- nents were endeavouring to form an association similar to the Primrose League. They were given to understand that it was to be called the "White Rose League" after the favourite flower of Mr. Gladstone. (Laughter.) Some had suggested that "The White Feather League" would be more ap- propriate considering on how many occasions Mr. Gladstone had shown the white feather in foreign as well as in. domestic affairs. (Laughter.) The objects of the Primrose League was, first of all, to supply voluntary workers at the time of elections. Then again a principle for which the. League was formed was to maintain religion and the constitu- tion of this country and the empire. All branches of religion, all kinds of religious feeling were alike welcome, and all tolerated. The only point which the league pressed upon the country was that there must be religion. (Hear, hear, and cheers.)—Captain NrerroLsoN said the league was something like Lord R. Churchill—it was young, but it was vigorous. (Cheers.) It was inexpen- enced perhaps, but it was going to be as vigorous and as powerful in the future as they hoped Lord Randolph would become. (Cheers.)—Mr. WYNNE JONES explained that it had been Mr. Parr's inten- .tion not only to invite them into the grounds, but to give them all a tea. He had written to London, and was told that it would be considered an act of bribery to give tea and would not be allowed, and they had therefore to be charged 3d each. Now they knew all about the matter. (Laughter.)_ After the speaking there was dancing, the music being supplied by the Foresters' band.
"Charming little, pink-tipped, shell-like ears you have, Miss Totty. Did you never have them pierced ?" "No; but I have had them bored."
A young man who was recently married to a girl, after proposing to her eighteen times, now wishes that he had asked her but seventeen times.

An Irish shoemaker advised a customer, when he com- plained of his new boots being tight, not to put them on until he had worn them for eday or two. "I walked the floor all night with the toothache," said he; to which his unfeeling listener replied, "You didn't expect to walk the ceiling with it, did you ?" A certain journal mentions James Clarke and wife, who were "born, died, and buried on the same day." He and his wife must have been awfully young. "Come here and tell me what the four seasons are?" Young prodigy answers: "Pepper, mustard, salt, and vinegar; them's what mother always seasons with." At an inquest held at Bath on Monday night respecting the death ot an old lady named Heard, it was ascertained that she had died from slaock to her system caused by the sting of a wasp.

_ The proprietor of a forge, not remarkable for correct- ness of language, but who by honest industry had realis- ed a comfortable independence, being called on at a social meeting for a toast, gave "Success to forgery." .Mr. Ruskin, alluding to children, says :—" Make them try always who shall speak truest, both as regards the fact he has to relate and the precision of the words he expresses it in, thus making truth the test of perfect language."
HINTS FOR THE HOME.

FIIIICKLIIS.—Powdered nitre moistened with watort applied to the face night and morning, will soon remove e.O traces of freckles. HICCOUGH in nine cases out of 10 can be stopped by an' effort of the will or by simply holding the breath. Sudden fright almost invariably stops it.

THERE are many people in the world who spend the first half of their existence trying to taste all the sweets of life, and the second half in trying to get the taste out of their mouths. PERSONS have derived great benefit from using the " Hop Villow," after a severe attack of teuralgis, and when in need of sleep. Take sufficient hops to half fill an ordinary pillow-ease, dry them well in the oven in 9' dish, and when cold put in the pillow-case. Use as an ordinary pillow.

-- A wurra in the British, Medical- Journal advises PeoPle not to slice up a pineapple with the same knife they use in peeling it, as the rind contains an acrid organic, substance which is likely to cause a swollen mouth end sore lips. In Cuba salt is used as •an antidote for the poison of pine-apple-peel.

-- EICLABGEMENT OF TONSILS.—Dr. Beresford writing I°' the Medical Advocate on the subject of chronic enlarge. ment of tonsils, recommends the injection two or three times a wpwL. of a strong solution of tannic acid, with the daily use of a gargle of the same, and states that if *ill course be followed the knife need never be resorted to.

TOOTHACHE. —A correspondent of the Electrician gives,. the following as an instant remedy for toothache : Witu a small piece of zinc and a bit of silver (any silver coill will do), the zinc placed on one side of the af"ted gurri and the silver on the other, by bringing tht7edgeB tcr. gether, the small current of electricity generate do immediately and painlessly stops the toothache.

THE great mistake of those who are ardent students is to trust too much to their books, and not to draw frosi their own resources, not recollecting that of all sophists our own reason is almost always that which abuses tti least. So soon as we choose to re-enter into our owvl breaists,_pach perceives what is good, each discerns whab is beautiful • we have no need to be taught to know either the one or the other, and we are never deceived in 51°11 matters unless we wish to be deceived.—Rosseau.

RHUBARB JAM.—To six pounds of rhubarb add ELI pounds of lump sugar and six large lemons; cut the rhubarb into small pieces about the size of a walnut ; then the lemons should be sliced and the peel cut yea fine. Put the rhubarb and lemons (taking out the PiPts from the latter) into a large bowl, then cover it with the sugar broken small; lot it stand 24 hours; Aker whicli boil it slowly for about three-quarters of an r, taking care that it does not stick to the pan, also not to stir mucl! so se to break the pieces of rhubarb, as the beauty of ID is in being whole. e— ' MONTREAL PUDDING.—Beat three eggs very light, sad strain through a sieve, add to them half a cup of !nag, one-fourth of a nutmeg grated, and two ounces of brovn! sugar ; then add one-quarter of a pound of flour anog seven ounces of finely rolled bread crumbs ; the flour to be stirred in gradually,and when that is well mixed stir io . the bread crumbs and beat altogether for at least 25. minutes-30 is still better—then put in half a pound a nicely stoned raisins. Put the whole into a pudding mould, tie it over tightly, put it into water, which mull! be kept steadily boiling for 3 hours; eat hot, with an/ sauce preferred. , . f SCOTCH OAT CARES.—Mix oatmeal and cold Watert with a seasoning of salt, into a rather stiff dough, which, after being kneaded,should be rolled into a cake as nearlY as thin as a half-crown as it can be made. Then put on A clean, dry, moderately-hot griddle. Bake on one Bid• till it is just beginning to brown, but be careful not to brown it. Then take the cake off the griddle and lay it 011 a clean board, baked side uppermost. After the cake has dried, and is almost cooled, lift carefully, and slowl/ toast the unbaked side before the fire. Oatcakes so pre' pared are delightfully crisp. The operatioti is a rather delicate one,but we have seen agirl of eight bake a cake in this fashion good enough to set before the Queen. TIA meal should neither be too coarse nor too fine. i • -- . DISCOURTEOUS FRIENDSHIP.—One of the most commons and no less one of the most irritating peculiarities of the growth of friendship is the corresponding and conse- quent growth of discourtesy which attends it. People who as mere acquaintances were civil enough to email other, become, after a very short progress toward Intimacy, rude ton degree hardly credible in people of any pretensions to good breeding. Of course we do not mean here simply the ordinary waiving of formalities,but a downright disregard of civilities, a wanton ignoring of personal tastes and peculiarities, and the indulgence in, native rudeness and selfishness. The true friend is HOS he who makes of friendship an excuse for greater laxity ill matters of gentleness and courtesy, but who finds in it * call to more exquisite courtesy, more careful thoughtful. ness, more absolute and minute self-denial—Bo:oo FRIENDS OLD AND NEW. Make new friends, but keep the old, . . Those are silver, these are gold; ' New-made friendships, like new wine, , Age will mellow and refine. Friendships that have stood the test... • • Time and change—are surely best; Brow may wrinkle, hair grow gray, Friendship never knows decay. - or 'mid old friends, tried and true, nce more we our youth renew. ut old friends, alas! may die, New friends must their place supply. - Cherish friendship in your breast, New is good, but old is best' • ' Make new friends, but keep the old. .., 1 Those are silver, these are gold.

LI/VON CHEESE, —Take one pound of powderttl sugar* two ounces of fresh butter, six lemons, and four eggs ; put the butter, sugar, and the grated rind of the lemonst with the juice, into a porcelain-lined saucepan (be carefW not to let any of the pips fall in) ' • stir them over the firs, and let bail for five minutes. Turn into a jug to coolest, little while you whip the eggs, yolks and whites together; strain, and add to the sugar. Place the jug in a saucepan of boiling water and stir the mixture continually until it thickens. Pour into small dry jars, cover, and use as r& quired. The reason for putting the mixture into a jug, and not into the saucepan, is to prevent it from boiling after the eggs are added, which would ause the cheese to crack. Another recipe: The juice of three lemons and the rind of two (grated well on to the sugar), 11b. lump sugar pounded, Vb. butter, six eggs, leaving out two whites; put butter and sugar in a large jar, then the rind and juice, then the eggs ; place the jar in a kettle of boil. jag water, keep stirring till it gets to the thickness of honey.

•• BOILED SAIZION. Salmon, when large,should be boiled in pieces or slices, for this reason—if the thick is cooked enough, the thitt part is cooked too much when a large piece is boiled. Double jowls therefore can never be properly cooked.; split jowls are to be recommended in preference. But, if the fish is a small one—six pounds or seven pounds, for instance—it may be trussed for boiling by bending ita head towards the centre of the body and its tail towards the same point on the opposite side. To secure the fish in this position it is necessary to use striug, and it maY then be boiled whole, removing the string after it iS cooked. The fish is sent to table resting on its belly. When boiled whole, it should be put into cold water and allowed to boil gently until it is cooked. When cooked in pieces, place the fish at once in boiling water, and, after it has been in a minute or two, lift it up on the strainer out of the water, and let it remain for a couple of minutes; return it to the water, and repeat the opera- tion twice more. This process is necessary to cause the curd to set, and will make the fish eat crisper, Let it boil at a gentle rate until it is cooked.

div.head: MAKING MINCEMEAT.
div.p: MAKING MINCEMEAT.

Before making mincemeat it must be determined whether " meat " from the butcher shall be put into the mixture. Properly speaking, there should be beef or veal in mincemeat, but it is becoming mcire and more the custom to omit the meat—that is, the lean meat—and use suet only with the various sweets. As for other ingrediente there is nothing to be said against them, and the proper' bons in which they are used is a matter of taste. The greatest care should be taken in selecting and preparing the suet, that it be perfectly sweet and freed from ever? particle of skin or membrane. Here are four recipes, all good, and differing in only trifling devrees : 1. Two pound/ of raisins, stoned, two pounds of currants, one pound of sultana raisins, ten pounds of apples, three-quarters of e pound of sugar, two pounds of suet, the juice of two lemonet and the rind of one chopped very fine, a quarter of a pound of mixed spice, a gill of brandy, two ounces of citron, and two ounces of candied lemonpeel. 2. Two pounds of the fillet of a sirlion of beef, boiled and freed from skilli together with four pounds and a half of suet, all mincea very fine; add eight large apples, chopped, six pounds of currants, washed and dried, two rounds of bread half aø inch thick, grated, an ounce of nutmeg, half an ounce of cloves, a pound and a half of sugar, and a little pepper and salt; grate the rind of an orange and a lemon, add the juice of six oranges and of two lemons; mix all these ingredients well together, pour over the whole a pint a port wine and a pint of brandy. 3. Three-quarters of pound of lean beef well boiled and finely minced, twn pounds of suet chopped small, one pound of moist sugars one pound of currants washed and dried, one pound of raisins stoned and minced, nine apples, the rind of a lemon crated; season with mixed spice and a teaspoonful of sale! incorporate the whole thoroughly, add a wine-glassful of port wine and a gill of brandy. 4. A pound each -1 currants, raisins, ribston pippins, calf's foot, and 'Nelda' ox tongue, the two latter boiled, and the whole minced; add half a pound of suet chopped fine, a quarters of a pound of sugar, half a pound of candied lemon Pee a pint of port wine, half a pint of brandy, the juice of qv° lemons, and a teaspoonful of mixed spice. When tbe _ mincing and mixing are completed, put the mixture in jars, press down and cover close. The mincemeat shouuld be kept 10 days at least before being used; if well 03013' i) will keep for months.
