REVOLUTION IN BULGARIA. PRINCE ALEX N DE a BETH RON E Ie—SUBMISSION TO RUSSIA.—ENGLAND AND THE REVOLUTION. SOFIA, SATURDAY —Prince Alexander's palace was this Morning surrounded by the populace and the troops quar- tered in the capital. His Highness abdicated at once, and was escorted out of the principality. Everything passed off quietly, not a shot being tired, and complete tranquility everywhere prevails. After the deposition of the Prince, a meeting was held by the inhabitants, at which a resolution was passed praying tee Czar to again extend his sympathy to the Bulgarian toile at this grave juncture. The entire assemblage thee proceeded to the palace of the Russian Agent, to whom the; communicated this resolution on their knees. The Russian repreeentative assured the people of the good feeling entertained by the Czar towards Bulgaria. The Provisional Government has been constituted as follows :-- Premier, without portfolio, Mgr. Clement, Metropolitan of lirnova arid Delegate of the Exarchate Minister for Foreign Affairs, M. - tojanoff ; Minister of Interior, H. Zankoff ; Minister of Finance. M. Burinof ; Minister of War, Nikiffo- rofi ; Minister ef Justice, M. Radoslavnoff ; Minister of Public Instruction, H. Vet ichkoff SOFIA, SUNDAY.—MonEignore Clement, President of the Provisional Government, has issued a pi oclamation to the Bulgarian nation announcing the antic ttion of Prince Alexander and the formation of a Provisional Government in the following terms r—" Prince Alexander of Battenburg has renounced tot ever the throne of Bulgaria, and has for- mally signed his abdication, being convinced that kis reign would ba fatal to the Bulearian nation. In view of these extraordinary event's a Provisional Gove!timent has been formed, which will carry on the administration of the coun- try, until the Great National Assembly shall have taken a decision. The Provisional Government declares that life. property, and the honour of Bulgarian citizens, as well as of strangers, are fully guaranteed, and is confident that Bal- garian citizens, without distinction of religion, nationality, Or political party, will co-operate for maintenance of order and tranquility. The Bulgarian nation may rest assured that the great Czar of Russia. the protector of Bulgaria, will not leave the country without his powerful protection. Long live the Bulgarian nation I" A second proclamation Was subsequently issued, which says:—" Prince Alexander rendered Bulgaria great services on the field of battle, but in politics he had too little regard for Bulgaria as a Slav State, and for the maintenance of good relations with Russia. His deposition therefore became a necessity." CONSTANTINOPLE, SUNDAY.—P.lrticnlars received here regarding the deposition of Prince Alexander state that a regiment from Kustendje. commanded by Colonel Stovanoff arrived at Sofia, and after the dethronement of the Prince escorted him to Lem Palanka on his way to Roumania. The regiments devoted to the Prine,e were at the time absent from Sofia, being ene.aged in the action of fortifications at Slivnitza. It is understood that the Porte will not change Its policy of moderation in consequence of the events in Bulgaria. but will await the action of the other Powers. BELGRADE, MONDAY.—rho Bulgarian Provisional Gov- ernment has blocked the Seivian frontier. The journey of King Milan to tilichenberg has been postponed owing to the crisis in the neighbouring principality. BUCHAREST, MONDAY.—it, is reported that M. Stambuloff, the President of t be 'Bulgarian Chamber, who is at Tirnova, has placed himself at the head of the protesting party, and is endeavouring to organise meetings in favour of Prince Alexander. Advicss from Widdin intimate that there is dissatisfaction in the army at the revolution, and that the lower classes of the population are still ignorant of what has happened. The garrison of Slaninla has remained faithful to Prince Alexander, and is stated to have refused to recog- nise the Provisional Government. On acconnt of the un- derstanding between Russia and the Provisional Govern- ment, a number of persons, fearing the consequences of Rus- sian predominance, have left Bulgaria and arrived in Rou- mania. Among tisern are M. Stojanoff, and several Russian Nihilists; who were serving as officers on board three Belga. rian war vessels. Accordiee to same private advices, the revolution broke out jest as Prince Alexander had inspected the Slivnitza positions and was about to proceed to inspect bhe troops at Widdin. ST. PETERSBURG. MONDAY.—The Russian newspapers. commenting on the deposition of Prince Alexander, express less surprise than was manifested concerning the Eastern Roumelian revolution of last year, it being considered that the political tensitm existing in Bulgaria foreshadowed a catastrophe for some time time past. VIENNA, MONDAY.—The independent Liberal press of Austria thinks the attitude of the Government, as far as it is known or supposed, to be a mistake. Reseim, it is pointed out, will not, or only for a short time, be satisfied with the mere removal of Prince Alexander. Then she will play:her part as the protector of Bulgaria, to accomplish formally the union with Eastern Roumelia. PARIS, MONDAY.—The " Temps " this evening, referring to the events in Bulgaria, believes that although peacs is not threatened, it would be going too far to suppose that the the revolution at Sofia will have no influence upon the rela- tions betweet the Great Powers. England had received a rebuff, and although she certainly will Rot make it a castes bel/i, it would he impossible for Lord Salisbury to purely and simply receive such a check. The Greek Minister, M. Gainadius, paid a visit to the Foreign Office on Sunday afternoon, and remained in con- sultation with Lord Iddesleigh for a considerable time. Rastern Pasha, at a later hour. paid a lengthened visit to Lord Iddesleigh at the Foreign Office. "{astern Pasha had previously paid a visit to the • Prime Minister at the Treasury. Later in the day M. Waddington, the French Ambassador, visited Lord Iddesleigh, and was engaged with his lordship some time on the Bulgarian question. Lord Salisbury, who received the news at Hatfield by telegraph, returned to London shortly after two o'cock on Sunday afternoon. His lordship at ence had a long interview at the Foreign Office with Lord Iddesleigh. Before the con- ference concluded, Sir Frederick Lascelles, British Minister at Sofia, who is now home on leave, called, and their lord- ships had the benefit of his opinion and local knowledge. Later on the Turkish Ambassador called upon Lord Salis- bury in Downing-street, and afterwards saw Lord Iddesleigh at the Foreign Office. The French and Greek Ministers likewise had interviews with the Foreign Secretary. It is understood that Lord Iddesleigh has no intention of taking any extraordinary measures, at any rate in the light of present information on the subject. and that it is improbable that any protest will be made by this country. HOW PRINCE ALEX teNDER WAS DEPOSED. CONSTANTINOPLE. MONDAY.—The Porte to-day for- warded a Circular Note to its representatives at the Courts of the signatory powers inviting them to communicate the Intentions of those Powers regarding Prince Alexander's de- position. The train service to Rouinetia was suspended to- day. The Consular reports state that the troops in Eastern Roumelia and the garrisons of Widdin and Shumla disap- prove of the deposition of the Prince, and that a contro- versy is proceeding at Sofia between the parties favourable to and against Prince Alexander, which threatens serious consequences. CONSTANTINOPLE, TUESDAY MORNING.—The greatest efforts have been made by the members of the Provisional Government to prevent the true position of affairs in Bul- garianfrom being known, all telegrams being stopped ex- cept such as are favourable to the conspirators. A second Provincial Government, in favour of Prince Alexander, has been formed and established at Tirnova, under the presi- dency of M. Stambouloff. Private despatches from an authentic source, which have just been received here, how- ever, leave little doubt as to how the revolution was ac- complished. The scare of the Servian war preparations helped the conspirators se far that all the troops were, by • order of the Minister of War, moved towerde the Servian frontier, except one regiment of cavelry which had to,Len effectually "Russianised " in view of the important work on hand. At two o'clock on Saturday morning this regi- ment surrounded the Royal Residence in full strength, and cried for the deposition of the Prince. Only a small crowd were present outside the Palace, and these were the sworn members of the conspiracy. The Prince was in bed at the time, but the rebel leaders forced themselves into the Palace, aud met his Royal Highness in the anti-chamber, where they demanded that he should sign his abdication. The Prince seemed stunned for the moment, and thee spoke some bitter words about the treachery of those whom he had led to victory, and of the ingratitude of the people for whom he had done so much. What followed is only known from the reembers of the Provisional Government. They assert that Prince Alexander signed his abdication under protest ; but rumours are not wanting that he distinctly refused to sign the document. What is certain, however, IS that at daybreak, and before the Bulgars of Scfia were stirring, the Prince, with a strong cavalry escort, started On the road to Sere Palanlea, the official aseertion being that he, would be sent thence across the Danube into Roumania. BUDAPEST, TOESDXY.—Despltcheg from Widdin' state that M. Stalbouloff, tho President of the Chamber of De- puties. strenuously opposed the revolution and subsequent despotism. It is further stated that the Bulgarian army is discontented with the revolutionary movement, and is dis- posed to re-establish Prince Alexander. Reports of Servian mobilisation and armament. are rife. The yacht with Prince Alexander on beard did not touch at Guirgevo, but proceeded past that place and was signalled this morning near Silistria. ST. PETERSBURG, TUESDAY. The Russian newspapers this morning generaPv express the c:enviction that the direct participation of Bassi in the pacification of Bulgaria will meet with no serious obstacles at the present political proposes juncture. The " N3VO9 Vremya that until the question of the appointment of a new Prince of Bulgaria has been settled. a Russian dignitary should be sent to Bulgaria to maintain order in that country. THE USURPING GOVERNMENT OVERTHROWN PRINCE ALFX kNDER RECALLED. VIENNA, WEDNESDtY.—THI Note Freie Presse publishes 1 intelligence from Kelafat, of yesterday's date, stating that the Provisional Government 'at Sofit has been overthrown, and that Monsignor Clement, Major Groutff, and M. Z in- koff have been arrested, and the former Ministry, under the presidency of M. Karaveloff. reinstated. The troops, who were led to take the oath of allegiance to the new Govern- ment easing to the announcement of the voluntary abdica- tion of the Princs, and the misleading proclamation which was issued, are, like the civil population, highly exaspera- ted, and refuse to acknowledge any new Government. De- putations are being sent from Sofia to Bucharest, Vienna, Berlin, and Darmstadt to assure Prince Alexander, should they meet hint at one of these places, of the loyal attach- ment of the people and the Army, and to beg him to return to Bulgaria. RUSTCITUCK, WEDNESDAY, 3 P.M.—The garrison of this i place has openly declared te;; submission to the Provisional .aovernment established at Tirnova, which is acting in the

name of Prince Alexander. Intelligence received here states that the head of the first Provisional Government estab- lished at Sofia on the deposition of the Prince haa fled into Servia, tegether with those who supported him in bringing about the revolution. The Sofia garrison is now under the orders of the Tirnovo Government, to which all other garri- sons have already signified their adherence. LONDON, WEDNESDAY NIGIIT.—The Press Association learns that the British Government has at length received direct information from Mr. Condie Stephen, at Sofia, stat- ing that the members of the Proyisionel Government have been arrested and imprisened, and that telegraphic orders have been despatched to the Royal yacht to return with the Prince to Soils. The important information from Mr. eon- die Stephen was at once telegraphed to the Queen at Bal. moral, her Majesty, in accordance with her request, having been kept constantly informed of the progress of events in Bulgaria. Lord Salisbury, who was at Hatfield, was also communicated with. The TurkA Ambassador, who called at the Foreign Office shortly after three o'clock. brought the same intelligence as th it sent by the British representative at Sofia. Both the British Government and Turkey were greatly plesse:i at the turn which events have taken. The telegraph wire from Soria being now free, the Government will be in receipt of dallied information as to the proceed- ings in the Bulgarian c tpital. The advices they have re- ceived are to the effect that the country is now all for Prince Alexander, and that he would be received back with a fer- vour of enthusiasm. THE SAFETY OF PRINCE ALEXINDER. BUCHAREST, VEDNESDAY, 6 P IL—According to the latest reports, Prince Alexereler remains at Renni, Russia. where the commander of the yacht had received instructions to leave him with or without the consent of Russia. The Prince requested that he might be landed on the Roumanian bank of the river. A deepatch from Galata states that Prince Alexander has been left free by the Russian Government to go wherever be pleases. It is added that at two o'clock this afternoon the Prince was still at 'tenni Russi. Sr. PETERSBURG, WEDIIESDA.Y.—It is announced here to-day that Prince Alexander, who arrived at Renni Russi yesterday, left that place on his way to Austria, via Volot- shisk, being in no way a prisoner. In tegard to the situa- tion of Bulgaria, it is semi-officially declared that the alarming reports published by the foreign press appear to be at least exaggerated. PIIILIFPOPOLIS, WEDNESDAY.—Immediately after the news of Prince Alexander's deposition reached this city, a large indignation meeting of the inhabitants and the troops in garrison was held, at which resolutions were unamimously and enthusiastically passed affirming loyalty to the Prince. Those present subsequently formed a procession and paraded the streets all night shouting "Long live Battenberg ! long live the Prince of Bulgaria! " Colonel Moutkoaroff, commander of troops in Bestern Roumelia, has issued a proclamation calling upon all pat- riots to defend the honour of the Prince and of Bulgaria. All the regiments in Bulgaria are declaring for the Prince. Per- fect order prevails everywhere. • POPULAR FEELING. PRILIPOPPOLIS, THURSDAY. Crowded meetings have been held throughout Eastern Roumelia in favour of Prince Alexander, at which resolutions were adopted advocating his immediate retuen, and demanding that no mercy sheuld be shown to the traltor3. Montkouroff has made an appli- cation to the authorities on the Turkish frontier requesting that the railway communication between Philipoppolis and Constantinople may not be interrupted and giving an assu- rance that no feeling inimical to Turkey is involved in the Government in Prince Alexander's favour. There is no diminution in the enthusiasm displayed for the Prince, and no Government will be recognised in Eastern Roumelia as having authority until his Highness is reinstated. . MESSAGE FROM PRINCE ALEX AN DER. The Press Association is officially informed that Prince Alexander has telegraphed to his father and some of the European Courts that he is safe and free, and on his road to Darmstadt. He was liberated at Reni-Russi, on Russian territory. The Press Association understands that it is pro- beble the Prince will not continue his journey to Darm- stadt when he hears of the counter revolution in his favour, but will return to Sofia and restore confidence and tran- quility. BURMAH.—INUNDATIONS.—GREAT LOSS OF LIFE AND PROPERTY. MANDALAY, FRIDAY.—Sir C. Bernard has arrived from Bhamo. The Engineers have cut the embankment south of Mandalay to let out the water in the town, which has been flooded owing to the bursting of the embankment. There is no result as yet. The river is stationary. It is reported from Bhamo that the water is falling there. When the river has fallen nine feet the upper portion of the town will be relieved. The lower portion will continue inunda- ted for a long period. It is useless to attempt to repair the embankment until November. The breach is now 300 Yards wide. In 1377 a portion of the embankment burst, but the inundation was not then nearly so extensive as now. The present catastrophe is undoubtedly largely due due to in- adequate provision for public works Only ton lakhs are allowed for the whole province, including railway survey. No funds were available for keeping the embankment in repair. The value of the property lost and the injury caused by the iaundatiou it is estimated will largely exceed 100 lakhs. A " Times" telegram, dated Mandalay, August 19th, says that great distress must ensue from the inundations. An enormous quantity of property, especially of provisions, is destroyed. The difficulty of people in obtaining food is greatly increased by the want of a market. Considerable loss of life has occurred, but it is impossible at present to obtain trustworthy information as to the number of deaths. The inundation will for a time greatly increase the diffi- culty of military operations, as communic ttion with the outposts and despatch of reinforcements will be very diffi- cult. The former English residency, lately occupied as a barrack by the 23rd Madras Regiment, and other posts have been temporarily abandoned owing to the inundation. De- sultory skirmishing with the insurgents continues. There is much sickness amongst the troops in Bhamo. RANGOON, SUNDAY.—Intelligence received here states that the steamer Ka.hbyoo, with troops, proceeded to a point five days' voyage above Kendal and captured a stockade, mak- ing prisoners of the rebel chief in command and 30 of his followers. In consequence of unusual finds the navigation of the river is difficult. Catzurra, SUNDAY.—The following officers have been ap- pointed to the command of the three new brigades which are to be formed in I3urmah in October :—Cavalry Brigade, Brigadier-General R. C. Stewart ; Ist Infantry Brigade, Brigadier-General C. J. East; Ead Infantry Brigade, Brigs- ! dier-General W. S. A. Lockhart. MORE FIGHTING IN BURMAH. MANDALAY, MONDAY.—The water here bscreesed eighteen inches last night. The breach ,in the embankment is 250 feet wide. The inundated district, which comprises the chief commercial portion of the town, is about five miles long by two miles. A portion of the inundated district was thinly inhabited, but there has been a heavy loss of life, although the exact number cannot be ascertained. The civil authori- ties appear to have neglected keeping the embankment in good order, a duty always carefully carried out by the Bur- mese Government. The death of the Myentzein Prince is reported from Yemoon and Kyouk3ai as having occurred from fever. The intelligence is not confirmed, but the report is widely believed. Desultory fighting continues. On the 18th, Lieutenant Higgins, of the 213 t Madras Regiment, with 360 Sepoys and military police, defeated the insurgents near Yeu, with a loss of 50 killed. On the same day, Lieut. Smith, of the Hampshire Regiment, with a body of Euro- peans. mounted infantry, and police, defeated the insurgents at Yemoon, with a loss of 32 killed. Our loss was one &pop killed, two of the Hants Regiment. and two Sepoys severely wounded. CALCUTTA, TUESDAY.—FaiIer despatches received here regarding t'se bursting of the bund of Mandalay estimate that 1,000 lives were lost by the inundation. It is further stated that the dangerous condition of the bund was pointed out to the authorities two months before, but nothing was done in the matter. THE AFGHAN BOUNDARY. VIENNA, SUNDAY. -- Considerable sensation has been aroused here by a telegram from St. Petersburg announcing that Russia's vissel, the Emir of Bokhara, has formally demanded of the Arneer of Afghanistan the cessien of the oasis of Khoja Saleh. The Bakbaran ruler adds lo his de- mand that the oasis shall be ceded to him without fighting, plainly implying that if this is not done hostilities will be begun. As it is manifest, however, that the Bokharan emir would stand no chance single-handed against the Ameer of Afghanistan, his demand is neturalle assumed to be actively backed ep by REuNssoiaL.—ANDjiyACNh DronicEl S. PETERSBURG, SUNDAY.--The Non Vrentya warns Eland not, to take any further measures tending to make Egypt an English province. Germmv and Austria, It says, would perhaps allow her to do so, hut Lord Salisbury ought to remember that these are not the only Powers who have to be reckoned with. INTERNATIONAL WORKING MEN'S CONFERENCE. Pkars, MoNiseele—The International Working Men's Conference was opened this evening in the Salle d Redoute. The seven English delegates, headed by Mr. Mawdsley, were present, and some delivered speeches in which they justified and praised the demands put forward by English working men--The invitation cent to workiug men by the French labour party states that the Conference "has for its object the amelioration of the condition of those who are being continually sacrificed and overwhelmed with burthens, and whose situation grows worse day by day. Our claims, when clearly formulated, were frequently dismissed when- ever they were not overwhelmed beneath the absurd denials of those who deliberately ignored the wretched condition of the people. We cannot, and we must not, make complaints separately. Let us neglect no ineaus to hasten the solution of social problems. It would be desertion from the com- mon cause were we to refuse th 3 opportunity offered for making our voices heard. We, the producers, must be con- scious of our rights and duties. Let us be homogeneous in our claims, and let its formulate in unison the specilication of work in a logical, precise, and energetic manner. We have also to prepare for the proper participation of workmen in the Labour Exhibition of 1839. We think that you will not be refused by your town councils or municipalities a pecuniary subsidy for the despatch thereto of delegates. Should it be refused to you, you can rest assured that those who are continually talking about the attenuation, depres- sion, and miserable condition of the working man, tee., are rnera phrasemongers, who do not etre about us, and who , deceive us when they get the chance." THE CHOLERA. ROME, MONDAY.—The returns for the last 21 hours are : —l5 cases and 9 deaths at Barletta; 6 cases at Acquaviva ; 11 cases and 4 deaths at Bisceglie ; 4 and 4 at Cerignola ; 6 and 2at Ruvo di Puglia: 3 and 2at Vicenza •, 2 and 2at Verona; 14 and 4 at Padua; and 10 and 2 at Bologna.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair shortly before 4-0. THE CHARGE AGAINST THE ORDNANCE DEPARTMENT.— Mr. W. H. SMITH, answering questions as to the charges of corruption, malversation, &c., made against the Ordnance Department, said he was prepared to receive statements from Colonel Hope or any other persons privately and in confi- dence, and if in the opinion of the law officers of the Crown they could be made the subject of judicial inquiry before any legal tribunal they should be brought before it. If there were no such tribunal now existing, he undertook that such a court should be formed. THE WOODEND COLLIERY EXPLOSION.—RepIving to Mr. Burt and Mr. C. Wright, Mr. MATTHEWS said that it ap- peared from the report of the inquest that the Woodend Colliery was worked generally with the Davy lamp. He was quite aware of the conclusions that had been arrived at by the Royal Commission on Accidents in Mines with re- gard to the use of the Davy lamp, and also of the corres- pondence between the Home Secretary in 188 C and the chairman of that Commission. The hon. member for More peth might perhaps be aware that in a bill which the right hon. gentleman opposite introduced last session for the regu- lation of coal mines special and elaborate provisions were made as to the construction of safety lamps used in mines. These or similar provisions be himself hoped to reintroduce in a bill which would be brought in at the first opportunity. Meanwhile the hon. member would feel that it would be in- expedient for the Home Office to prescribe the use of any particular lamp of any particular manufacturer, because Parliament might not approve of that recommendation, and the expense incurred by colliery owners would be thrown away. But what he could do was to issue a circular to col- liery owners drawing their attention to the conditions laid down by the Commission on Mines with reference to the paramount importance of safety lamps, and also to those portions of the report which dealt with the relative advan- tages mad disadvantages of the different lamps now in use. Further, he meant to issue instructions to the inspectors of mines to insist upon the discontiouence of the lamps now in use in any case where the circumstances were such as to render the use of those lamps dangerous. He might aid that work at the Woodend Colliery had been resumed with the sanction of the inspector, and that the Marshall lamp was in use. The present decision of the Home Offiee WAS that it was not necessary to attend the inquest Isy counsel, seeing that the inspector and deputy-inspector were both present, who were fully competent to elicit all the facts which in their view were material. EVICTION'S IN IRELAND.—SiT M. HICKS-BE(C11, in reply to Mr. A. O'Connor, said that there had been 16 evictions on the estate of Mr. Nixon at Gweedore, county Donegal, but in all cases the persons were re-admitted as caretakers. On the estate of Captain Hill 67 were evicted, of whom 31 were re-admitted as caretakers. Many of the persons had received poor law relief, and out of an amount of £2OO owing only £4 had been realised. THE STATE OF KERRY.—Sif M. HICKS-BEACH informed Mr. E. Russell that Sir Redvers Buller will receive, in con- nection with his mission to Kerry, the civil powers of a divisional magistrate, which will give him every control over the local censtebulary ; and the resident magistrates will be directed to aid him in his efforts to detect and pre- vent crime. THE BELFAST RIOTS. The ArronerEr-Gewenee for IRELAND, questioned by Mr. Sexton, said the eight con- stables and one sergeant arrested at Belfast had been apprehended under a coroner's warrant, over which the Geivernment had no control. Care, however, had been taken that they should have the advantage of adequate legal assistance.—Sir M. HICKS- BEACH, replying to Mr. Sexton, said that the Commission on the Belfast riots comprised, as at present constituted, General Bulwer and two members of the Irish Bar—Mr. French and Mr. Adams. The Government, however. thought that it ought to be strengthened by the addition of a police officer of experience and standing who had had some practice in dealing with a population rather akin to that of Belfast. Therefore they proposed to add Mr. Wal- lace Mc.Herdy, Chief-Constable of Lanarkshire. NEW MEMDERS.—Mr. Munro Ferguson, entering amid Opposition cheers, took the oath and his seat for the Leith Burghs, in the room of Mr. Gladstone, who had elected to sit for Midlothian. Mr. Evershed took his seat for the Burton Division of Staffordshire, in the room of Sir M. A. Bass, advanced to the Peerage. THE ADDRESS. The adjourned debate on the Address was resumed. Mr. LABOUCHERE, after some caustic references to the Queen's Speech, discussed, in a racy, discursive vein, the conduct and pesition of the dissident Liberals, Lord R. Churchill's insulting election address, and the decaying in- fluence of the Whig party. Sir M. Hicirs-Beaca thought Mr. Labouchere's caricature of the policy of the Government hardly called for comment, but in answer to more serious accusations he maintained that it was a plain and sober one, and its object was to se- cure the material welfare of the people of Ireland. Referring to the speech of Sir W. Harcourt, he denied that measures for the redress of grievances must of necessity eccompany repressive legislation. This principle was a novel discovery, and it had not been carried out in practice by Liberal Governments either in Ireland or in the case of the Crofters in Scotland. Moreover, the Irish grievance which it was now desired to redress—the denial of a separate Parliament --was one which the country had clearly and distinctly pronounced upon, and he asked whether moonlighting in Kerry and rioting in Belfast were to continue until the country altered its opinion. • As regar- ded the first of the Commissions proposed, fie admitted that the Irish land question could not remain as it was, and the scope of the inquiry, he said, would be so narrowed that he conceived it would be quite possible that the Commission would be able to report in time for legisla- tion to be submitted to the House early next year. He in- dignantly disclaimed the existence of any desire on the part of the Government to encourage evictions. He hoped, and believed, that lasidlords would act fairly towards their tenants, and all he desired was that they should be left to deal with each other free from outside influence. As to tenants liable to judicial rents, he doubted whether the hard- ships alleged existed, and, while emphasising the necessity of enforcing legal obligations, he had no doubt that a scheme would be found possible whereby a system of peasant pro- prietorship might take the place of the present dual owner- ship. He next entered into a detailed E. xplanation of the scope of the second inquiry, which he said wotild be under- taken by men of experience in engineering, drainage, and agriculture, not so much in Ireland, perhaps, as elsewhere, and expressed greet confidence in the advantages to be de- rived from extending the natural resources of Ireland and improving the arterial drainage of the country. &Ir. BRADLAUGH challenged Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain to state their views on the land purchase policy of the Government, and energetically declaimed against the taxation of English artisans for the purpose of buying out Irish Landlords. Mr. RADCLIFFE COOKE spoke in support of the Gov- ernment policy ; and Mr. PINKERTON complained that, as a Commission WAS to inquire into the question of the rents, the Chancellor of the Exchequer had already prejudged the case by declaring existing judicial rents to be fair. Mr. SHIRLEY contended that the country bad not declared against a subordinate Parliament for Ireland. Mr. P. Mc DONALD enlarged upon the necessity of im- mediate legislation with a view to stop evictions ; Mr. JENNINGS argued that the working-men of the North of Eneland were opposed to the time of Pediment being en- tirely monopolised by Irish questions, and Mr. ILLINGWORTH charged the Government with pandering to the la ndlord classes. Lord HARTINOTON. who rose amidst much cheering. be- gan by referring to the observations of Mr. Labouchere with respect to the action of the Liberal Unionists, which he characterised as unfair and not justified. As to the policy which had been announced by the Government, he remarked that the House was not asked now to commit itself to the , legislative projects which they contemplated ; and as to the executive measures, nobody proposed now te challer.ge them. They had been disparaged—end no doubt u sturally— by the Irish members. They had been ridiculed and dis- paraged by the hon. member for the Scotland Division of Liverpool (Mr. T. P. O'Connor), and those Irish members who agree with him, very fairly from their point of view, 1 for it was perfectly natural for them not to desire tee resto- ration of social order in Ireland. (Cries of "No, no," and 0 Withdraw" from the Irish benches.) Mr. T. P. O'CONNOR : Shame; shame. Lord Heasenewrrne, continuing: Before crying shame. would the hon. member allow him to complete the sentence?
THE EXAMINER,. SATURDAY, AUGUST 28, 1886.

It was natural to suppose that they did not desire to see the complete restoration of social order until the political cttanges upon which their hearts were set, and upon which they alleged the permanent prosperity of Ireland depended, had been adopted—(cheers)—because social disorder un- doubtedly constituted one of the chief arguments upon whiela they depended for advocating those political changes. (Hear, hear.) He could not expect that they should de- sire that even a fair rent should be punctually and peace- fully paid, because they never accepted the Land Act of 1881 or the amended Acts as a complete and final solution of the land question. (Irish cheers.) He did not agree with Sir William Harcourt's sweeping doctrines about "social order," and pointed out that he had not always held them or acted on them, as was shown by hie speech on the Arms Act, Sir W. Harcourt said that he and his friends denounced the Land Purchase Bill introduced by the late Government. As a matter of fact he said very little indeed about land purchase. What he said more than once was that if the Government of Ireland Bill was passed, some Act founded upon a similar principle to that contained in the Land Purchase iII was a measure which certainly was called for by equity and justice. If the principle of dual ownership had failed, and if any amendment of the Land Act were desirable, it mast be ia the direction of in- creasing the efficiency of the purchase clauses. Any such attempt ought to be preceded by careful inquiry. As to the inquiry into public works—though he was against offering any disguised or demoralising alms to Ireland—he maintained that Parliament did not possess sufficient in- formation. Mr. J. MORLEY could discern very little in the noble lord's speech to lead to a hope of the speedy removal of the embarassments and discords of the Liberal party. As re- gards the scientific commission of experts, which was to investigate the possibility of developing the natural resour- ces of the country, he anticipated the probability of ina• mense expense being incurred, and contended that the re- port of a Committee which recently sat had provided all the information necessary. He also saw grave dangers in the propesed system of local government, and argued that disastrous results would follow unless the local authori- ties were guided and controlled by a national central authority. Mr. W. F. LAWRENCE also made same remarks; and on the motion of Mr. PeutrELL the debate was adjourned.
Several new bills were brought in and read a first time. After other business the House adjourned at 12-50.
HOUSE OF CONIMONS.-TIIESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QUE,TlONG.—Replying to questions from Mr. Howard Vincent and Mr. Mundella, Baron DE W0r2313 could give no pledge as to the re-introduction of the Merchandise Marks Bill of last session, but every matter connected therewith had received, and was re- ceiving, close attention at the Board of Trade.— In answer to Mr. Powell Williams, Mr. MATTHEWS would not undertake to issue the commission promised by Mr. Hib- bert on the subject of Quarter Sessions c3ntributions of towns to county rates, but the subject would have careful consideration in connection with a scheme of local govern- men".—ln answer to Mr. E. Russell, Sir MICHAEL Lucas- BEACH said the appointment of Sir Redvers Buller would involve no curtailment of the powers of the Inspector- General in Ireland.

THE BULG&RIAN Riavourrrow.—ln reply to Mr. Bryce, Sir James FERGUSON said: As to the events in Bulgaria, her Majesty's Government are not in a position to give the House much more information than that which has ap- peared in the newspapers. Direct communication with Soda has been interrupted, but a despatch has been received from her Majesty's acting agent at Sofia to the effect that at 3 a.m. on Saturday a small detachment of infantry sur- rounded the palace and secured the person of Prince Alex- ander, who is said to have signed an abdication. His High- ness was taken to the War Office, and at 3 o'clock he was sent under escort to a destination which is unknown. A provisional Government was then formed. Of course, many reports have reached us, but nothing authentic or direct.

in relief either of the landlords or tenants of Ireland. (Home Rule cheers.) At the instance of Mr. W. Redmond the House was counted. More than forty members were present, but most of them went out immediately after.

Mr. CRILLY regarded the Irish proposals of the Govern- ment as totally inadequate. They formed a somnolent policy, put forward by a Cabinet of Rip Van Winkles, who intended to go to sleep for the next six months and expected on awakening to find every difficulty smoothed away, and every danger overcome. Mr. G. W. Betroue said the expectation of the Irish party was that they could convert the agrarian system into a lever by which they could force Home Rule upon this country. If the difficulty were settled the trade of the bon. member for Cork would be at an end. Mr. STUART supported the amendment of the bon. mem- ber for Cork, observing that it was proposed to supersede by a Royal Commission the best commission in the world, and that was the commission composed of the Irish repre- sentatives. _ _ . _ . _ _ _

Colonel SAI:DIDERSON theught after the debate the Irish landlords would be judged by the country not to be sa black as they were painted. He entered the House the other night when the member of East Galway (Mr. Harris) was speaking, and he heard him say" landlords are an abomin- able class." The hon. member had always been consistent. (Laughter.) He held exactly the same opinion six years ago, and six years IVAS a great strain on political consis- tency.. (Laughter.) By a quotation from a reported speech Mr. Harris was made to appear to be indifferent to the shooting down of landlords like partridges in September. A Personal explanation by Mr. Harris was smartly seized by Colonel Baunderson as giving him a greater advantage ever his opponent, whom he held to be committed to the confes- sion that he had been a member of the Ribbon Society. Mr. Harris and his friends now boiled over with indignation. The Speaker, to calm the storm, soothingly suggested that Colonel Senn- derson might accept a repudiation.—Mr. HARRIS, with refreshing innoeence, availed himself of this hint to repudi- ate the bon. and,gallant major's words as "a most infamous falsehood."—Of course, the Speaker had then to call Mr. Harris to order. The scene ended in mutual withdrawals, but was revivel soon afterwards when Colonel Saunderson accused Mr. Parnell of holding the throttle-valve of crime, " which he kad turned on before." The hon. member was compelled to withdraw this observation. Mr. Harris was afterwards allowed in self-vindication to explain that he bad followed up the quotation given by Major Sannderson with the assurance to his bearers that be was not inciting to crime, and was a foe to the shedding of blood. The de- batewas, on the motion of Mr. Chamberlain, again ad- journed. Mr. Howl= introduced a bill to consolidate and to amend the law relating to Parliamentary elections, which was read a first time.
The Bosse adjourned at half-past five. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TITURSDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. NEW MEMBER.-Sir M. White Ridley, who was received with Ministerial cheers, took the oath and his seat for the Blackpool Division of Lancashire in the room of Colonel Stanley.

QCBSTIONS, &c.—lt was stated that the committee ap- pointed to consider M. Pasteur's method of treatment for hydrophobia had examined a large number of per- Bens operated unon, and were of opinion that the treatment was effectual. In reply to a question, Sir R. GOBST communicated to the House the information received from the Viceroy in regard to the inun- dation of Mandalay. The givinz way of the bend was due to an unprecedented rise in the river, and the total loss of life was under 25. The Under-Secretary, answering another question, said the cost of the military operations in Barmah to 31st March last was 39 lacs of rupees (£390,000). The expenditure for the current year, estimated at 30 lacs (.E300,000), would be exceeded—The Holm SECRETARY, answering Mr. Dillwyn and Mr. Kenyon, said his infor- mation was that the resistance to the collection of tithe in Denbighshire was of an organised nature, but it was impos- sible to say at present whether it would extend to other parishes. SIR R. BITLLER'S APPOINTMENT.

A lengthy discussion arose in connection with the ap- pointment of General Sir R. Buller to the supreme command In Clare and Kerry. Replying to Mr. Russell, the Chief Secretary said General Boiler's appointment was a purely civil one ;he was not going to Ireland. as had been sugges- ted, to enforce martial law, but he was being sent to take measures for detesting and punishing crime.—Mr. RUSSELL moved the adjournment of the House in order .to discuss the appointment of Sir R. Buller, which he described as con- trary to constitutional principle, adverse to the future peace of Ireland, and calculated to introduce a bad precedent in England. The prevalence of ci inn in Kerry was a sign of ill-government, and that could not be improved by sending a military man with undefined powers to administer the country. The spirit of the mea- sures proposed by the Government showed that they intended to treat Ireland as a savage and barbarous country.—Lord R. CHURCHILL failed to see what practical benefit could ensue from the course now adopted. The proper method would have been to move an amendment to the Addrese, and that, if adopted, would have put an end to the appointment and also to the Government. He con- sidered that the late Government had lost their right to cavil at General Butler's despatch to Ireland, because they themselves appointed an officer on the active list—Sir C. Warren—to command the Metropolitan police. The present Government thought that possibly there had been some failure and want of energy on the part of the police in Kerry, and they selected Sir R. Buller to remedy the defect. The Government declined to discuss the merits of the ap- pointment, or to take part in proceedings which seemed to be intended only to occupy time unprofitably. —Sir WILLIAM BARCOURT taunted the Chancellor of the Exchequer with " flying in the face of the rules" by reffislng to discuss a question properly introduced, and said this came with a bad grace from one who had, to an ex- tent which was a great abuse, taken advantage of motions for adjournment on every possible subject. He accused Minis- ters of having introduced the appointment in terms calcu- lated to stir up public misgiving and to creat3 an impres- sion that the moonlighters of Kerry were to be treated as rebels taken with arms, and shot without trial. It was fallacious to compare General Buller with Sir C. Warren, whose military capacity was absolutely in abeyance, whilst the Ministry could not deny that General Buller would be empowered to give orders to the soldiers in Kerry. He hoped the House would accept the Chief Secretary's milder version, and, paying no attention to the " flare-up " of Lord R. Churchill, permit the discustion to clese.—Mr. H. J. WILSON drew attention to descriptions of Colonel Buller 's operations in Zululand, where he com- manded a force of what k were called "indiscriminate ruffians" and " levied toll on Zulu blood."—Sir M. HICKS- BEACH said he was impelled to interpose on behalf of a gallant and distinguished officer who had been outrageously attacked. During the Zulu war Colonel Buller was as humane 29 be was brave, and bad been selected to go to KFrry because the Government believed be would act con- stitutionally, justly, humanely, and firmly in the task , before him.—Mr. DILLON said the people of Kerry regarded the. appointment as intended in the landlord interest, to assist them in the work of extermination.—The House divided, and the motion for adjournment was _rejected by 1241 to 146 votes.

div.head: ADJOURNED DEBATE.
div.p: THE ADJOURNED DEBATE.

In some conversation between Mr. Parnell and the Leader of the House, the prospect of the debate on the trtesent amendment lasting till next Tuesday was opened out, but Lord Randolph refused to contemplate such a coating - I ency. Mr. PARNELL resumed the debate on the Address, and moved to add the following clause to the Address: Humbly to assure her Majesty that we fear that, owing to the heavy fall in the price of agricultural produce, the greatest dill- culty will be experienced in the coming winter by the Irish tenant farmers in the paytnent of their present rents, and many will be unable to pay those rents; that numerous I evictions, confiscating the rights vested in the tenants by the Land Act of 1881, causing widespread suffering and endangering the maintenance of social order, will be the , result; that we deprecate any attempt to transfer the loss ' due to inability to pay the present rents from the owners of land to the taxpayers of Great Britain and Ireland by any extension of State-assisted purchase on the basis of rents fixed when prices were higher than they now are. The leader of the Parnellites spoke with his accustomed ' cram self-posession, but said he shuddered to think what the state of Ireland would be two or three months hence under the policy announced by the Chancellor of the Exchequer. He admitted that he and his party had every reason to be patient and to do all they could to keep their people within the limits of legality, theirs being now a winning cause. But 1, from an examination of the Ministerial programme he de- , duced that evictions would take place in Ireland, exaspera- tion would follow, and order would not be restored without coercion. He counselled the Chief Seeretary.with bitter defiance to " urge his fires, sharpen his pincers, and prepare his scorpion wnips," but to remember that the Irish people would never submit to be governed by a Government which was not their own. The Irish people would utterly refuse to sell their national birthright for a mess of pottage. He advised a triennial revision of rents according to prices, and the admiesion of leaseholders to the benefit of the Land Act, as measures of temporary relief, but declared that the ques- tion of autonomy would now always be-first in the hearts of the Irish people. (Cheer 3. Mr. PLUNKET subjecteu Mr. Parnell's argument to some criticism and comparison with his former declarations re- garding Lord Ashbourne's Land Purchase Act. He charged the hon. member with taking upon himself a terrible res- ponsibility in publishing" in his cold-blooded manner" the declaration that the Government policy must fail, and that he would and must have stringent coercion in Ireland. , Mr. GearesToNX, who was enthusiastically cheered, an- nounced his intention to take no part in the division, but was preceading to carry out a proposal to subject the Minis- terial programme to "free comment" when the Chancellor of the Exchequer hastily intervened, and procured a deci- sion of the Speaker that the debate must be limited to the amendment. Reproachful exclamations, intended to shame the Leader of the House. greeted these tactics and Mr. Glad- stone himself commented sharply on the fact that he had been debarred from his epportunity ,of criticising the policy of the Government as leader of the Opposition by the fact ;of that policy being developed by Lord Randolph after he (ar. Gladstone) had epoken, instead of in the Queen's i Speech, according to usage. In further discussion on the point of order, Sir W. Harcourt opened up the prospect of another amendment being brought forward to provide Mr. Gladstone with his lost opportunity. This suggestion had i a miraculous effect in removing difficulties, aneMr. Glad- ! stone was suffered to continue his speech by "indulgence of the House." In its coarse, be criticised severely the lend purchase scheme shadowed forth by the Ministry, and warned them that no power on earth would succeed in carry- ing a measure which would throw the difference between , the judicial and the agricultural rent on the taxpayers. He argued that Ministerial obligations to Lord Hartington ' should incline them to go as far as he did in conceding i that as a modes vivendi between themselves and the Irish I people a central body in Dublin might be made a feature of their local government scheme. , For himself, he treated it as no reproach. but as a matter of delight, that he should be taunted with becoming either leader or follower in any movement that tended to soothe the people of Ireland and encourage them to hope for the realization of their just de- mands. lie feared only the dark prospect due to the post- ponement of that consummation which alone could give rest and repose to Ireland, and which alone could bring to a close the period of its political agitation. (Cheers.) In the course of subsequent discussion Mr. Chaplin paid homage to his new leader, and resumed his old role of de- tractor of of Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Mlcdonald, the blind member of the House, made his maiden speech, which was distinguished by clearness of utterance, warmth in defence of his leader, Mr. Parnell, aed boldness in attack of Minis- ters.—Mr. T. W. RUSSELL, though quoting an (morn-let's fall in Irish prices, gave energetic support to the Ministry.—Mr. MenoNy's support of Mr. Parnell derived special significance from the fact that he, as one who had assisted in fixing the judicial rents, now declared them to be too high.—On Sir T. ESMONDE'S motjon, the debate was adjourned, Mr. SEX- TON assuring the Chancellor of the Exchequer that the ne- cessity of discussing his cenduct in connection with the Belfast riots precluded any hopes of the debate terminat- ing on Thursday. The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for IRELAND having brought .in his Bill for creating the Belfast Riot Commission, the House adjourned at ten minutes to one.

THE ADJOURNED DEBATE. Sir T. ESMONDE, resuming the adjourned debate on the Address, contended that no amount of Coercion Acts would prevent the Irish from agitating for their own Parliament and the making of their own laws. (Hear, hear.) Mr. W. REDMOND considered that in the pressing nature of the case it was the duty of each representative of the Irish people one after another to endorse emphatically on behalf of those they represented the sentiments contained in the speech of the leader of the party to which they had the honour to belong. Mr. HOWARTH said in better parts of Ireland the natural remedy for distress was that rents should go up and down with the price of produce. He was ot opinion that if fur- , ther sacrifices should become necessary in the interests of peace the community at large would not desire to see the whole loss fall upon the landlords of Ireland, and would be quite prepared to share in paying a national fine. (" Oh, ob.") Tile only permanent remedy:for the evils that afflic- ted that country was that of emigration. (" Oh, ob.") Mr. G. HOWELL said if the Government would but under- take to follow the advice of the hon, member for Cork they at any rate might be able to prevent some of the distress that was sure to arise in Ireland.
- —. Mr. ADDISON protested against the notion that the work- ing men, or the "classes," in his constitaene7 would be willing that one shilling of English taxation should be paid

div.head: ADJOURNEb DEBATE.
div.p: THE ADJOURNEb DEBATE.

The adjourned debate on the Address was then resumed. After remarks from Mr. Flynn and Lord Cranborne, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN addressed the House, objecting to Mr. Paneli's amendment as superfluous. He would support no attempt to transfer the loss which might fall upon the land- lords to the pockets of the British taxi:layers. He could not, however, vote for an amendment wkich was equivalent to a vets of censure on the Government, and was not going to do anything to turn them out so long as the alternative Government was committed to a Separatist policy. It was only by the creation of a great scheme of peasant proprietor- ship that they could deal with the Irish question, and this could only be done by confiscation or by State purchase. He was prepared to give a favourable consideration and even a cordial support to any proposition that the Government might make for the establishment of a peasant proprietary in Ireland, provided that the whole arrangement was under the effectual control of the Imperial Government and re- cured by the intervention of municipal authorities. In reference to the appointment of Commissions, he said Royal Commissions were in these matters of the greatest service, and the only objection to them was when they were evi- dentiv proposed with the view of delay. He admitted there I had been a fall in prices, but for that evil a sliding scale was the fair remedy. It was the duty of the Government to maintain social order, and while it did that it would also, he expected, endeavour in every way to promote the pros- perity and happiness of the people, and do for them all and more than an Irish Parliament could reasonably and justly do. For these reasons he was prepared to wait for the full development of the Government's policy, and to give them a fair trial. (Cheers.) Sir C. RUSSELL said the speech of the right bon. gentle- man was less concerned with the amendment before the House than with a justification of his own conduct. It was a speech in which the right hon. gentleman sought for and received the cheers of ;gentlemen opposite by language in- sulting to his former coffeagues- Mr. SEXTON moved the adjournment of the debate, and, on the understanding that tile discussion of the amend- ment would be concluded to-morrow night, the motion was . agreed to. The House adjourned at 12.32.

A CHINESE Commisstox.—The Chinese Ambassador, the Marquis Tsemt, has commissioned Messrs. John Brinsmead and Sons, of London, to manufacture a pianoforte for the special use of the Marchioness Tseng in China. The Great Ebor Handicap race was decided on Wednes- day over the Knavesmire course, and resulted in a victory for the favourite, Mr. Childwick's Le Caissier, who beat King Monmouth by a neck in a most exciting finish. _

THE CARDIFF ELECTION Riors.—A letter from the Home Secretary, accompanying the report of the Commissiener, Mr. Bridge. who recently held an inquiry into the elect'on disturbances at Cardiff, was read on Monday at a meeting of the Cardiff Town Council. Tne Home Secretary re- frained from comment on the report, but suggested that at future elections, when serious disturbance of the public peace might be apprehended on polling dap, the counting of votes and declaration of the poll should be made on the day following, a course which experience had shown to be more conducive to the preservation of the peace than the declaration of the poll on the night of the election. The police received great provocation, and, except in one or two cases, their conduct was very good. WHAT HUNGER CAN Do.--Ibe Dade county coal mines in the State of Georgia are worked by 500 long-term con- victs. For several days these convicts had complained of excessive labour under the great heat. One morning, when the stockades in which they are kept in chains, were opened, the men refused to go to work. They said they were ready, to die. and would as soon die as live in torture. The keeper telegraphed to the governor that he must either shoot several of the men, or starve all into submission. The governor sent back word to use the latter course. For two days and one night the prisoners were kept without bread or water, and still maintained a defiant front. The third morning several of them declared their wish to surrender. They were set upon by the leaders and maltreated. But hunger had done its work, and before dark all but one had surren- dered. At last accounts this one still held out, and was re- ported to be on the verge of derangement. THE RED DEATH SECT.—The Peculiar People often cause a painful sensation in this country by refusing to call in a medical man when a member of the sect is seriously ill; but much more shocking (says a contemporary) is the doctrine respecting sickness which is propounded by the Red Death sect, one of the numerous bodies of religious innovators to be found in Russia. The leading principle of this sect is that, as God cannot be pleased at the sight of human crea- tures suffering, religion imposes the obligation of putting an end to their lives when they are enduring pain. All sick members are, therefore, put to death. The sect derives its title from the ghastly ceremony of despatching the doomed., member. The executioner is dressed in a crimson garb, and the patient is strangled with a red thong, after being laid on a catafalque in a room lighted by a solitary lamp. The law has intervened to put a stop te the butcheries of the sect, and 40 of the members have been arrested by the police. A Rovea, PIANOFORTE —ln prospect of the marriage of Don Carlos of Portugal with the Princess Marie Amilie, the English residents in Lisbon resolved to present the Prince with a grand pianoforte made in their own country. The commission was given to Messrs .Lihn Brinsmead and Sons, by whom a first-class instrument has been specially con- structed, and is now to be seen at their establishment in Wigmore-street. The exterior has a handsome appearance, the case being rosewood of a beautiful grain, relieved by gilding, and bearing a plate, on which is inscribed, " Pre- sented to His Royal Highness the Prince Don Carlos on the auspicious occasion of his marriage with her Royal High- ness the Princess Marie Amelie, with profound respect and earnest good wishes, by the British community in Lisbon. May 22. 1880." It is hardly necessary to say that the manufacturers have done their best to turn out a pianoforte which shall be a credit to the country of its origin. The instrument contains all the improvements patented by the firm, and by the perfection of its touch, the beauty of its tone, and the ease with which it answers to every mood of the player, is eminently fitted for the destiny which awaits it.—Daily Telegraph. _ _ _ _

EVICTIONS IN IRELIND.—.I most determined resistance is being given to an evicting party which has been at work for the last few days on the Marquis of Clanricarde's estate, near Woodford, county Galway. About 1,000 police have been drafted into Portunana, whence they go each morning to the scene of the intended evictions. During the last fortnight evictions on an extensive scale have been going on in Gweedore, county Donegal. The total nearly rental involved is only £5O, and the cost of the 150 policemen, bailiffs, dr.c., including the hire of some sixty cars, has amounted to £lOO a day. In some instances the evicted persons were reinstated in their holdings as caretakers. The people are said to be hopelessly in arrears with their rent. A New Ross correspondent sends particulars of extraordin- ary eviction scenes which took place in that neighbourhood on Monday afternoon. At four o'clock an immense pro- cession entered the town from Fethard, county Wexford. First came the Ross Brass Band, then three waggonettes containing 62 persons, the wives and children of 13 small farmers evicted last week from their holdings on the Mar- quis of Ely's estates. The waggonettes were followed by 300 horsemen, four deep, a number of priests on cars, headed by Father Tom Doyle, the friend of Sir Chas Gavin Duffy, the procession being clostd by a string of care in single file, said to be several miles long. The procession was interspersed with some five or six bands, the bandsmen Carrying green flags on gilded pikes. The object of this extraordinary gathering was to escort the evicted families to New Ross Workhouse, where a "ward of honour " has been set apart for their uee. Notices had been previously posted about the town calling on the people to assemble in their thousands "to witness the last resource of landlord oppression, and to comfort the poor evicted on their way to the workhouse." In compliance with this suggestion all the shops were shut and the town was decorated. A plat- form was erected from which Nationalist orators harangued the people. An extra force of police were drafted into the town, and about one o'clock a battery of artillery from Dungannon Fort, en route to Clonmel, arrived, and were assigned quarters for the night in view of possible disturb- ances.

A PERILOUS NIGHT ON A WELSH MOUNTAIN. --s The greatest excitement has been created at Towvn, on the Welsh coast, by the thrilling adventures of a minister and his family. The Rev. W. E. Heningsoe, M.A.. of Coven- try, who, with the members of his family and a friend, were staving at this quiet watering place, made an ascent of Caaer Idris. After spending the day upon the great moun- tain, they attempted at four o'clock to descend by the re- nowned foxes' path, a precipitous stone-strewn slope lead- ing down to Lake Llyngader. Instead of striking the path, however, the party went beyond and got separated, ulti- mately finding themselves in positions el such danger that they had to seek shelter for the night amid the rocks. At nightfall the minister and his wife found themselves standing upon a precipice so deep that a fall over it would have resulted in their being dashed to pieces. Three other members of the party, who were hidden from sight by a huge piece of rock, also got into a situation where they could move neither backwards nor forwards. They cried aloud for help, but without avail, and were compelled to remain in their perilous locations throughout the night. For many hours the mountain was enveloped in a dense mist, and the mother cried out at intervals to her children for fear they would fall asleep and roll over into the abyss. With an almost superhuman effort Mr. Heningson at length dragged himself from his place and clambered up the cliff. After a long and weary journey he succeeded in getting a strong band of men, who hurried to the mountain with ropes to rescue the affrighted famTly from their hazar• dous positions. With great difficulty the party were drawn up the rocks by the ropes, and were subsequently lodged in a cottage at the foot of the mountain. After partaking of refreshments and lying down to rest the ladies seemed little the worse for the extraordinary adventure, but Mr. Henirm- son suffered severely. He lost his voice by continually shouting for help, and became utterly prostrated by the mental anxiety of the long night and his physical exer- tions.

MR. GLADSTONE ON THE IRISH QUESTION.—On Saturday Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone arrived at Chislehurst on a short visit to Mr. Charles Morley. They were accompanied by Mr. Herbert Gladstone, Mr. Arnold Morley, and Mr. Majors- banks. During the afternoon Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone drove to Frogmore to call upon Lord and Lady Sydney, whom they stayed with about half an hour. In the evening about 150 members of the Chislehurst Working Men's Liberal As. sociation assembled outside Mr. Morley's residence, and, in response to a request for a short speech. Mr. Gladstone pre- sented himself. After the cheering had subsided, he thanked the company for the kindness with which they had greeted him. He had always said he had seen nothing on any occa- sion that he could recollect equal to the enthusiasm with which the late Government's proposals of the present year had been welcomed by their friends, and he had been very much struck to find in the South of England, where he bad visited, although undoubtedly the late Government occu- pied almost universally the wrong position on the poll—(a voice, "For a time")—vet those who were with them were heartily with them. That enthusiasm appeared to him to show that they were all of the same type of Englishmen as those of whom it was originally said that "An Englishman did not know when he was beaten." That was, he never meant to be beaten—(hear, hear,)—and although he was beaten on a particular occasion, he meant to continue to struggle till his efforts were crowned with victory. The Irish proposals of the late Government claimed from him a primary position, because the happiness of Ireland depended upon them, and although there might have been prejudices and antipathies between thoge countries, the fact that be- tween 1,300,000 and 1,400,000 Englishmen and Scotchtnen had been to the poll to vote on behalf of Ireland showed that those prejudices were fast disappearing. Let them go all over the world and ask any man in any country, Euro- pean or American, let them consult any book that had been written on the subject, and they would not find one of them that did not say those relations had been miserable for Ire- land and dishonourable for England. (Hear, hear.) There- fore, for the honour of their country,they should continue to labour as long as they could for the interests of Ireland, and so redeem England's honour in the history of the world. If the country had any desire for the House of Commons to do its work, for its character to be maintained, the Irish , question must be got out of the way. There would never be any progress in English legislation until that was settled. Turning to the guests, Mr. Gladstone complimented Mr. A. Morley, saying that he bore a name which was connected with everything that was Christian-like, honourable and patriotic, and concluded by saying that although they were a reduced party, they were a happy one. (Cheers.) It is in the provinc of .Sazhurg is the Austrian Alps, and it is rot far distant from Bad Gasteio, the famous meeting place of the Eninerois ; rmr from the Gross Grochner, where the recent mountaineering accideet occurred. A ST. HELENS CYCLIST'S FRAT.—Mr. J. B Warren a member of the St. Helevs Cyclists Club, started at mid- night, on Wednesday week, on one of Rudge's " Royal Crescent Tricycles" for shrewsbury and back, via Warring- ton, linutsford. Holmes Chapel, Sandbach, Crewe, Nant. wich, Whitchutch, and \Vern, a distance of 75 miles, re- turning bf Chester and Frodshatn, but unfortanately he missed his way from Wbitchurch, and passed through Tar. porley and Tarvin to Chester and Frodsbarn, thus making the return journey 78 miles This was a total of 153 miles in 18 hours 15 minutes; excellent performance, especially

A CHILD DBOWNED LT .RLINPORD —About half -past two on Saturday afternoon, James Yates, two years old, son of Daniel Yates, a collier residinz in Chapel Fields, Rain— ford, was found dead in Randle Brook, Rainford. Deceased had been missing from about two o'clock on the ptevious day, when he was last seem playing with a number of other children near the house. Some time afterwards he was
missed, and information was given to the police. Inquiries

were made, and the pits in ihe vicinity were dragged, but without avail. On Saturday afrernoon, at the time stated, however, two men named John Cotton and James Harrison • were searching for decea.ed, and found him lying face down- wards in Randle Brook. The body was afterwards removed to the parents' home. A RAILWAY TRAGEDY AND MYSTBRY.—The dead body of a gentleman was found in a first-class carriage of a Midland express from London on its arrival at Leicester at 2-40 a.m., on Saturday. On the step of the carriage lay a six-cham- bered revolver, and death had been caused by a shot in the ,head, where there was a severe wound. A season ticket from London to Manchester was found on the deceased, and bore the name of James G. Lowe. 4, Langley-place, Victoria Park, Manchester. An inquest was held on Monday. The guard of the train stated that he purchased a ticket for the deceased at St. Panora., and gave him 15s change. He rode alone in the compartment of a first-class carriage, and wit- ness noticed the blinds drawn at various stopping places. Mr. Lowe, of Noryond, broth.r of the deceased, produced a letter written on Friday by the deceased to his wife, sayin& he had succeeded in collecting £1.200. On the body being " searched at Leicester, no money was found. The medical witness expressed an opinion that a murder had been com- mitted, and the inquiry was adjourned in order that further inquiry might be instituted._

, QUARTERLY SESSION OF GOOD TEXPLARS.—The quar- terly session of the South-West Lancashire District Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Public Hall, Hindley, ou Saturday afternoon, tinder the presidency of Brother .1. W. Hall, , of Warrington. After the opening cere- mony the quarterly reports of the district officers were sub- mitted. The report of the D.C.T. (Brother Hall) referred to the work of the Order, and urged that it needed earnestness and devotion to ensure success. He pointed out the advan- tages of individual efforts on the part of the members, and asked each lodge to do its best during the com- ing winter session.—The report of the W.D. Secre- tary (Brother M. Jones) showed that there was a slight decrease in the number of members com- pared with last quarter. the number of ledges being 56, with a total of 2.650 members. The financial re. port of the 1,17.0. Treasarer (Brother J. J. Wright) was of a favourable character, as were also the reports of the Dis- trict Electoral Superintendent (Brother J. Pickersgill), the District Superintent of Juvenile Temple (Brother R. An- ders), which showed there were 26 temples with a total of 2;055 members', and urged the importance of a closer 'anion between the adult end juvenile sections of the order. The reports of the Executive and Credential Committees were next received. All the reports were unanimously adopted, and a discussion ensued as to the next place of meeting. Oa the motion of Brother J. W. Hall, it was decided that it be held at Warrington on the 27th November next. An open-air demonstration and procession was afterwards held. and at a public meeting Bro. A. E. Eccles, Past Grand Worthy Treasurer, preelded. .

TERRIBLE FIRE IN LONDON.—A terribly destructive nre broke out on Friday morning in the Isle of Dogs, opposite to Greenwich Hospital. The Oil Storage Company occu- pied about eight acres with its warehouses, receptacles, and storage ground, with a frontage of 100 yards in Manchester- road, whence the premises extended 100 yards back to the river, the premises thus forming a square. Here in ware- houses, tanks, barrels, &c., there was stored an enormous quantity of petroleum, paraffin, kerosene, and various kinds of vegetable and other oils. At a quarter to four o'clock on Friday morning the watchman citecorered flame in the receiving-house, near the entrance gates, and immediately raised an alarm. Assistance was quickly summoned by mes- sengers from the police station, close at hand, and steam fire engines and fire floats were speedily on the scene. Meanwhile, however, the flames had spread with frightful rapidity, and when the firemen arrived they found the buildings, stocked to the roof with oil, burning furiously, whilst the terrified residents in the vicinity, everwhelmed by the spectacle of the far-reaching flames and the intense heat, were shrieking for help, fleeing from their homes, and fainting in the streets. The fire brigade had no ordinary foe to encounter, and the battle for some time went against them. Supt. Campbell fell between a tank and the wall, but was quickly dtagged from his perilous position, aad imme- diately afterwards the flames burst with a roar over the spot. After this the fire burned with renewed strength, and continued well into 9_ttorday. The manager of the Oil Storage state the buildinge were fullt insured, and that the greater portion of the We suffered by the destruction of oil, time is also covered by insurance. INGENIOUS FRAUDS ON THE RAILWAY COMPANY.-- Before Alderman J. Harrison and Mr. J. C. Gamble, at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, Thomas Woods, an elderly man, respectably dressed, was charged with travel- lino' on the London and North-Western Railway from Liver- pool to tit. Helens without having paid leis fare and with intent to avoid payment.—Mr. Ferrand, of Liverpool, who , prosecuted, said that case showed a very ingenious fraud, and the defendant must have practised it well before be carried it out so effectively. Defendant, he added, resided at Clock Face, and travelled for some firm in the lard trade. He took a return ticket frotn Clock Face to Liverpool, which ticket would be available for six days. After going to Liver- pool he would return to St. Helens, show to the ticket- collector at the door his return half from Liverpool to Clock Face and ask permission to go in the town on business, until the time for the departure of the train from St. Helens to Clock Face. Defendant on coming back to the station pur- chased a single ticket from St. Helens to Clock Face, and would give that ticket up on his arrival at Clock Face. On his next journey to Liverpool defendant would only take a single ticket from Clock Face to Liverpool, and would re- turn with the return half of the ticket he had paid for on the previous occasion. By that means defendant would travel from Liverpool to St. Helens on two occasions with the same half of a return ticket. Mr. Ferrand added that they had been suspicious of the defendant's conduct for some time, and the detective officer was directed to watch his movements.—Evidence in support of the charge was Riven by Samuel Jones, station master, Clock Face; L. Battersby, station master, Walton ; Ticket-collector Wilding, St. Helens ; and Railway-detective Petkins.—The Bench inflic- ted a fine of 40s and costs upon the defendant. A SWIM THROUGH THE NIAGARA RAPIDS.—The feat of swimming the whirlpool rapids of Niaffara, which Captain Webb died in attempting, was successfully accompliEhed on Sunday by an ex-policeman from Boston named William J. Kendall. He wore nothing save an ordinary cork life pre- server. Diving into the water, Kev,dall swam half a dozen strokes towards the centre ef the river, when be was caught in the eddy, which first carried him back towards the Falls, then down the rapids in the counter current. As he reached the boiling water, Kendall assumed a perpendicular position, treading the water. In this way he struck the first breaker. which submerged him for a moment ; then his hands ap- peared with a swimming motion as the huge waves dashed him high ain the air. Then began the race between life and death. Kendall did not try to dive, because he believed that Webb split his head her striking a rock while diving through the breakers. The rapids tumbled him about, keep- ing him most of the time submerged and once tossing him ten feet out of the water. Then he was sucked under for half a minute, reeppearing several hundred yards further down. "That's killed him !" shouted an eve-witness, and as his body was apparently lifeless when be entered the whirlpool a few minutes later everybody believed him dead. Up to that time he had been ebout three minutes going three•quarters of a mile. Soon after entering the whirlpool he was drawn under, re-appearing a few hundred feet away. Two minutes later, to the surprise of eyerbody. he was seen to be alive, and began to swim towards the Canada shore. In ten minutes he reached the rock, clinging to it, but he,, not haying strength to climb upon it, was helped ashore, completely exhausted. The trip through the rapids occu- pied just five minutes. He was taken to the hotel, where brandy soon revived him. He made this statement of his experiences :—" I was induced to make the attempt by bets amounting te three thousand dollars. There isn't enough money in the whole world for me to make the trip again. While going through the rapids I was tossed and tumbled until I knew not where I was. The weight of the waves was terrible, and I was pounded until I was sore all over. I knew hardly nothing. oh ! nothing while going through, though I realised that I turned three complete somersaults, such was the force of the back waves. Once I was carried near the American shore and saw some rocks close to me. made a desperate effort to get away from them, but with what effect I don't know. It ie certain that I did not strike a rock during the whole swim. When I entered the whirl- pool I was in pretty good condition, hut when I found my- self spinning around like a top and b, ing drawn down with irresistible force I thought I would Fell out my bets for three cents and consider I was doing well. I lost conscious- ness for a few moments then. When I was shot up it was, I should judge, fifty feet from where I was drown down. I was completely exhausted and knew that tow it was a struggle for life. Then it was that I threw myself on my back and pushed for the shore. It was that terrible whirl that made me so sick."
