- "Ireland, Ireland, always Ireland," is the despairing cry of the politician who wants to see something done by Parliament for England, Scotland, and Wales, We have got a new Government and a new policy; but the policy, so far as it can as yet be defined, is one that chiefly relates to Ireland. Unhappily, so long as the Irish problem is unsolved, there is no setting it aside; it will remain at our doors, and continue to press for a solp- tion. The majority of the electors of tse United Kingdom are not yet convinced that Home Rule is the best way out of the difficulty; but we venture to predict that if the present Government carry out the policy they have thus far outlined it will breed so much confusion and produce so much dis- gust that the prospect of government in Ire- land by a purely Irish Parliament will begin by comparison to look exceedingly bright. In the first place, the Salisbury Government are resolved to put off doing anything as long as they can. This is wise on their part, seeing that they practically confess that they haven't a definite idea of their own as to what should be done. And then they have the Liberal Unionists to consider. It would never do to begin doing something which might not be approved by Lord HAW. TINGTON and his followers, for in that case the patronage upon which they exist might be withdrawn, and the Minisfry might find themselves, as the phrase is, in the streets. They are in a fix, and, like other people similarly situated, they want time to consider how best to get out of their dilemma. They were, it is worth while to remember, in office at the beginning of the year; and on the 26th January they made it known that their policy was the policy of suppressing the National League. Since then there has been an increase rather than a decrease in agrarian crime in Ireland; but we hear nothing now of suppressing the League. But a Salisbury. Churchill Government is nothing:if it cannot "jump Jim Crow ; " it is only crotchet- mongers like Mr. GLADSTONE who trouble themselves with adherence to principle. So the immediate policy of the new Government is to be a Policy of Delay, with Government in the meantime by Royal Commission; there isto be a big Commission and alittle Commis- sion—a big commission to inquire into the Irish land question, and a little one to make a report as to the developement of the material resources of Ireland. It is not easy to say why the large Commission should not have included the smaller one. Perhaps the Cabinet were in the position of the carpenter who, having made a large hole in the door for the use of the cat, thought it necessary to make a small hole for the use of the kitten. The Royal Commission on Trade Depression, appointed by the Tories when

they were previously in office, is still at Work; and if it is doing its work properly it ought to have covered a good deal of the ground to be traversed by the new Commis- sions. Perhaps the Commissioners have not Spent money enough; and besides, a ball of this kind once set rolling must be kept rolling. The immature opinions of the Government on the Irish Land Question have been set forth by Lord SALISBURY, Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL, and by Sir MICHAEL HICKS- ' BEACH, as Irish Secretary. They are not very clear' as the speakers are not in agree- ment with each other. They await the light to be given by the Royal Commission to get them out of the fog. But the principle thus far laid down is a bad one; it is proposed to get rid of dual ownership by a system of land Purchase, the British Parliament findinr, the Inon.ey, and local authorities providing the security. How this local authority is to be set up, or to operate when set up, is not , evident; but this much is evident, namely, that in this case local security cannot be so good as national security. English electors Showed aversion to AIL GLADSTONE'S Irish Land Bill because they were afraid that, if Parliament advanced money on the purchase of Irish land, it would never get it back again. But it must be remembered that the EX-PREMIER, as the greatest financier of this generation, provided, as security for the pay- ment of the interest, the whole of the revenue from Irish customs and imposts, as well as the amount to be collected in the shape of rent; and he left such a margin •as would have more than covered every penny of in- terest, even if not a shilling of rent had been Paid. Lord SALISBURY offers no such security; the guarantee, such as it is, will 'kit a local guarantee; and as the purchases, 'to I be of service, will have to be effected in the I Poorest districts, it is obvious that the guar- antee will be a pcor one. It is further sug- gested that, where the judicial rent is found to be greater than the tenant can pay, the amount to be paid will be reduced; but, Hi order that the landlord may not suffer, the . difference between the real rent and the. judi- cial rent will be met by the State. In other viords, if this doctrine be .carried out, the British taxpayer, whatever his own losses in business may be, will be called upon to make good the losses of the Irish landlords! A bait of this kind is sure to be snapped at by the landlords of Ireland; and as to the People at large they are to be humoured by expenditure on harbours of refuge for fishing boats, though, as Mr. PARNELL says, "the Pboard of Works has strewn the Irish coast With monuments of its incapacity as an engi- neering body." The sum of £750,000 has been named as the amount which the Govern- Might also be prepared to spend in lowering the great arterial beds of Ireland; but the estimate given in Dublin for lowering one bed £600,000 ; while in the opinion of the leader of the Irish party the total sum re- quired would be not three quarters ofa million, but at least ten millions ot money! Let the taxpayers of this country ask themselves Whether they are prepared to bribe Irishmen Hi this way to forego their demand for Home Rule; and whether they are willing to ensure that Irish landlords, however bad the times ta ay be, shall suffer no loss? If they are not Willing to commit themselves to follies of this kind, let them speak with no uncertain sound, and induce their representatives to take the earliest opportunity of dismissing a Government which includes propositions of this kind in their plans for settling the Irish question.

TEE Rev. EVAN EVANS, Rector of Llan- rmon, Denbighshire, is likely to be- , come famous as the person whose , Conduct led to a war against tithe rent , Which may spread from Wales to every other Part of the United Kingdom. Farmers have long suffered the pinch of the hard times, and it is not unnatural that they. Should feel that the tithe payment constitutes a burden which should, if possible, be les- sened, if not got rid of altogether. They , Perceive that, under existing arrangements, tt is always well with the tithe-supported par- , son however it may be with themselves; he , gets his tithe rent even when that and the ' landlord's rent have to come out of capital. Some landlords have shown themselves con- siderate by making reductions in rent, vary- /rig' generally from ten to twenty-five per cent. Noting this, the farmers of Llanar- Mon conceived the idea of asking the Rector to forego twenty-five per cent of the tithe charge they were under obligation to pay him; but the reverend gentleman refused point blank to consider such a proposition. The farmers thereupon determined to absent themselves from the next rent audit, saying the Rector must get in the tithe as best he could. But as it 'transpires they were not indisposed to concede something if the Rev. EVAN EVANS would also make a concession. A second interview was sought, and the sug- gestion was made that there should be a re- duction on the tithe charge of ten per cent., but still the Rector was inexorable. It was "not to nominated in the bond" that he should abate a single farthing under such circum- stances; let them go to the landlord if they wanted relief in the shape of reduction of rent. This kind of talk didn't improve the, temper of the suffering Welsh farmers; having been met with a stiff upper lip, they, too, would show fight," and the result was a resolution to pay no tithe rent at all. The Rector, thus set at defiance, has had recourse to the law, notices have been served, and an attempt has been made to distrain ; but on Monday a solicitor's clerk and two bailiffs were driven out of the district, one of the bailiffs being badly injured. Violent resis- tance is of course to be condemned; but we can well understand why the colliers of the neighbourhood and the people generally should sympathise with the farmers, and be in arms against the Vicar. They must feel that that is a scandalous state of things which permits of the Rev. EVAN EVANS exacting some £3OO or £4.00 in the shape of tithe when he cannot command a congregation of more than 3o in a population of 1,600.. The evil of the Establishment —.the grinding tyranny of a law which permits of such a ,thing—is brought home to them in a most re- pulsive form. The Welsh are not averse to paying for the support of a minister ; they are exceedingly liberal in their maintenance of a Church in which they believe; but, having done this voluntarily, they can have little respect for a further demand which is en- forced by solicitors and bailiffs. It is some- times said that the tithe charge stands on the same footing as the rent charge of the land- lord; but there is a great difference between the two. Up to 1836, it was customary tol take tithe in kind - a tenth sheaf of corn, a' tenth pig, or a tenth calf being surrendered ;1 but the landlord was not paid in this way. Originally, too, a portion of the tithe was for the maintenance ot the poor; but the clergy, neglecting the poor, have appropriated it all

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. There is a story by Mr. Louis Stevenson, called "Prince Otto," which has been strangely called to recollection this week. Otto is a German Princling who has a very clever wife. and who is ruled by a very able Minister. At a certain stage of the history wife and Minister agree that Otto is no longer to be trusted with the direction of affairs in the princi- pality, and they decide to depose him, which they do m the simplest and most, matter of fact manner, and is accepted by Prince Otto as an ordinary part lof the day's proceedings. 1 remember when reading the book feeling that herein the author's imagina- tion had led him astray, and that his story was weakened by the strong improbability of the situa- tion. But what was fabled to have happened to Prince Otto has actually occurred to Prince Alex- ander of Bulgaria. One day a sovereign prince, the next morning a corporal's guard present themselves lat his chamber door, he is quietly deposed and I spirited away from his capital without any fuss or bloodshed! _ .

It is true that more recent intelligence varies the similitude of the cases of Prince Otto and Prince Alexander. In the news which reached the public on Monday morning the incident was set forth as being completed. The Prince had been deposed apparently without protest, the people had gone down on their knees to beseech the Czai to reign over them, Bulgaria was content, and things were going on in the capital and throughout the country exactly as they had proceeded whilst the Prince was still omnipotent. We know now that these were all lying telegrams. The plot to depose the Prince was the work of a comparatively small band of con- spirators acting under directions from St. Peters- burg. Europe was shocked to hear how the Bul- garian nation had deserted the gallant Prince who - led them to victory against Servia. Europe is delighted to learn that, on the contrary, Bulgaria is faithful to its Prince, and that the tables have I already been turned upon the conspirators. What would be the result of the episode as affecting .the I peace of Europe is yet a moot point. - It is difficult Ito believe that Russia has moved in the matter without the cognisance, not to say the consent, of Germany and Austria. If that be so, the Czar will work his will, for, it is no particular business of ours. England is neither the policeman of Europe, nor its knight errant, that it should go about pre serving order and righting wronged Princes. It is Austria's affair, and above all Turkey's—Turkey, which might with a little exercise of common sense and ordinary prescience, have made the thing im- possible by cordially supporting the movement for the union of Bulgaria and Roumelia. But Turkey °will not go to war on her own account. Austria his apparently been squared; even the valiant Jingoes could not drag England into war for this particular cause, and Russia will accordingly get her ruthless way. Mr. Gladstone, like a wise man, has gone off holiday-making to Bavaria.. The selection of holi- day ground is admirable, being out of the ordinary track, whilst- the country is delightful, and the cli- mate healthy. Parliament is still sitting. and to- night Mr. Chamberlain breaks silence as to his position with a Conservative Government that have , already indicated a scheme of reimbursing the Irish landlords cut of public revenues. But, practi- cally, political interest in the proceedings of the session has reached its climax. The mere fact of Mr. Gladstone's departure is indicative of the end of the first act. He would not have left the post of duty if there were anything of material import- ance to keep him there. His example has already been widely followea, and day by day, after to- night's division, we shall see the attendance at the House of Commons dwindle. The stars in their course fight for Lord Salisbury. It is only in the fiercest heat of political warfare that it is possible to keep the House of. Commons in session during the last week of August. It is now known that the Liberal Opposition, more generous than their oppo- nents in similar circumstances, have determined to give the Government full opportunity of preparing their Irish policy. The tug of war is by common consent postponed to February next, and in the meanwhile there is nothing to be gained except personal discomfort in worrying round the Esti- mates of the present year. The Irish members are, of course, bound to make some show of opposititm, and they may be depended upon to do what is ex- i-pected 61 them. But even with them moderation is the order of the day, and the battle will, after all, be but a sham fight. I should not be at all sur- prised if Saturday fortnight witnessed the cere- mony of the Prorogation. It is to be hoped that no one glancing at the car- toon in" Punch "this week will miss its most deli- cate point. Naturally enough the bear "on the prowl S' in the foreground Will focus attention. Thi- of course, represents Russia prowling round

ig _ about Afghanistan, Bulgaria, Armenia, and other happy hunting grounds more or less nearly connec- ted with the way to Constantinople. The point of the picture is, Lowever, shown by the shadow of the head of the British Lion delicately displayed on the rock behind the unconscious bear. This goes to make up one of the most striking cartoons Ten- niel has lately done. Another point, which is even more certain to escape attention, is the singular appositeness of the picture. On Monday morning the world is startled by the news of the kidnapping of Prince Alexander of Bulgaria, unquestionably at the instigation of Russia. On Wednesday morning " Punch " comes out with an elaborate picture pat on the situation. The 'ordinary reader of" Punch" will see nothing remarkable in this. I know many well-informed people who, without too closely con- sidering the matter, are under the impression that " Punch "is prepared on the Tuesday night, coming out on Wednesday like the daily papers with the latest information. The fact is that this picture of the current week was designed in the councils of the "Punch" staff exactly a week before it was pub- lished, and was out of Mr. Tenniel's hands last Fri- day, sixteen hours before Prince Alexander was arrested, and forty-eight haters before the news reached London. This week's work, though a striking example of -political -prescience, is by no means exceptional. knowing the circumstances of time under which the cartoon is settled., I have often been struck with its extraordinary appro- priateness to the circstances of the politics of the day of publication. The House ef Lords once more numbers Earl Rus- sell among its members. The long minority of the r grandson of th.e great earl closed last month, and the new Earl has taken the oath and his seat. He is, it will be remembered, the son of Viscount Am- berley, from whom much vas expected by an an.xious father, but who died before the promise , could be fulfilled, leaving a son and heir eleven :years old. The present Earl is a mild-looking youth who, as yet, has given iso sign of ability to add to the far-reaching fame of the Russell family. He has strong Parliamentary predilections, and has been of late years a constant visitor at the House of ICommons. His attempts at instruction in this di- rection were at the outset comically frustrated. As a peer, though still a miner, he had the right to sit lin the front gallery to the left of the clock. The rst night he came down he was walking straight in when old Mr. Hartley, the doorkeeper, now re- tired, thinking he•was a young man from the coun- try, with an order for the strangers' gallery, seized him by the arm and roughly demanded where he was going. Earl Russell was so alarmed that he ' made no answer but left the lobby. A week later he made another attempt and was again seized by the irate door-keeper. This time he gave his name and was allowed to pass. Oddly enough, on pre- senting himself some nights later, Mr. Hartley did not recognise him, and once more he was reminded of the enormity of the offence of a common person passing the doorway. After this he for some time gave up the attempt to avail kimEelf of his privi-

ileges; but by this time he is well known to the guardians of the door, and passes in and out at pleasure. The intended retirement of Sir James Tlannen from the Court of Probate and Divorce will be a great loss to the public service. Sir James is only, in his sixty-fifth year, a comparatively early age for a judge to seek repose. But since he succeeded Lord Penzance In the Divorce Court fourteen years ago, he has had very hard work of a particularly dis- tasteful character. I have heard from an intimate friend of Sir James's that in spite of his daily prac- tice he finds it impossible to become inured to his position, and is personally borne down by the stream of human misery that incessantly rin4s through his court. Like Charles Dickens, Sir James Hannen was at one time a reporter in the Press Gallery of the House of Commons, a sanctuary at this day for much, as yet, undeveloped legal ability. As I men- tioned last week, Mr. Justice Llannen is just now at • Royat in contiguity, if not actually in company, with Mr. Inderwick apd Sir Charles Dilke. I have heard of a most excellent scheme—l can- not call it charity—which has just been set on foot. There has been latterly an extraordinary dearth of servants in London. The cause is America. Twice a year a great agency sends over from New Yosk a matron who organises arrangements for young ser- vants to leave who are. hired actually before they arrive in New York. The result is that London is quite undersupplied. To try and meet this several ladies have formed a sort ot association, taking young girls from the East and getting them em- ployment in the West. This has been going onnow for some years. The success has not been complete. East End servants are not popular in South Ken- sington. It seemed necessary that they should pass through some medium, some civilizing lir- , fluence, before their services were quite what was wanted. Now there is another great want in West End London. It is what may be called Ladies Chambers. The num- ber of single ladies who work for their 1 livelihood has enormously increased, is enormously increasing, and cannot be coped with or kept downll Houses are dear, flats are dearer, hotels are dearest of all. It would be a charity to do also something to relieve these- toilers from their distress. And this is just what the charity that has been planned, or rather the two charities that have been combined, effects. Houses are to be taken and let off in fiats, or sets of ro6ms, and the servants are to be these East End girls. Thus to two classes of poor, the one institution will bring relief. The experiment ' begins in Carlyle-square. The house has been taken and the institution set going. Thus, all things are working from both ends of the social pole to the continentalising of London. The Duval restaurant, near the Temple, has been so great a success that others are to be started this coming winter. Soon °tie will be able to live as cheaply in bondon as in Paris. .

WARRINGTON BREWSTER SESSIONS. A sitting of the Warrington Borough Magistrates was held at the Sessions Room in Irlam-street on Tuesday morning for the purpose of granting the renewal of existing licenses, and to hear objections, should there be any, to such renewals being made. Mr. C. Broadbent was in the chair, and Alderman Davies, Councillor Greening, Mr. R. Garnett. and Mr. F. Monks were also on the Bench. There were not many people in court, more interest being at- tached to the sessional meeting to be held next Monday, when applications for fresh licenses are to be heard. The Chairman said that there had been a memorial handed to him, which he would read. It was from the ladies in connection with the Girls Club, John-st., Warrington, and read—" On behalf of the above: named organisation, we (the secretaries of the same) beg to remind your worshipful bench of magistrates of our continued efforts to lessen the idle and intem- perate habits of the working girls of our town, and ask for your help and co-operation towards this most desirable end, in reducing, as far as in you lies, their facilities for drinking. Not wishing again to appeal personally to you, we take this method of approaching you, in the hope that our very earnest petition may have due consideration from you.— Secretaries, Mary Garnett and Maria Cutting. August 24, 1886." The Chairman added that he was sure that the objects the ladies had in view had the pathy of everyone on the bench.—Mr. H. B. "kite (magistrates' clerk): There was only one con- viction during the last year, that of a licensed victualler, John Mather, for permitting betting in his house. Mather has left the house, and there is a fresh tenant, so practically there are no defaulters. --Chief Constable Hunt: The landlord of the Gun beerhouse was brought up, but he has removed, and there is another one in his stead.—No objections were offered to the renewal of any of the licences, which were granted, Mr. Hunt stating that in regard to off-licenses holders to sell beer and wine not to be consumed on the premises, there had not been a single complaint of a nature to come before the magistrates:—The Chairman: I suppose it does not follow that because there is no complaint there is nothing in any way objectionable ?—Chief Con- stable Hunt: They have all been very well con- ducted as far as I know.—The Chairman: I am -eery glad to hear that, Mr. Hunt. lam glad to see from your returns that there is a great decrease, in the drunkenness over last year.—Chief Constable Hunt; lathe number of people proceeded against there its a reduction.—The Chairman: Yes, and that is satis- factory to the magistrates andthetowngenerally— Chief Constable Hunt: 718 last year, and 574 this year.--Mr. Monks: Hard times?—Chief Constable Hunt: Pertaps, but at the same time 1 believe there is a decided improvement.—The Chairman: The question has been asked on the Bench whether theinstructions of the police as regards their mode of dealing with licensed houses of all kinds, are the same as ten or twelve years ago.—Chief Constable Hunt: Exactly the same.—Mr. White: I think the owners of the houses have become more particular. —Chief Constable Hunt: Invariably the tenants en- , gage to go into a house on a certain condition, an it has a wonderful effect on the conduct of ti house. It .there is a complaint the landlord or. landlady expect to have th go.—The Chairman: it the opinion of the police that the off-licenses ' .cted t t to an increase of drunlcenness?—Chief Cons' ,abie, Hunt: I have spoken rather strongly about tltat some time ago. but they are now well condi:, ier better than they have ever been. The fac hat there has been two convictions during th a year. ink. against persons occuping licensed premis and both are removed, goes to show what is ti usual mode with these cases.—Mr. Monks: I th' there is no doubt the houses are better conduc xed than. they used to be. The Chief Constable then presented a rt to , the magistrates, which gave a table for the hist ten years ot the number of licensed vict mailers, beer, house keepers, and off-license holders , with number- of offences committed by theM, ar Ad convicted or - dismissed, also the number brought ,up for drunken- ness and convicted or dismissed. The transfers for the year had been :—licensed Vi tuallers* 16, beer- house keepers 12, off-license h( )Iders 18, total 46. The report appended stated tha'is in 1886 there were, 87 licensed houses, and there 1' ad been one convic- ted, as compared with five 1 Ast year. There were 48 beerhouses, and one conviction was recorded. The shopkeepers' licenses numbered 71, none of whom had been summor.ed to appear before the magistrates 574 persons, as compared with 718, had during the year been charged with drunken- ness. Of these 336 males and 120 females, as com- pared with 417 males and 174 females had been con- victed. Sixty-three males and 55 females, as com- pared with 74 'males and 53 females, had been dis- missed. The figures in 1877 were: Convicted, 672' males and 113 females • dismissed, 86 males and 66 females; total 937. The totals for the last ten ;years were :-1877, 937; lB7B, 833 • 1879, 773; 1880, 776 • 1881, 706; 1882, 897; 1883,717; 1884, 651; 188 g, 718; 1886, 574. The report also stated that on Monday next applications would be made for two new victuallers' provisional licenses, and. for two full alehouse licenses. The magistrates on Monday granted the follow- ing transfers :—From Thomas W. Reynolds, Mason? Arms, Mill-street, to Mary Reynolds; James Rath- bone, Farmers' Arms, Dallam-lane, to Charlotte Rathbone : John Mather, Rose and Crown, Bridge.. street, to Alfred Woodhead ; Alfred Woodhead, Higher Angel, Buttermarket-street, to James Thomas Higginson ; William Rowe, Rifle Volunteer, Cockhedge, to Elizabeth Rowe • William Dunbob- bin Old House at Home, Friar's-green to Henry Bridge.

Gladstone, accom- panied by his daughter and Lord Acton. arrived here this evening, and at 11-40 p.m. continued his journey to Cologne, FraukfOrt, and Munich. His destination is See, where where the right hon. gentleman intends to reFnain some weeks. The length of his stay will, however, depend, Mr. Gladstone informed a representative of the Brussels press, on the state of politinel affairs, and notably on the c•Jurse events take in the East of Europe. Mr. Glacis'one ap,Ared in very good health. He travelled hence ia au ordinary carriage, preferring it to a sleeping car.

, . Ito themselves. The farmer who pays tithe is doubly taxed for the support of the poor ; he is taxed in the poor's rate, and taxed in the tithe charge; and when he is bard pressed to make ends meet, it is not to be wondered at that he should begin to think there is some- thing wrong with an ecclesiastical system which renders such a state of things possible. There is something wrong; and, whilst depre- cating any resort to violence, we trust the agita- tion against tithe rent will be continued until -English as well as Welsh farmers are brought to see that the road to reform in this matter is in the separation of Church and State.

div.p: 'TOUCH AND GO."

The death of Canon Barclay removes from Runcorn a figure no less prominent than be- loved. He was a father not only of the church, but of the people, and secured— that which should accompany old age, As honour, love, obedience, troops of friends.

John Thorpe, an Orangeman of Garston, has been sent to gaol for four months for assaulting P.C. Grimshaw, of Widnes, and a labourer named Keogh. These Orangemen must fight—at Widnes if not at Belfast. It is a pity they don't take Lord Palmerston's ad- vice, and disband themselves.

Is it too much to hope that Orangemen may in time tone down, and become members ot the Primrose League? It is true that the League, having regard to its colour and its character, has been described as a sickly and effeminate imitation of the Orange Society. But sickly and effeminate people don't as a rule assault policemen; and there would there- fore bp a little less likOlhool of their being sent to gaol,

The magistrates of Runcorn have issued an order requiring all dogs in the district to be confined or kept under control by a strap or muzzle. This has been done in consequence of a case of hydrophobia; and it would be worth the while of magistrates in other places to follow suit. They do not need to wait until some one is bitten and dies to know that it would be a good thing at this time of the year.

In another column we give soul.) particu- lars of a man named James Higham, who has been the means, during his career, of saving from drowning no less than eighteen persons. If it could be shown that he had killed as many in battle, he would be made much of, and presented most likely with a sword of honour. As it is, he is out of work, and in want of a job. Can nothing be done for him? He is a humble simple-minded man, but he is none thc less a hero.

Here is another epigram on " the gutter sparrow of politics." It is the outcome of a prize competition offered by a weekly paper An empty Exchequer, where Churchill holds sway, Is a state that can ne'er come to pass; For, whatever his blunders, it's clear as the day He can never be wanting in "brass."

It is agreeable to observe that there is at least one Tory member who is not to be led by the nose in the matter of securing Irish landlords their judicial rents at the expense of the British taxpayer. Speaking in the debate on the Address on Wednesday, Mr. Addison, 0.C., and M.P. for Ashton- under-Lyne, said: "Certainly the large manu- facturing constituency of 8,000 persons whom I represent would never consent to be taxed for a guarantee to Irish landlords."

The Reports presented at the Brewster Sessions held during the week at Warrington, St. Helens, Runcorn, and Prescot all show a decrease in convictions for drunkenness. It is suggested that the hard times have had something to do with this—that there has been less money to spend in drink. Brewers and publicans, too, are getting more careful; they are afraid of repeated convictions result- ing in loss of license. Magistrates have be- came more stringent, houses are somewhat better conducted, and there is less drunken- ness. There is still, unhappily, plenty of room for improvement.

If people would take to thinking, there would be less drinking, and to this end they should have freedom of access to books rather than bottles. This is one reason, and no small one, in favour of making the War- rington Lending Library free to the public. A contemporary suggests that the Jubilee of the Queen should be commemorated by raising sufficient money to endow a " Queen Victoria Free Lending Library." But what does this mean—a brand new Library in addition to that belonging to the ratepayers ; or the en- dowment and freeing of the present Library? Our contemporary should explain.

A CONSERVATITE CLUE TX)RWIDNES.—A meeting of Wid- nes Conservatives have decided to form a Conservative club for the town. The share capital is to amount to £2,000 in shares of £1 each. It is proposed to erect a building fitted np in the most approved style, including a hall for concerts, lectures, ice RUNCORN (406TH) STARIZ BONS'KETT BUILDING SOCIETT. —The fifth annual report states that during the past year the sum of £1,179 238 d had been received as subscriptions, and repayments amounted to £505 4s. The total income was £1,717 183 rid. The sum of .E 1,412 113 6i had been advanced on mortgage of property, making with other small sums a total expenditure of £1;505 9s 2d. Since the forma- tion of the society £4,577 us 61 had been advanced on property. I ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—On Wednesday evening, as Mr. Edwardson, mineral water manufacturer. Hibbert-street, was driving home with his wife in a trap from Prescot, the vehicle overturned, a-id the occupants were thrown out. Mr. Edwardson received serious injuries to his head, and broke one of his ankles. and he was conveyed home in an Insensible condition. He is new progressing as feyourably as can be expected. Mrs. Edwardson escaped with a severe sleeking. Tax LATE MR. HUN'TER, or WIDNES.—At the mentbly meeting of Widnes School Board, held on Thursday, under the presidency of Mr. T. S. Timmis, Mr. J. B. Imison moved " that the Board expresees its deep regret at the loss the Warrington-road Board school has sustained by the death of Mr. Hunter, the late head master, and the members beg to tender to Mrs. Hunter and family their sympathy and condolence. The Chairman seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. The other business was of a merely formal character. TEE ELECTION ou COMMISSIONERS.—The annual elec- tion of Commissioners takes place on Thursday next. The retiring members are—Messrs. R. Shaw, T. Harris, H. J. Grice, P. Speakman, and H. White. It was at one time thought that these gentlemen would be returned unopposed, but Mr. S. Yarwood, auctioneer, has declared his intention to seek the suffrages of the ratepayers Mr. Yarwood, who has been a tradesman in the town for a very long period, claims in leis address that he is fully conversant with the desires and needs of the ratepayers, and that he has the time at his disposal to carry out the duties of a commis- sioner satisfactorily. CHANGE-RINGING AT DARESBURY.—On Sunday last the Daresbury Society of Change-ringers rang for morning ser- vice at the Parish Church a :touch of 720 changes of Bob Minor in 28 minutes. The ringers stood in the following order, viz.:—Thomas Houghton, senr., treble; Peter John- son, 2nd ; Peter Hamblett, 3rd ; Charles Hartley (his first 720), 4th; Edward de Prez, sth; and Thomas Houghton, junr., tenor. The conductor was Mr. Thomas Houghton, sem, who has just completed his 39th year as clerk and 1, sexton of this parish, and who has only once been absent from his duties during the whole of that period. The office of clerk and sexton has been held in the same family from the year 1777 down to the present date, by the above-named Thomas Houghton 39 years, John Houghton (his father) 30 years, and John Houghton (his grandfather) 40 years, making a total of 100 years.

Thomas, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Jesse Autrolnie, 10 years of age, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street, on the 14th August. P.C. Barber said the defendant had his cost off, was using most fearful language', and threatening to thrash some boys. Mr. Brundrit, in ini• • posing a tne of 5s and costs, 9s 6,1, said he was tweet to see a boy of his age in such a disgraceful position. It did not augur well for his future, but he hoped this would be a lesson to him—Far a like offence Thomas Bate was fined 10$ and costs, James McTurk 5s and costs, and Wm. Dunning 103 and costs. THE SCENX PAINTER AND ms CflanacrEn.—Saninel Watson, a shabbily dressed man, was charged, at toe Rencorn Police Court on Monday, with beg:ging in Bridge-street on the 22nd inst. P.C. *Barber iroved the ease. The prisoner, who trembled violently, sai the was a scene painter by profession. It would, he added. ruin his character if the magistrates sent him to prison. Superin- tendent Hollim,sworth said nothing was known of the pri- soner. He had instructions to put begging down.—The Pri- soner : If your worships would let Ing if ; it would be a great stain on my charaeter.—Mr. Brundrit : Where do you come from ?—The Prisoner: I came from Newpeen Monmouthshire. last. I was at the Victoria Theatre there. He stated that he bad been rather unsteady lately, or he should not have been in that•position. Professionals would give him drink but they would not give money. He prom- ised to go at once to Liverpool if disci:are:ed.—Mr. Bran. lint said begging was on the increase in the county, and the ' Bench could not oYerlook the case.—He was sentenced to seven days' hard labour. RUNCORN POLICE Coterer.—On Wednesday, before Mejor rlaziehurst and Mr. James Handley the following were lined 10s aEd costs for drunkenness and disorderly conduct: —Elizabeth Smith, Mary Kennedy, Peter Rogers, and Geo. Joseph Wilson. James Portlock and John Atherton were charged with stealing 103 from a till in the shop of Isaac Saunders, grocer, I,Vnitlev Inferior, on the 20th August. The prisoners were remanded to Walton gaol until the 31st instant, when they will be brought up at Daresbnry Ses- sions—Yesterday, .before Major Hazlehurst, Maggie Jones was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour for disorderly con- duct. —Elizabeth H. Oxworth, a married woman, was charged with stealing a counterpane and two sheets, the property of John Pakeman, a labourer, living in Holloway- road. •On Thursday night Pakeman was removing his fur- niture to another house. About midnight he left in the va- cant house the rtieles mentioned for a few minut,ss and wht he returned tLy were not to be loun2, but informa- tion being given to P.C. Millington, that officer shortly afterwards found them in the prisoner's house.—The pri- soner, who is a convicted thief, said she took the articles for a "lark," was committed to the sessions for trial. • ASSAULT ON A SALVATIONIST AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, William Hodgkinson was charged with assaulting his wife, who is sixty years of age. —Mr. Knowles appeared for the complainant, and stated that she had been married to the defendant 25 or 33 years. For some years he had hablually ill-trcated her, and had lately threatened to cut her throat and marder her. AbcOet three months ago he turned his wife out, and she bad Since been dependent upon her son. She belonged to the Salva- tion Army, of which the defendant was until lately a mem- ben Formerly he was a sober steady man, but he bad taken to drinking, and now objected to her going to the meetings of the Army. On the 14th inst. complainant was taking part in a procession, when the defendant took bold of her by the neck and shook her violently, and it was Alleged would have choked her had not several members of the Army rescued her. She had been unwell since.—ln cross-examination, the complainant denied that her husband , had offered her a leg of mutton if she would only give up' walking the xreets.—The defendant, who complained that he ought to be protected from the vio'ence of his son, was ordered to find sureties, himself in £lO and two in £3, to .keep the peace for six months, or in default 14 days.

• Re:Nana: WAS'ERWORICS COXPANY.—The half-yearly meeting of the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks Company was held on Monday at the Public Hall. Mr. W. Hayes occupied the chair, and there were present Messrs.W. Whittaker, T. Bankes, James Shaw, and W. F. Salkeld. In moving the adoption of the directors report (which was pub- lished in the "Examiner" last Saturday) and the state- ment of accounts, the Chairman said the accounts were in a very satisfactory state, and the directors were pleased to he able to recommend a dividend of 4 eer cent. per annum. Probably, if they had not earned that dividend, there would have been more proprietors coming to the meeting to ask the reespn, and he took the small attendance as being com- plimentary to the directors rather than otherwise. He was pleased to say that the wages were less during the half year, although A greater amount of pumping had been done. The amount shown on the balance sheet as being due for water rates at the end of June was £638 is 101. Since then be was glad to say that £470 of that amount had bEen collected, and it was a pleasant thing to fled that their clerks were doing their duty.—Mr. Bankes Eeconded the motion, which was carried, and a dividend of 4 Per cent. was declared.. 'Votes of thanks. were accorded to the channel' and the secretary, and the meeting was adjourned for a week, as there was not a quorum present to elect the retiring direc- tors, Messrs. Bankes and Timmins.

A PITIFUL CASE AT RuNcons.—A t Runcorn Police Court. on Monday, Ambrose Bate, a boy, was charged with steal- ing a coat, value 10s, the property of Mr. Robert Garet, Greenway-road. Mary Ellen Bate, his mother, was charged with receiving the coat, knowing it to have been stolen. Mrs. Bate appeared ta feel her position acutely. Charles Gorst stated that he went to Mr. Juke's school, Irwell-lane, on the morning of the 12th August. Before the commencement of school he played outside, and placed his coat on a rail near the brickfield. When the bell rang the coat had disappeared. Mr. Marsh, pawnbroker, deposal to Mrs. Bate pawning the coat at his shop on the 17th Inst. He added that she had dealt with him for many years, and he had always found her a honest, straigtfor- ward woman, and she had never been in disgrace. Eleanor Waterworth, a married woman, of Hartley-street, said she saw the boy wearing the coat on Sunday the 15th lust, and said "You have got a coat on like Gorst's boys." He made no reply. P.S. Neild, on the 20th, went to BAte's holm in Hartley-street, and Mrs. Bate then denied that the coat was in the house. The boy pleaded not guilty, and said he found the coat on some rails. His mother also pleaded not guilty, and said when the ofifieer called she had pawned the coat, as she was very poor. Superintendent Hollings- worth said this was a pitiable case. The woman's husband was a drunken fellow. The charge against the boy was dis- missed, and that against the mother was altered to illegally pawning, and she was fined 5s and costs. THE REPRESENTATION OF NORTHIVICH —Writing to Mr. E. H. Moss, president of the Northwich Division Liberal Association. Mr, Brun- ner declares that whenever the Liberal party in the constituency had need of his services, those ser- vices should be heartily and entirely at their dis- posal.

Mn. FRENCH, Q.C., AND THE NEWTON DIVISION. —ln a circular letter just issued to the Liberal workers of the Newton Division, Mr. French, Q.C., the candidate at the recent election, says—" The fact that we are again beaten makes no difference to me. You need not think that you have worked in vain—the recent poll still shows what I have so often urged, that if the apathetic stayaways had only voted there was a margin for a majority of 1,000 in our favour. So I should venture to say to you and to all our friends—work away among the people from the local centres, and look upon New- ton as a fight in which, by pegging away, you will win the next time.—Yours faithfully, D. O'C. FRENCH."

ANOTHER PRIZE FIGHT IN LANCASHIRE.—A cor- respondent writes :—About five o'clock on Sunday morning a prize fight for £2O a side took place one and a half miles from Colne, between a Keighley pugilist and a man from Burnley.. The. combatsnts were driven to the place, acccompanied by their respective hackers. Twenty rounds were fought, and both men were much punished. After about two rounds had been fought it was evident that the Keighley man was getting the best of it, but his op- ponent suddenly hit him heavily below the left eye, and until the end of the fight planted his blows there. The time occupied. was nearly an hour rand a half, and the Burnley man was ultimately pro- claimed victor. The gang got clear away.

_ PRIMITIVE METHODIST CAMP MEETING, HAT- TON.—On Sunday the Primitive Methodists held their annual Camp Meeting in Hatton. The morn- ing and afternoon services were well attended by large congregations, the Wesleyans considerately giving up their services for the day on this account. The services were conducted by the respected cir- cuit steward, Mr. T. Rollison, of Sims Cross, Wid- nes. Short sermons and earnest addresses were given by Messrs. Malkin, Butler, Arnold, Parker, Wibberly, Swales, and Dutton, the Wesleyan preacher for the day. In the .evening a lovefeast was held in the chapel, which was. comfortably filled. This was considered to be the best Camp Meeting and lovefeast ever held at Hatton.

FAILURE OF A LOCAL TRADESMAN.-At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court on Wednesday, a re- ceiving order was granted, on a petition of the debtor himself, against Mr. E. Johnson, an alder- man of the borough of St. Helens, wholesale and retail grocer, carrying on business at St. Helens, Widnes, Runcorn, Earlestown, and Warrington. A. private meeting of the creditors was held on Mon- day. when it was unanimously agreed to accept 65. Bd. in the pound, and sympathy was expressed with Mr. Johnson in his position. .It was subsequently found that several creditors would not fall in with this arrangement, and consequently 111 r. Johnson had no other alternative than to file his petition'. At Monday's meeting the liabilities were set down at X 10,129, and the realisable assets £3,600, in addi- tion to claims which the debtor had upon certain. collieries. Mr. H. L. Riley acts for the debtor, whose public examination will take place on the ath September.

THE TRANMERE TRAGEDY.—Travis, the Sutton hotel keeper, who was convicted at the Spring Assizes at Chester, and sentenced to death for the murder of Elizabeth Platt, .at Mersey-road, Tran- mere, but whose sentence was afterwards commuted to penal servitude for life, has just been removed from Knutsford prison, Cheshire,where he has since been incarcerated, to Stafford. From there he wili proceed to one of Her Majezty's convict estab- lishments.

I%,sterday afternoon a special meeting of Widnes Local Board was held for the purpose of considering the question of the completion of the To mu Hall, cr such portion of it as might be considered advisable. Mr. F. H. Gossage pre- sided, and thre were present— Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Houghton, 'Gasket!, Heves, W. W. Gossage, D. Wright, T Handley, Cook, Mi3woed, Sadler, and Allen (clerk.)—D:. O'Keeffe moved that the town hall be erected according to the plans first submitted by the architect. He pointed out that Wilnes was a growing town, and would probably in the near future possess a charter of incorporation, and he maintained that a town hall was necessary as there were no other buildings suitable for public demonstrations. He also argued that it would be a source of revenne.—Mr. Wright seconded the motion, on the ground that it would be more economical to build ihe hall at the same time as the public offices.—Mr. Gaskell opposed the propoial. He said the condition of the alkali trade was such that no additional burden should be pet on the ratepayers of the town. The alkali trade of , Widnes was in a critical state. The Board had already in- curred expenses in connection with the public offices that . meant 31 in the on the rates —The Chairman supported Mr. Ciaskell's viaw.—Mr. Thomas Handley moved an amendment that the tower shown on the plan should be added to the public offices at a cost of £6so.—Mr. .Heyes - seconded the motion—Both motions were lost.—Tne Beard had also met to consider the adopticea of a court of arms for Widnes. hut the conSiderstion of this subject was left to the General Purposes Committee.

SERIOUS OUTBREAK OF HYDROPHOBIA IN RUN- CORN DISTRICT.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Superintendent Hollirgs;vorth asked the magistrates to issue an order under the Dogs Act requiring all dogs to be confined or kept under control by a strap or muzzle. A serious outbreak of hydro. phobia had taken place at Aston. A dog had escaped from Runcorn, got amongst a herd of (tattle on the farm of Messrs Percival, at Asten, and bitten several of the animals. Since then three cows had suffered from hydrophobia and had been destroyed. There bad also been a mad dog at Aston Grange, beloneing to Mr. Buxton, des- te ,yed. An order similar to the one for which he was now applying by the desire of the Chief Constabe, ex- pired on the sth August, and he asked for the present order to extend to the 23rd October. Similar orders were in force in the Northwich and Nantwich Divisions, and he should ask for the Daresbury District to be included next Tuesday. —Mr. Linaker, solicitor, said he was consulted by Messrs. Percival, on Thursday, with reference to these cases of hy- drophobia in cattle; and he wrote to the Home Secretary, suggesting, after giving the facts, that they should send an inspector down to inquire into the matter. On Friday he got a telegram from tne Clerk to the Privy Council stating that an inspector would be sent down with instructions to report. The Inspector (Mr. Wynn) visited the farm on Saturday, and told him (Mr. Linaker) that he had known cases of hydrophobia to develop in a dog kept under con- trol, 13 months after receiving a bite. The slog which bit these cattle left Runcorn on a Saturday night, and must have travelled by Weston and Clifton, or by Halton to Sut- ton and Aston ; and be thought it was in the interests of the public that dogs should be kept up.—Mr. Brundrit: The question is what will be done with sporting dogs? He ap- pealed to Mr. Fletcher.—Mr. Flether said he was of opinion that sporting does on land were not at large.—Mr. Brun- drit : Yes, I thick that is so.—Mr. Linaker: You might ex- cept sporting dogs.—Mr. Fletcher thought it would be in- vidious to do that, and Mr. Brundrit concurred.—Ultimately the order asked for was granted.

RUNCORN BREWSTER SESSIONS. The annual sessions for the renewal and granting of licenses in the Runcorn Petty Sessional Division, were held at Runcorn Police Court on Monday. The magia:rates on the Beach were Messrs. 4. Brundrit, chairman, James Rey- nolds, A. Thomas, Jas. Handley, and G. L. Davies. SUPERINTENDENT'S REMELT.

Superintenden-t-ifolllngswortla presented the following report :—I have the honour to submit the annual report with reference to the conduct ef the licensed victuallers and beer .retailers in this division daring the past year. There are 45 licensed victuallers, 53 beer sellers, and five others who sell off the premises; total 103, which gives an average of 185 of the population to each license. Four licensed victuallers have been proceeded against dzring the year, two of whom were convicted, being the same number proceeded against and convicted as in 1835. Two beer sellers have been proceeded against and two convicted, as compared with three proceeded against and three convicted in 1885. 156 persons have been convieted of drunkenness during the year, as compered with 199 in 1835. Superintendent Hollingworth said he bad given notice o objection to the renewal of the license of the Blue Ball Inn, Fryer-street, occupied by William Treverton. The grounds of the objection were that the house tad been generally badly conducted during the past year, that a conviction had been recorded against the holder of the license during that period, and against previous occupiers, and that the house was the resort of thieves and women of ill fame—P.C. Smith deposed that Treverton TM fined £1 and costs on the Ist of May for permitting drunkenness. Daring the past twelve months he had frequently visited the house, and on every occasion there had been thieves and prostitutes there. He did not consider the house necessary.—Cross-examined by Mr. Linaker, witness said thieves and prottitues were en- titled to refreshments if they behaved themselves. Cates of harbouring bad characters in the house had been reporttd to the Superintendent, but no proceedings had been taken.— Mr. Linaker said no doubt the evidence world not jueeify the cases being brought before the court. Dealing with the "statement that the house was not necessary, Mr. Linaker asked if there were not in the town public houses as close to each other as the Blue Ball was to those in the neighbour- hood ? Witness : Yes. There might be some closer.—Are these necessary or unnecessary for the requirements of the ptblic ? They are not patronised by such a class of people. —ln answer to further questions, witnees said he had known Treverton three years. He kept the Bird-in-Hand several years, and he was not convicted during that time,—Soper- intendent Hollingsworth asked how often there had been convictions against this house for the past three yearn 2—Mr Linaker objected to this question as unfair, but the Bench decided that it should be answerGd.—Witness could not tell the exact number of times.—Mr. Linaker contended that the Bench could not deal with the question as to whether the house was requisite or not.—Mr. Brundret : Have we no power to refuse or grant licences. It is licensing day; what are we here for ?—P.O. Smith said the " house " had been summoned for harbouring prostitutes. Respectable people would not go into the house.—Mr. Linaker said the evidence given by the police had not shown any reasonable ground to induce the Bench to refuse the renewal of the license. With reference to the contention that the house was not necessary for the requirements of the neighbourhood in which it was situated, the same argument and stronger evi- dence could be brought forward against any licenseo house in Runcorn. He asked them to deal honestly and straight- forwardly towards all landlords; and oomnasnc: at oue end

The Blue Ball was further from Any other licensed house than the majority of other public houses were from their neighbours. It was the only public house in the etreet, and if the thieves and other persons. described could net go tl the Blue Ball, they were entitled to refreshment, and vrou:d go into mere respectable houses, and spread the nuisance to other neigh- bourheads which were at present free. BRUNNER, MOliD, AND CO., LIMITED,
WINNINGTON.

The half-yearly ordinary general meeting of the shareholders of Messrs. Brunner, Mond, and Co., Limited, alkali manufacturers. Virinnington, was held at the Law Association Rooms, Liverpool, onl Thursday week. Mr. John Crosileld, of Warrington, presided, and amongst others present were—Messrs. E. Milner, Walmsley, Law, Anderson, James Simp- I son, Jones, C. M. Holland, H. Coghill, Marshall, T. ; W. Read, Galloway, Mayer, Antrobus, T. H. Fergan (secretary), &c. The notice convening the meeting!, having been read by the Secretary, the following report of the directors was taken as read, a copy having been forwarded to each shareholder:—The balance sheet and profit and loss account, certified by the auditor, and now presented;shows a balance to the credit of profit and loss account on the work- ing.of the half-year ended on the 30th June, 1886, £81,961 6s 10d, which, with the amount of £0,165 3s 3d, brought forward from the previous half-yen?, makes a total of £112,127 10s Id. The directors propose to deal with the above balance as follows: —lnterim quarterly dividend on the preference capital, at 7 per cent. per annum, paid on the 22nd May, 1886, £4,367; dividend to be now paid on the preference capital at 7 per cent. per annum, £4,651 65—£9,018 6s; interim quarterly dividend on the ordinary capital, at 20 per cent. per annum, paid on the 22nd May, 1886, £26,000; dividend to be now paid on the ordinary capital, at 20 per cent. per an- num. £26,000—.52,000; amount to be written off -patents account, £7,500; amount to •be placed to reserve fund, £10,000; balance to be carried for- ward, £33,6094s id; total, 112,127 lOs ld. The auditor retires, but is eligible for re-election.—JOHN CROSFIBLD, Chairman. The CIIAIR/SAN said the directors had very great pleasure in being able to lay before the shareholders a satisfactory balance sheet for the past half-year. It Would be seen that they had earned their divi- dend, and that they were carrying forward a larger balance than they did previously. The condition of the company was perfectly satisfactory. He moved the following resolution:—" That the directors' re- port and statement of accounts be adopted, and that a dividend be paid the holders of the preference shares at the rate of 7 per cent. per annum on the amount paid up on such shares, and that a dividend be paid the holders of the ordinary shares at the rate of 20 per cent. per annum on the amount paid up on such shares, free of income tax, for the half- year ended 30th June, 1886, less the interim dividend in each case declared on the 22nd May, 1886." Mr. 11. COGHILL seconded the resolution, which was unanimously carried. On the proposition of Mr. ANDERSON, seconded by Mr. SatesoN, Mr. T. W. Read, accountant, Castle- street, Liverpool, was unanimously re-appointed auditor.for the ensuing half-year. This concluded the business.

div.head: MR. BRUNNER AND THE NORTHWICH
div.p: MR. BRUNNER AND THE NORTHWICH
DIVISION.

A meeting of the members of the Runcorn Dis- trict Council of the Northwich Division Liberal Association was held on Thursday night to consider the draft of an address proposed to be presented to Mr. Brunner, the late Liberal candidate. The ad- dress had been previously approved of by the dis- trict councils of Winsford, Northwich, and Middle- wich. After some discussion, the address was adopted, but may be subjected to several slight alterations. It reads as follows:

"To John Tomlinson Brunner:, Esquire, J.P., Winnington Old Hall, Northwich. The Council of the Liberal Associa- tion for the Northwich Division of Cheshire desires to ex- press its unabated confidence in you as the Parliamentary candidate selected by it to do battle on behalf of true Liberalism in this constituency, and its appreciation of the valuable services you have rendered as the first member of Parliament for this division. The council recognises in yon a politician who has never swerved from the Liberal prin— ciples yon profess. No personal ambition or selfish purpose has influenced you in your public action. When Liberalism was struggling to assert itself in this county, long prior to the passing of the last Franchise Acts, it had no stronger or more earnest supporter than yourself. You have never been affected by the social and political inflaerces which have so often prevented men of wealth and position in this county declaring their Liberal allegianze. You have throughout keen firm on the question of the rights of the people as against the privileged classes, and your name more tharf any other in this constituency is associated with the cause of true and sound politica progress. The council of this asso- ciation hasnever had any reason to regret its choice of yru as its candidate. Your exposition of your political faith hae been so clear, so simple, and so straightforward as to leave no doubt on the minds cf those whom you addressed as to your political convictions. Your Parliamentary action has fully justified the confidence reposed in you. A slight defection from the Liberal party has brought about a tem- porary representation of this Division whiah the association cannot regard as satisfactory, and this council with coml.- dence asserts its belief that the candidate of its choicawill at tat) far disttnt date be returned to Westminster by the overwhelming vote of the re-united Liberals of this ad- mittedly Liberal constituency-"

fsTTENFTEB Mt-DER IND SIITCKDE.—At Salford Prilice Co-art, on Thursiay, a journeyman printer named lEfolcroft was charged attempting to murder his wife, and also with attempting to commit snici ie. Priaoner attacked his wife while she lay in bed, and stabbed her in the face and head. She escaped after a desperate struggle, and retunising with assistance found the prisoner lying unconscious on the bed; with dangerous .stabs on the throat and wrist. He wascom- mitted to the finites. RENEWED DISTURBANCES IX BrnrisT.—At Belfast, as the queen's IsLandrum were going home on Tuesday evening from -work, they were attacked by a crowd of roughs in North-street. For a time the wildest confusion prevailed, women screaming, and men ehenting. The police, however, who were present in strong force, succeeded in separating the combatants, and arrested one of the ringleaders of the attacking party, and promptly conveyed him to the central police station. At the moment of the attack, the main body of Islandmen had passed into Shankbili-road. hearinc: 1 cries for assistance from their comrades, they attempted to go back, but were prevented by a strong body of troops who weft!, drawn across the roadway.—After service on Sunday evening, in Albert-street Presbyterian Church, Belfast, situ- ated in a Catholic district, the members of the congregation were attacked with stones, groaned at, and threatenei, and most insulting epithets were shouted at them. The Rey. Hy. Montgomery, the pastor of the church, was very roughly handled, notwithstanding the presence of the military and constabulary. Occasional shots were fired between two and three o'clock on Thursday morning in Grosvenor-road a.istrict. but Shankhill-road has remained perfectly quiet since midnight. when the military- and extra pollee were withdrawn. The scene of Wednesday night's conflict is literally covered with large paving atones, which render certain streets almost impassable. All parts of the town are now quiet. Thirty persons were charged at Belfast on Thursday with rioting and attacking places. Most of the pnsoners were oemmitted for trial.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Beforo the Mayor_(llderman Harrison) and

Alderman Holmes. DESERTlON.—Frederick etansley, who pleaded guilty to being a deserter from Her Majesty's East Yorkshire Regi- ment, stationed at Beverley, was remanded to Strangeways to await an escort. CIIIIINE7 ote FlRE.—William P. Chorley was summoned for allowing his chimney to be on fire on the 13th inst. He was fined 2e 63, including costs. DItrICKENNESS—Jarres Ward was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Crown-street on Saturday evening. He said that he was a stoker, born in Montreal, and was making his way to Liverpool to try to get a boat. He was allowed to go on promising to leave the town.—John Con- way, for being drunk and disorderly in Dial-court on Satur- day night, was fined 5s and costs.—John Clare, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Brittermarket-street on Satur- day night, was dismissed.—Michael McDonough was charged with being guilty of similar offence in Fennel-street on Saturday night.—John Higgins, charged on a warrant with- being drunk and di3orderly on the 291 h March, 1884, was fined Sc and at sts.—Bridget Rooney pleaded not guilty to a charge of drunkenness and disorderly conduct in Bridge- street on the 14th inst. She was fined 2s 63, including roate.—Bridget McDonough was sent to gaol for fourteen days for drunkenness in Scotland-road on the 12th inst. Teen EDUCATION Acr.—The following persons were sum- moned fer not sending their children regularly to school : Peter Molyneux, fined 55: George Daniels, fined ss; Thos. Griffin, sent to the Workhouse.—ln the case of Jeseph Granger, his sons, George and Benjamin, were sent to the ship Clio •' and Patrick Barklev's son was sent to St. Ann's Industrial School, Liverpod.— Henry Wadsworth was charged with neglecting to send his son William Henry to school. It Was proved that the lad was incorrigible, and he was ordered to be birched.—Geerge Goodehild was charged with a like offence The lad made 36 out of a possible 101 attendances, and a letter was read from a schoolmaster in which the lad was referred to as "sue of the worst truants in the town." The parent was fined ss.—William Back- house's son net having been to school since November last, the pareet was fined Sc; and William Cliff was fined 5s in respect of hi 3 sere James. SLEET,: co Orre.—A soldier, named O'Brien, and a girl named Mabel Gandy. were charged with sleeping out on the premi ,e 3 of John Williams, farmer, Folly-lane, and doing damege to s straw stack to the amount of 24. O'Brien, who received a good character, was ordered to pa,' se, no convic- tion being recorded, and Gandy was fined 51, including CORts. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds and Mr. R. Garnett. RFFOSING TO WORlt.—Henry Smith ',NS charged with refusing to perform his task of work while a casual inmate of the vagrant ward at the Union Workhouse.—He was sent to prison for fourteen days. AS,,AULTS —Jonathan Buckley Mellor was summoned by Margaret Barlow for assaulting her, on the 21st inst. COM.. pleinant stated that she was standing speaking with a neigh- bour, and defendant commenced threatening her. He then ran at her and struck her three times. Defendant said that compiainant and her husband assaulted him, and he only defended hie:self. The case was dismissed.—Ann Machin was summoned for assaulting Mary Peers, and a cross-sum- mons charged Peers with aseaulting Machin. Mr. Yearsley appeared for Mrs. Machin, who was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace, and the cross-summons against Peers was dismissed.—Elizaheth Adams summoned Elia I Cullen for assaulting her. div.head: GREAT FIRES AT EARLE STOWN AND
div.p: GREAT FIRES AT EARLE STOWN AND
NE WTON , CHARGE OP INOENDIA.RISg.

On Sunday two sericua fires occurred near Earles • I town, one at Newton early in the morning, and the second at Vitriol-square, in the evening. A singular coincidence is the fact that both fires occurred on the premises of two marine store dealers, and the respec- tive properties of two brothers. This circumstance is rendered all the more remarkable by the fact that outbreaks of fire of small magnitude are of very rare occurrence in the district, and two conflagrations in one day is stated to be unprecedented in local his- tory. The first fire was discovered at an early hour en ,ianday morning, though it is supposed to have Lad its origin at a late hour on the Saturday night. About half-past eight on Saturday night, James Gregson, in the employ of William Ronayne, marine store dealer, High-street, Newton, noticed some smoke issuing from the building. He entered the building and discovered that a few old bags were burning. He at once extinguished ale fire with a few buckets of water, and he again locked up the place, leaving all safe. At that time Mr. and Mrs. Ronayne were away from home, but returnee about midnight, and on being apprised of what had occurred, entered the premises and satisfied themselves that everything was right. But shortly after half-pet four on the Sunday morning, his man, Gregson, who lives near the building, again noticed that the contents of the place were on lire, but on this occasion much more seriously. He gave an al am, and Ronayne, with several neighbours, were quickly on the spot. Buckets of water were carried from neighbouring houses and poured on the flames vrhicla quick- ly spread. The building was one storey high, and the roof soon caught fire. In the meantime messengers had proceeded to the gasworks of the Newton Improvement Commissioners in Crow-lane, and here a stand and hose pipes were ob- tained. These were affixed to one of the street mains, and a plentiful supply of water was thus secured. The entire building and its contents had then been destroyed, the roof and walls having fallen in. The smouldering embers were played upon for a considerable time, and the fire was pre- vented spreading to adjoining property. The damage amounted to about £430. which was covered by insurance. The cause of the fire is supposed to have bees a spark from the chimney having alighted upon the roof of the buildins, which was not in the best state of repair, or that some of the bags of the paper stored therein had spontaneously ignited. The second fire, which created an unparalleled excite- ment for many miles round, occurred on the premises of Patrick Ronavne, brother to the Mr. William Ronayne just alluded to, marine store, bag and waste paper dealer, Vitriol Square, near Earlestown. Patrick Rooayne's premises are situated near to the famous "Vitriol mountains," and within a short distance of the now unused Sankey Paper Mill, and the more widely celebrated Sankey Sugar Works. One of Mr. Ronayoe's speculations is the purchase of the many thousands of bags and baskets in which raw sugar is I brought to the Sankey Works, and these he had stored in an open yard adjoining his premises. The " baskets " are manufactured of Indian cane of a light rushy nature, and having been used to convey the raw sugar from India they were of a highly inflammable character. These baskets, which numbered scores of thousands, were piled to the height of five or six yards, and in some places higher, and occupied an area measuring nearly a hundred yards by over fifty yards. Shortly after half-past seven on Sunday night the discovery was made that these baskets were on fire. The alarming news spread with lightning-like rapidity, and crowds began to flock to the neighbourhood. Almost in the course of a few minutes the fire was known all over Eerles- town, while as the flames spread in all directions, the con- flegration was seen a considerable distance around. Is the meantime, hewever, several willing workers were putting forth efforts to prevent any destruction which it was possi- ble to avert. Police-constable Hunt, stationed at Earlestowr, and Mr. Herbert Thompson, of Sankey House, were mostly prominent, and the officer mentioned secured commendation from the many thousands of specta- tors by his untiring energy. Mr. Thompson also rendered conspicuous help, and their efforts were supplemsnted by P.S. Commins (Newton) and several constables, who were I attracted to the spot from surrounding districts by the 'flames, which about nine o'clock shot up to a tremendous heieht in the air. The entire' neighbourhood was lit up, and many hundreds if not thousands of persons were at- tracted from Haydock, Ashton, and Golborne. The universal impression for miles around was that the extensive Sankey Suer Works or the Viaduct Waggon Works, a few hun- dred verde away from the scene, were on fire. ' The rapidly disappearing baskets were situated in a hollow at the foot of the "Vitriol Mountains," and being in an open spot, the assembled crowds had a splendid view of the fire. To the sightseers the spectacle was a grand one. For an area of about 50 yards square there was nothing but one seething mass of flame, which, towering many yards high over head, threw out an intense heat, and rendered a reflection visible even so far away as St. Helens, Warrington, and other sur- rounding places. The efforts put forth were chietis directed to prevent the destruction of a portion of the baskets, and this was success- fully carried out by cutting a passage through the immense pile of unburnt baskets. This was done under the direction of Constable Hunt. Commencing a few yards from where the flames were raging the baskets were thrown on one side, and a pissage of about five yards was quickly made through the stack. Ibis confined the limits of the conflagration and from ten o'click danger of further damage was at an end. Shortly after the outbreak was dis- covered information was conveyed to the members of the Viaduct Works Fire Brigade, and about a dozen men, dressed in their uniform, were present during the evening. They obtained the Viaduct Works hose, and laid a hose pipe from a stand-hydrant in the Works to the scene of the fire, where water was poured on the flames. These operations were carried out under the direction of Mr. Samuel Barrow, Captain of the Fire Brigade. The flickering embers con- tinued to burn until about midnight, when they burnt themselves out. The baskets were piled near a wooden fence which divided them from the branch railway to Messrs. Richard Evans and,Co's coal wharfe on the Sankey canal, and this fence was also partially destroyed. Many thousands of the baskets were burned to ashes, but, it is stated, the actual damage only amounted to about £l6O. Fortunately this is covered by insurance. The police authorities subsequently made diligent enquiries into the origin of the fire, and, as a result of their investigations, a boy named Barlow was taken into custody on Monday night, when, it is stated, he acknowledged having set the baskets on fire, though, he added, it was done accidentally.

div.head: CHARGE OF INCENDIARISM.
div.p: CHARGE OF INCENDIARISM.

Mr. W. F. Gooch, J.P., attended at the Newton Town Hall, on Tuesday, when Alfred Barlow, 13 years of age, re- siding at 20, Booth-street. Earlestown, was brought up in custody on a charge of "having at Newton, on Sunday the 22nd just, maliciously set fire to certain sugar baskets, the property of Ratrick Ronayne, whereby damage to the amount of .£l6O was done." P.S. Commina said the pri- soner was charged with wilfully setting fire to the baskets in an open yard in Vitriol-square, about 7-45 p.m., under the following circumstances. The prisoner, in company with several other boys, were playing on the " Vitriol mountains," near to where the babkets were stored by Mr. Ronayne, a marine gore dealer. He was known to have had some matches in his possession, and he went to one of the baskets lit a match. and then lit the basket. He after- wards returned to his comrades and said they were going to haye a fire, qualifying the expression with a strong ad- jective. Immediately afterwards the basket blazed up and the result was that nearly all the baskets in the vicinity were consumed, with the exception of a portion saved by the exertions of several men of the district. The fire was of a very serious nature, and was seen for miles around. He (P.S. Commins) in company with several constables were attrac- ted there, and it was not until half-past twelve that the fire was got out. After a good deal of inquiry on the pre- vious day (Monday) he, in company with P.C. Hunt, appre- hended the prisoner at 0-45 p.m., and he was taken to the police statioo, where he admitted that he had set the baskets on fire, but lie said he did not do it wilfully. He said he lit a match and dropped it and the baskets took fire. He (P.S: Cemmins) wished to ask for a remand until the Petty Sessions, to ba held at the Town Hall on Saterday.—Pri- soner's father, who was present in court, asked that his son millat be admitted to bail.—Mr. Gooch, J.P., decided to re- mand. the prisoner as asked. and said he would be admitted to bail in one surety of £50.-----Mr. Thomas Molyneux, of Market-street, Earlestown, informed the mazistratos that he was willing to act as surety for the boy, who was formerly one of his e4unday sesolars. He (Mr. Melyntire) was very sorry to see him in that position.—The boy was afterwards liberated.
