div.head: DETERMINED SUICIDE AT NEWTON
div.p: DETERMINED SUICIDE AT NEWTON
LAKE.

A determined suicide was ccomrnitted in Newton Like on Thursday about noon. John Shaughnessy, a labourer, lately living at Croft, was observed near Old Pin-fold, off Southworth-road, and which ad- joins the lake, about nine o'clock in the morning, and he subsequently-lay down on the grass as if he was sleeping. Two hours afterwards an acquain- tance named King met him coming from the direc- tion of Lowton village, and deceased was again go big towards the lake. At twelve 0?elock another man named Francis Edward Clarke residing at Manchester, was walking along Southworth-road when he saw some clothes lying on the grass near the side of the water. He afterwards saw deceased in the water and making attempts to hold his head beneath the surface. Clarke called out to him, and then took off a portion of his clothing and entered the lake with the view of bringing Shaugh- nessey to the side. The latter had then disappeared, however, and Clarke was unable to find the body. Information of the occurrence was con-eyed to Newton by a girl named Baxendale, and P.C. Spencer appeared on the scene. A boat was ob- tained, and Mr. John Lane, with grappling hooks, rowed to the spot. Shortly afterwards the body was recovered, but the poor man was quite dead. The body was removed to the Legh Arms to await, the inquest.

div.head: POLICE ASSAULT AT HOUGHTON
div.p: POLICE ASSAULT AT HOUGHTON

GREEN, At Liverpool County Sessions, on ',Tuesday, before Mr. Hugh Perkins (chairman), Mr. Eckersley, Mr. James, Tinsley. and Captain Withington, Thomas Flaherty and Michael Flaherty, who had been com- mitted from Warrington, were put up for trial on a charge of assaulting Police-Sergeant Barnes, at Houghton Green, on the Ist lust, and Thomas Flaherty was also charged with causing bodily harm to P.C. Stead at the same lime and place. Mr. Welshy was the prosecuting counted, and fully stated the circumstances of the case which have already beau reported in our columns. The principal allegation was that prisoner tore open the cheek of Stead, who was severely tnaltreated. Sergeant Barnes, P.C. Stead, John Ryder, and William HOWAtii, farmers, were called as witnesses. Dr. Crimmins, M.P. (instructed by Mr. EL J. Longton, solicitor, Warrington'', was counsel for the prisoners, and denied that they were to blame for the affray. The police, he said, brought it about through their own conduct. He stated that prisoners, with Patrick Flaherty, were standing quietly talking together at about half-past ten on the night in question, on the road leading from Houghton Green to Winwick, near Jacks- on's farm, where Patrick Flaherty was working- Some burning wood was thrown towards them from the garden, of a cottage near one piece coming over the hedge on to the road near them. Stead came up and asked Flaherty what he was throwing that fire up for, and he replied denying the charge, and offering to submit to a search for fireworks or matches. Stead roughly ordered them off, and streak with his stick Thomas Flaherty, who struck back in his own de- fence, when &teed closed upon him, and they fell to the ground, Stead uppermost. Stead's wound was then caused accidentally in the struggle. Dr. Cornmins denied that Thomas Flaherty assaulted Barnes, but simply did his best tb get out of the officer's hands. As to Michael Flaherty, he committed no assault, but on the contrary was struck by Birnes; and then he retired from the scene. The statement W 55 spoken to by witness Patrick Flaherty, the third, man present, and John Hewitt, a lad of Houghton Green, gave evidence that he threw the burning wood in question. The prisoners were raid to be men of good character by their employer,.Mr.nter Longton, of Winetick, and others —The jnry fannd both prisoners not guilty, and they were accord- ingly discharged.

div.head: TERRIBLE ACCIDENT IN SINT,' FIELD. • EIG4IT CHILDREN KILLED.
div.p: TERRIBLE ACCIDENT IN SINT,' FIELD. • EIG4IT CHILDREN KILLED.

On Wednescfisy afternoon, by the falling of a wall in Neadotr-street, Sheffield, eight children were hilled and one in;ifred. The wall formed part of the boundary of' the works of Messrs. Daniel Doncaster and Sons, steel manufacturers. It was built in 1872 as the outer aide of an iron and steel warehouse where bars of iron weighing altogether several hundred tons were stacked: About four o'clock the weight proved too powerful, and the wall, to a length of 25 yards, fell into the street. Behind it came thousands of bars of iron, weighing several hundred tons, the whole be- ing piled up across the street many feet high. At the moment of the accident several children were playing beneath the wall. They were caught by the 7Svicks and iron, and crushed to death in an instant. Hardly anyone was about at the moment, and for a long time It was uncertain how many lives had been lost. A gang of 150•Imen immediately set to work to remove the ddlti,l4, but it was seven o'clock before the first body was recovixed. It was that of a child crushed beyond all recognition, the head being completely 116.ttened, and'identification was only arrived at by the character of the clothing. One by one six more bodies were recovered. At nine o'clock work ceased for the night,. The following are the names of the five children whose remsins have been identified :-- Martha Armitage, aged 10 years, and John Armitage, aged two. children of John Armitage, 9 Court, Hoyle- street ; Henry Crisp, aged two, parents living in Adelphi-street 7. William Cullingworth, aged three years, son of Henry Cullinstworth, of the Burnt Tree Tavern, Hoylt-street ; and Gilford Andersoa; aged seven, son of Septimus Anderson, Burnt Tree Lane. The disaster has occasioned great excitement in Shef- field,' and universal sympathy is expressed towards the friends and relatives of the killed.

The work oi removing the debris of the wall and the fallen iron bars at the scene .f the terrible disas- ter at Sheffiild was resumed by a number of, Messrs. Doncaster" employ 69 and others shortly after five o'clock on Thursday morning. Another body, that of Herbert Crookes, was found about eight o'clock, dreadfullyinjured. The father, who had been among the crow&of onlookers, was only able to identify it by the peen:istr description of his little lad's shirt. By half-past nine the road was sufficiently clear to show that the bodies of all those killed had been recovered. It is exceedingly fortunate that the accident did not happen two hours later than it did, otherwise the loss of life would have been very heavy, as the path run- ning along the wall was nightly the rendeavons of a hundred or more children.

div.head: WELSH TITHE RENT AGITATION. EXTRAORDINARY PROCEEDINGT-S.
div.p: THE WELSH TITHE RENT AGITATION. EXTRAORDINARY PROCEEDINGT-S.

A remarkable series of scenes have been enacted during the week at Llanarmon -y-Yale. a remote little village perched among the Denbighshire hills, and situate about equal distance from tlte towns of Mold and Ruthin, in North Wales. On July 16th the rector's rent audit was held at the village inn, Lien- armon, and little or no money was paid by the far- mers. After the usual notice had been sent the tithe payers summoned a meeting and appointed a deputa- tion, consisting of Messrs. John Jones and Francis Beech. farmers, to wait upon the rector, the Rev. Evan Evans, to demand a reduction of 25 per cent. IThe interview was very stormy, and the deputation left the vicarage somewhat hurriedly. The result of the confevence was reported to a meeting of farmers,, and it was resolved not to attend the rent audit, the farmers declaring that if the rector required his !tithes he shonld fetch them as the tax gatherer fetched' the ,taxes. This phase of the strained relationship ! did not long continue. Mr. 0. Edwards, solicitor, having been instructed by the rector to distrain for the amount of tithes due to him, a second meeting of farmers was held, at which it was decided to send a ifinal deputation to the rector demanding a return of ,to per cent. on all tithes. Accordingly. Messrs. ;Roberts and John Lanton, farmers, -visited the vicar- age. and again saw the Rev. R‘s-an Evans. They ; represented that as hill farmers they were mainly I engaged in cattle breeding, and that now prices had fallen so low they were ansolutely unable to pay the tithes in fulL The rector listened to their applica- tion, an then inquired why they sought relief from him—why not apply to the land- lords. The tithes were light enough now, and he could not and would not grant any abatement. The deputation again reported to the tithe payers, and on this occasion a majority of the farmers re- solved to pay no tithes whatever. The meeting broke nu amid some excitement, and a letter of defiance was despatched to the vicarage. On August 17th three bailiffs from Chester, a head bailiff and two 1, under bailiff., drove from Ruthin to Llanarmon to I dietrain for the tithes. Their reception was anything , ! but cordial. The farmers armed themselves, and ! resolutely refused to permit them to enter their houses. The bailiffs, however, threw down their ' !write, and at each farm formally diatrained on e.ertain cattle. At the farms of Mr. jones and Mr. Francis Bee oh some cows were seized. Mr. Beech occupies about eighty acres of land, and the amount for which. the distraint was levied was £.9 los and expenses. At Mr. Jones's farm the amount due on forty-eight acres of land is between £8 and 4. The usual five (lays grace was allowed in which to pay the money, and on Saturday the time expired, but in the mean- while the bailiffs had hurriedly shaken the dust of Llanartnon from off their feet. The bltter feeling' which has been aroused at Llanarmon is illustrated by the fact that tenants paying sums as small as 25 in tithes absolutely decline to do so. In all there are 26 farmers and occupiers who have refused to pay tithes under any circumstances. Others have agreed to pay if the rector does not also insist on the pay- ment of the lezal expenses incurred. A few others again. have paid the tithes, and these have been sub- jected to nightly serenades of an unpopular character from the angry villagers. It is gleefully announced 'that the rector has been unable to obtain the services ! of a Welsh auctioneer to oonduct the sales.

Although on Monday the time expired under the writs, Mr. Whaley, auctioneer, of Chester, whose ser- vices bad been secured, did not deem it advisable to proceed with the sales. The unruly and turbulent spirit displayed by the colliers would undoubtedly have led to violent proceedings had Mr. Whaley ap- peared. He states that the farmers themselves would off or no opposition to the sales, as they are anxious to enter their protest only against paying tithes to the church. It is the colliers who constitute the rough element. Three of his. bailiffs have been so alarmed that they have returned to Cheater. The vicar declares that the conduct of the anti-tithe agita- tors has been meat violent. When they visited him at the rectory they shouted "Woe upon you ex- tortioners and robbers," and otherwise insulted him. At Llandegla, near Llanartnon, some very riotous proceedings occurred on Monday evening. An anti- tithe meeting was convened and attended by most of , the farmers in the district. Mr. Davies, of -Manches- ter, staangly urged those present to preserve a peace- ful attitude and to endeavour to accomplish their ()ads by constitutional means. A reeolutiora was unani- mouely passed in this spirit. During the proceedings 50, quarrymen from Bwlchgwytn, who had struck work on purpose to attend the meeting, marched in, and they were received with cheers. Trp to this mo• ment everything had passed off quietly. Shortly afterwaras, however, a conveyance, containing two fresh bailiffs from Chester and a clerk from the office of Mr. Edwards. solicitor, Ruthin, drove into Lien- d.egla. Mr. Edwards's clerk was follawed into the yard by Mr. Beech, a farmer, whose goods had been distrained upon. Hero one of the quarrymen struck I him 'a heavy blow with a cudgel on tlie back of the head, and he had to run to the house. Mr. Beech's son called upon the crowd to desist from further vio- lence, and it was then ascertained that he was em- powered on behalf of the Vicar to offer the farmers that if they would pay the tithes ho would withdraw the writs and pay all the costs. The' farmers discussed the-offer, and came to the unanimous determination to refuse it. They wanted a reduction of 26 per cent., as originally demanded. In the meantime the crovvd, espied the conveyance which contained the two. bailiffs and the driver. A hovel of execration was raised, and the mob started off ia pursuit of them.. The horse was lashed into a r allop, but by running across the fields the quarrymen intercepted the party and a severe struggle took place. The bailiffs were badly hustled and then beaten, with clubs. The horse was again whipped up, and, the discomfited bailiffs eventually escaped to Llandeght.' The tithe-rent dispute betwaen the Rector of Mau- armon and the farmers of that parish remaa'naun- sealed. Major Cornwallis West, who represents the division in the House of Gammons, has arrived on the scone and undertaken tke part of mediator. The colliers and quarrymen of the district have announced their intention of supporting the farmers, arid have resolved to do all they possibly can to prevent the threatened sales taking, plasm. On Thursday two cows belonging to vito of the 1 farmers were sold, but in each case the animals were hougat by the owners. The agitation against the payment of what the farmers are said to regard as "an iniquitous impost" appears to be assuming serious proportions. At the conclusion of the second sale on Thursday an indignation meeting, attended hy farmers from all parts of the Vale of Clwyd, was held in the farmyard. Several of the speakers stated that in the districts they came from notice had been given to the clergymen that in future no tithes would be paid, one farmer remarking that no less than 150 of his neighbours had taken this course.

THE COTTON TRADE —The Bolton Master Spinners' Association on Wednesday resolved to join the o!dham and Ahton masters in enforcing a reduction of wages of five per cent., provided the masters in the three districts repre- senting three-fourths of the spindles make an agreement to that cff -et. The leaders of the operatives assert that should the masters enforce the reduction a strike will result. •

div.p: THE LIBERAL PARTY IN NEWTON DIVISION.

DuT,l.7',ig the present week the Liberal party of the Newtoti.Division, under the auspices of the Liberal' 300, have 'wen taking steps to place themselves on a better footing, in view of any future elections in the constituemey. On each of the three elections, and more particularly in the cases of the last two, the Liberals fought at a serious disadvantage, in having no candidate raund whom ta rally until their opponents had loudly prvtiaimed their champion, and almost completed their arrangernents for the polling. This has been keenly felt to b a drawback to the success of .a Lineral candidate, and it is expected that the present efforts will to a great extent nmedy the former state of affairs. T;) considor this question a meeting of the Earles,t ,wn and Vulcan portion of the Liberal "300" was held in the Earlestown and Mstrict Liberal Club, Fairclough-street, on Tues:tay evening, and there, was a large attendance. A resolution was passed that they con- sidered it necessary that stepe should be taken to have a Liberal candidate in the field at the earliest possible trio. mexl, ready to commence a campaign in the division when- ever such might be deemed necessary. It was also decided that this should be raged upon the Liberal "300." A meeting of the latter body, prinepally for business purposes, was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, on Tnnrsday evening. The meeting was largely attended, and Mr. G.- W. Rawlins (Kaintrill), presided. The matter was discussed, and ulti- mately left in the hands of a sub-committee. Subjects of a purely business character were' afterwards considered.

EIGHTEEN LIVES SAVED BY A WARRINGTON MAN. James Higham, a glass bottle maker, who-lives in Mill-lane, Bank Quay, Warrington, has gained dis- tinction' by rescuing from death by drowning_ no less a number than eighteen persons. Higham is a• man of unassuming manners, and does not seem. to attach very great importance to the noble efforts he has made in saving life. He has, however, plenty of pluck, and a spice of daring in his com- position:. about thirty-five years of age. In conversation with a representative of this journal, on Wednesday, he gave a few particulars of his achievements.. He appears to be of an amphibious nature, and cars scarcely remember the time that he firsttound himself able to swim. " When I. first commenced swimming," he says, "I should be about six years old. I learned in the Mersey, at Bank Quay, where I was bred and born." The propensity of Higham, when a youngster, to be in the water, •in season or out of season, provoked the wrath of his father, who frequently ordered him away from ' the bank of the-river, and, if a surmise may be per-, milted, no doubt often emphasised his instructions in an unpleasantly practical manner. When about eight years old, Higham saved the life of a young- ster named Jim. Potts who was of an age similar to himself, and ams•dr4a-ning in the Mersey. A lad of the name. of William Douglas was the second re- cipient of his favour, "'Next," Higham remarked, 'in a business-like manner, "was a chap named 1 Joseph 'Wainwright,. and I saved the same person ! again in - the year following. He would be 1 about eleven years old, and I should be ! about the saane,. Then there was Jim By- lands in the-• Sankey Canal. Jim would !be about eight years old. :Next to him came :fed Greenali. He would. be about thirteen or four- teen, and was pulled out ofahe Mersey. Alf More- ton, thirteen or fOurteen years- of age, was drown- ing in a brickfielit near. where Cartwright's bottle house is built; I; jumped in and two more tied their scarves, and :so we pulled him out. The next one was William Webb,.in. Canines Hole, Irisht•own, Dublin. I was then about twenty years old and Webb about eighteen.. He was working in the bottle-house at the same- trade as me, and when I 1 saved him he was learning.ta, swim. It's a curious !thing, but he had two brothers drowned, one of 'em ! at Manchester, and we thought holv funny it would I have been if he had been: drowned as well. The next was :Margaret Johnson,, about six or seven years; she was got out of th& canal at Buttermilk Bridge... Then there was the- wife of a sergeant at Dublin, where I was working.. Me and some mates were on a .wall and a chap: came up and said Can any of you chaps swim.' Laays can,' and then he says 'there's a woman out yonder (in Dublin Bay), and can't' get back?. L pulled off and I went in. .It was a bit lumpy in the bay and, he said go to her and I'll send a boat for her: I got to her and held her up with my arms as•vaell as I could, and I told her she must put her two arms at the back of my neck. and she could kick as hard as she liked. Just as the boat came to us, we- were both about giving up, and I had a tight struggle as it was. The husband gave me 10a- when I landed and a tumblerful of whisky. That's, all ever I got. Harry ! Groves—l gothim out of the.•Merseyhere. He would be about nine-years old. Cant think of any more.' IThis narrative was given -with. great simplicity of manner, and in reply to repeated questions Iligham, who is not a tutored mai4.having kept no dates or particulars,- and consequently having nothing but memory to rely on. When ha' has succeeded in say- lag a life, ha seems to have-thought no further about the matter. "The oldest pemon I recollect saving," he continued, "was a forge-chap out of the canal, and the one in Dublin Bay was the next to my thinking.. I used to get 'emout and take no notice; never bothered my head about 'am. It was touch and go with that there fellows Moreton. A fellow named Jack Rylands helped me out when I was drowning :myself one day.. I had had a longish swim, and the tide was running. I was tired, and gave up about four yard's from the side. I was only a little chap then. That •in Dublin Bay was the toughest, struggle, and the-nextt was with the ice at the brickJield. It has been-hard pulling against the tide in the Mersey, and running from here to But- ! termilk Bridge and then juanping in with my 1 clothes an. Moreton was-sacapital swimmer, but he could not:make- a way to the side because of the ice, which he kept breaking with his hand. I I jumped; in, and two others got us both out. with their handkerchiefs,. William Lee, six years old, I saved on Thursdayalhaa in 'Sankey Brook, at a place where it is rather chop All us lads in Bank Quay!were like ducks; we could swim as soon as we aatra; hatched. Mr.:. Bolton, Bank Quay Glasi wrork, used to be a terrible one for swimming, and got sports up amongst!! his men. He gave me a book,ta learn swimming,but I took no notice of it andlused to learn myself.. I never took a prize. Werused to go to the. water and play 'about, and when-the tide came in. we would go to Walton !Arches. I have learned a good many to swim. I nassEto get chaps on ray back, knock them off in the•middle of the river, and then take them to the side! when they Well 3, tired."—" You have not Ataished this sort of work yet? "—" There's no tel- ling;. I may have one or two More this summer. Sometimes they stickZke leeches. I never had any difficulty in knocking them off, but I had to knock one off in the river here. I was getting tired. I 'turned,on my back' nut my hands against his sto- mach, and knocked &irn away. When I recovered myself I tackled hi=l: again and fetched him out. That, and the one in Dublin Bay were the only times when I was fairly tired. When I got Lee out he; lay on his back about a foot deep in the . water, as stiff as a,: crutch, as though he could not sink." It may be mentioned that Ingham has in his house a framed certificate . given by the Royal humane Society, and dated 16th October, 1877. It is awarded him for saving Margazet Johnson out of the Sankey Canal, on a Sunday afternoon, at luttermilla Bridge. A clergyman of the neighbour- hood, and his wife, at the time interested them- selves in the matter, and it was mainly through their instrumentality that the society became ac- quainted with Higham's exploits and awarded the certificate. It was desired to make the presenta- tion publicly, but to this Higham objected on the ground of diffidence. The people he has saved have mostly been the children of poor people, and the lOs given him in Dublin seems to be the only pecuniary reward that has attended his exertions, He has for some time been out of work, and seems anxious to pick up a jo:b.

THE CITY. OW Ripos.—The one thousandth anniversary of the foundation of the city of Ripon and the jubilee of the See of Ripon are being celebrated this week. The procee.l- - began on Wednesday, and were taken part in by Cie Archbishop of York. the Bishop of Ripon, the Marqt;is, of Ripon, the Bishop of Chester, the Bishop of Durham, and others.

TERRIDLE FOREST FIRES.---Accounts received of the forest fires about Milwaukee (United States) shove that several towns in the vicinity were completely consumed by the flames. The fires wbitzb were raging in the Mara- thon and Clark Counties communicated to Spencer and Colby. The former olace was soon reduced to ashes. The buildings consumed were churches, school-house, the greit wood turning factory, saw mills, depot, and valuable reel- denees. Two hundred thousand dollars worth of ploperty In Spencer Town alone was destroyed. The fires were raging in the outskirts of Chipperwa Falls, and the citiz.ens were in readiness to fieht with the flames. Spencer town has a population of i,OOO, inhabitants, most of whom were rendered homeless. The district affected is the heart of flourishing country. The information was dated on the 9th inst. Many other places were expected to fall into the terrible embrace of the flames. The cause of the fire was the dry weather experienc.ed, not a drcp ol rain falling for many weeks.,

div.p: THE ORANGE RIOT AT WIDNES; • POLICE PROCEEDINGS. On Monday at the Widnes Police Court, before Ittnesrs. F. H. Gossaee ant John Brock, John Thorpe, labourer, Wood-strnet.'Gerston, was charged on a warrant with er saulting Police-constable Orimsbaw, and damaging his felt hat to the amount of ss; and also with assaulting Bernsen Keogh, Of Grenfel-street. Widnee., Mr. QuiMan) (Liver- ; pool) appeared for the defence.—Police-conetable Grimsnatv said that on the evening of the 14th inst., at about tevee o'clock, be stood at the end of Grenfenstreet, in plain cloth' watching a proceseion of Orangemen, most of whom bad come from Gersten. and when they were near the OrifFee Hotel he saw a roan rueh• into the midst of the band. 00 coming out of the band the man was followed by .two bands" men and severe.' members of the procession. The man ran on to the waste ground, and when the men were about eight yards from where witness was standing, one of the reef) kicked the runaway on the ankle, knocking him to the ground. Witness went to where the struggle was taking place, and with the aid of the crowd separated the men. A* witness was going away the prisoner made a rush at him, and struck him a violent blow on the right side of the head- 'His hat was knocked einn.and he reeled and fell 'to the ground, where Tleorpe kicked him several times in the ribn,' , He managed to get upon hie feet and ran towards his ova door to put on his uniform. He was again etruck several times by the crowd, but at last succeeded in bolting the door and putting on his uniform. On coming out and go- ing round the cerner he again saw the prisoner, who set up-- lon him again, knocking :Am down and kicking him. 116 followed the crowd to the London and North-Western i Station, wnere he saw the prisoner, whom he identified, and' Inspector Wood had him taken into custody. In reply IP Inspector Wood, witness saki his injuries were such that be' had to leave duty, and heeves scarcely yet fit to do in-- Police-constable Liptrot said he saw the assault, and he could identify the prisonar.—Bernard Keogh, labourer, said, he heard the prisoner say nee would give Grimshaw police officer, and he then knocked hitu down. Prisoner also as- saulted him (witness), kicking him about the ribs.—Ellen Keogh, Annie Muldoon, an Gritnshaw gave corroborative evidence.—Mr. Quilliam called James Burrows, of 5, Rue- eel-place, Garston, who raid he was with the prisoner in . the procession and never left his side. It was not true 00. , he assaulted anyone.—Ptieoner was sent to gaol for three months for the assault on Glitnshaw, and one moat!) for . the assault on Keogh. FIFTEEN GARS'FON MEN SUMMONED. At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, before Mr. H. S. Hall and Mn F. H. Goesage, fifteen men, mostly members of the band connected with the Garston True Blue Orange Lodge, were summoned for having, on the 14th inst., coal- mined a breach of the peace by marching along certain atreets in Widnes with a nand of music playing party tunean brandishing a stick, shouting and making a disturbance to toe alarm divers of the Queen's subjects. The names of the defendants are :—George _Richard Edge, John Wain' wrigbt, William Grimeee• J. G. Woodtborpe, John Yater Thomas Sparkee, Frederick Dean, Hamilton Mason, Josenla Grimes, William Woodthorpe Henry Jenkineou, George Fitton, William Brown, no3eph' Bartoe, and Francis Jacin• son. Mr, Swift (St. lle:ens) appeared for the police; MT Shepherd Little (barrister, Liverpool.) defended Edge, and , Mr. Quilliatu (Liverpool) the other defendants. The case against Indge was first taken, but he declined to plead.--t Mr. Swift, in opening the case, said up to tbe present the Orangemen and Catholics bad managed to live quietly to- gether in Widnes, though they bad each had their respective gala days and anniversaries. It therefore seemed to the police of Widnes that irruptions of Oraegemen from Garston or any other neighbouring town should be prevented. The defendant Edge was drum major of the Garston Orange Band. On the evening of the 14th inst. a party of Orange- men arrived from Garston. There were about forty members Of the band, who were dressed in blue sailor suits, with white facings, and they also wore broad brimmed yellow straw hats. Lefendant carried a pole about six feet in lengths which had the Orange emblems, a crown and a bible, on the top of it. The bendarrived at the London and North- Western station, and accompanied by about 200 followers, who wore Orange favours and lilies, they walked on towards Farnworth, and as they passed the Widnes Police Station the band played the "Boyne Water." Nothing more was seen of then) by the police until about seven o'clock ;when the band returned from Farnworth by way of Simms Cross. NVhen near the Board Schools a great disturbance took' place. Inspector Wood prteeeded to the spot and saw the Orangemen in their otiginal force, with a number of spiv* pathisers. In fact a large crowd of about 2,000.,0r 3,000 ! people had assembled, many of whom were hostile to the lOrangemen. The defendant Edge was seen to gesticulate I very violently, and brandish his staff, and heard to.make • great noise. •Araegemen from Garston were fighting Wici- !'nes people, policemeinwere attacked and stones were thrown. The police got between the rival parties, but not before a con- , siderable number of people were injured and damage done. Ultimately the police got the band to the railway station, but even there stones were thrown from their train, and stones were thrown in reply from the streets below. The Orangemen as they left the station were good enough to promise the Widnes people that they would visit them on future occasion, and they went off shrieking ".3oyne "and " King William." The first witness. called was ! Inspector Wood, who said the defendant walked through the streets in the afternoon in a very defiant attitude, and in such a way as to arouse the feelings of the opposite natty: In the evening he saw de- fendant waving the pole he held, as if he were inciting the Orangemen to attack Ike Widnes people. For about five minutes there was a regular riot. He (Inspector Wood) was much alarmed for the safety of the town. A number of windows wete broken, and the inhabitants were in • great fear as to what might happen.—P.Cns Grimshaw and Middleton gave evidence as to the violence used by the Oraagemen.-1701:. Little argued that nacasa bad been made out, and asserted that no judge had ever yet held that an Orange band was not entitled to march through any part of England playing party tunes and wearing emblems.—Supt. Barker stated that in April defendant was bound over at Islington (quarter sessions) in his own recognizences of £2o' te keep the peace for six months for an exactly similar of- fence committed at Garston.—The defendant was ordered to be bound over, himself in £4O, and two sureties in £2O, ta keep the peace for six months, or go to gaol for two months- -John Wainwright, William Grimes, J. Woodthorp, John Yates, Wm. Sparkes, and Frederick Dean were also boauct over in sureties of £2O to keep the peace for six months', er go to neat for a montb.—lu the remainder of the case Supt. B7aner agreed to withdraw the summonses on pa,ypaeut of ct. st.s.

Not to be beaten—Oil-cloth. Strange proceeding—Employment of contractors to enlarge buildings. Why is a prudent banker like a bicyclist P—Because he balances carefully and prepares for a run. Too BASHFUL.—A modest youth was he—He kissed her finger-tips; she softly said, "Ah me! Why was I born with lips ?" In newspaper wedding reports every bride is beautiful. It is a mystery, says a rejected one, where all the plain married women come from. He, tenderly: And what do you think of the engage- ment-ring I sent you, Gertie ?—She, delightedly: Oh, it is beautiful—in fact, the handsomest one I ever had given me! NEW MATRIMONIAL WEAPON.—"-My wife is practising with dumb-bells!" proudly exclaimed a -w,ould-be athlete. "Do you find them any softer, than flat-irons ?" queried a wag who overheard the remark. . UTILISING THE DEAR DEPARTED AS AN ADVERTISING MEDIUM.—The following epitaph may be seen in the cemetery of a parish in the environs of Paris—" Here lies Madame N—, wife of M. N—, master blacksmith. The railing around this tomb was manufactured by her husband." A vulgar nouveau riche was lunching with a new acquaintance whose little boy was at table. During a pause in the conversation the enfant terrible spoke up. "I wish I was you." "Do you my little boy? And why do you wish you were me?" "Cos you don't get your ears pinched when you put your knife in your mouth !" LOVE AND LAW.—He: It was natural, you know, that I should be attracted to you.—She, shyly: Indeed! Why P—He : Well, you know your brother studied law in the same chambers with me, and we were admitted to the bar together—She: But what had that to do with me ?—He: Why, don't you see? I looked upon him as a brother-in-law.—She, blushing: Oh, I see! Portly old gentleman to articled clerk in lawyer's office: "Is Mr. Buzf us in ?" Articled clerk: "He is at present engaged in a consultation, sir; he will be at liberty in a moment, if you will wait." Portly old gentleman, taking a chair: "Do you smoke?" pulling a cigar from his vest pocket. Articled clerk, rising eagerly: "Yes, sir." Portly old gentleman : "Then you won't object to my lighting a cigar! First newspaper humourist, at dinner party: "I flatter myself that is not a bad story." Second newspaper humourist, without smiling : "Yes, it will do." First newspaper humourist: "Then,' why don't you laugh? That is a nice way to treat a friend's joke !" Second newspaper humourist, laughing: "Oh, I didn't know this was a socid matter! I thought you wanted my professional opinion. Pray, pardon me !" THE ART or SHOPPING." What's the price of this article ?" inquired a deaf old lady. "Seven shillings," said the draper. "Sevenbein shillings !" she exclaimed ; "I will give you thirteen." "Seven shillings," replied the honest tradesman in a louder tone, "is the price of the article." "Oh ! seven shillings,' the lady sharply rejoined; "11l give you five." A GOOD JUDGE OF A DlNNER.—Cawder got a good dinner at home the other day by telling: his wife that he was going to bring a judge home with him to that meal. When he arrived alone, and Mrs. Cawder asked him where the judge was, he triumphantly pointed to him- self, and remarking, "I'm a good judge of a dinner." An American justice's first charge: " Gentlemen of the jury, charging a jury is a new business to me, as this is my first case. You have heard all the evidence as well as myself; you have also heard what the learned counsel have said. If you believe what the counsel for the plaintiff has told you, your verdict will be for the plaintiff; but if, on the other hand, you believe what the defendant's counsel has told you, then you will give a verdict for the defendant. But, if you are like me, and don't believe what either of them has said, then I'll be hanged if I know what you will do! Constable, take char.ge of the jury !"

Wife: "Can you tell me, my dear, why a widower is like a young baby ?" Husband: " Er—er—because----" Wife: "The first six months he cries a great•deal, the second six months he begins to take notice, and lie always experiences great difficulty in getting through his second summer." A German school teacher was instructing his pupils how to act when the Grand Duke should pass through on the railroad, an event which was to occur the next day. "Remember, children," said the pedagogue, "that as soon as the train arrives you are to shout as loud as you can, 'Long live the Grand Duke!' until he leaves." The next day, when the Grand Duke arrived at the station, and bowed graciously from the platform of the special carriage, the school children made the welkin ' ring with—" Long live the Grand Duke until he leaves !" LETTING HIM DOWN.—Scene--Board School, not a , hundred miles from Glasgow. Inspector, to schoolgirl, during reading examination: "What is meant when it says here, He was amply rewarded'?" Schoolgirl: "Paid for't." Inspector: "Paid for it! No, no! You don't know that. Suppose you were to go into 4 baker's shop and buy a half-quartern loaf, and lay down four- pence; would you say you had amply rewarded' the baker ?" Girl: "Yes, sir." Inspector: Why ?" Girl: "Because it's only twopence-threefarthings." Collapse of inspector. Canon Bagot once, seeing in a groceg:s shop window a card with "This sugar given away" on it, had a stone of it made up in two parcels, and walked out with one under each arm. Demanding payment, and explaining that the sugar was given away only to purchasers of • tea, the assistant jumped over the counter, followed the reverend gentleman, and gave him into custody for larceny. Pointing to the cunning tradesman's lure, Canon Bagot asked the constable whether any one could steal sugar which was given away, and the intelligent officer discomfited the shopman by declaring, "No, in- deed; and I'll have a stone of it myself !"

div.head: PRESENTATIONS TO THE REV. J. AIcTLTRIC
div.p: PRESENTATIONS TO THE REV. J. AIcTLTRIC

The Rev. J. McTurk, who has been superinten- dent minister of the Warrington Wesleyan Circuit during the past two years, but who is now remov- ing to Walsall to fill a similar office, was on Satur- day evening presented with a token of the respect and esteem in which they held him by the members of the Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel. The pre- sent consisted of a handsome leather travelling bag, suitably furnished with brushes, &c., and the pre- sentation took place in the chapel. Although, ow- ing to the annual excursion of the employees of Messrs. Monks Hall, and Co., taking place on Satur- day, a considerable number of the members of the chapel wore out of town, there was a good attendance at the presentation. Mr. Sum- mersgill, who presented the bag to Mr. McTurk, said that they all knew that the rules of Methodism I required that after a minister had laboured in a circuit for three years it was an inexorable law that the minister should remove to another sphere of labour. Their superintendent, the Rev. J. Mc- Turk, had to fall in with that rule, and knowing he had been labouring amongst them in a way which had commanded their esteem and love dur- ing his three years, they thought it right and pro- per that they should not merely have a formal part- ing, but that they should give expression to the feelings of their hearts by presenting him with some small token, but which, however, would by no means evidence the full amount of their grati- tude. (Hear, hear.) Of all the men that he had known he knew of none who had laboured amongst them who had raised a feeling of respect so univer- sal as their esteemed superintendent. He did not know that he had made a single enemy—and.he felt more especially called upon to express on behalf of that church their gratitude to God for Mr. McTurk's presence with them. During the last three years they had had a very important work accomplished amongst them in the building of that chapel, and there was perhaps none amongst them knew better than he (Mr. Summersgill) did, the value of the work which Mr. McTurk had rendered them in regard to that building. At every meeting of the building committee, with the exception of three, they had had Mr. McTurk to preside over them, and two of these three meetings took place before he was superintendent, and on the other occasion he was out of town, when he deputed the Rev. Mr. Cut- ting to act as chairman. (Hear, hear.) Mr. McTurk ruled those meetings in such a way that they were harmonious and resulted beneficially for their in- terests. (Applause.) That church had greatly grown since Mr. McTurk came amongst them, and his presence and support had been always duly given and faithfully rendered with regard to every- thing connected with the establishment and growth of their church there. He might say, speaking from the subject a little, that Methodism had proved herself to be a most fitting, and he might almost say the post fitting, church that he knew of to meet the requirements of the working classes. That was evidenced by the fact that they now had. there a church so strong and in- fluential, the most powerful, and, indeed, the only i church n Sankey Bridges. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Summersgill having humorously commented on the various contents of the bag and their uses proceed- ed to make the presentation, reminding his hearers at the same time that they must not regard the bag as a hint to Mr. McTurkto quit, (Laughter.) The fact was that they knew he was leaving before they bought it, and they thought they would make him as comfortable and look as respectable as they could on his leaving Warring-ton. (Laughter.)—The Rev. i J. McTunx, on rising to acknowledge the gift was cordially received. He said they had done him a great honour in presenting him with so handsome a bag, and it was a very great pleasure to him to re- ceive it. That evening would be a pleasant memory to him, and he had a good many pleasant memories in connection with Sankey Bridges. (Hear, hear.) He should not readily forget the speech made at the quarterly meeting by Mr. Summersgill on the pro- rsal that there should be a new chapel there; and was sure it must have been a very great gratifi- cation to their friend as well as to them all to watch the growth of that new chapel—the erection 'of the material building, and the growth of the church within it. (Applause.) For his own part he was glad he was going among working-men again, and into a manufacturing town. (Hear, 1-ear.) He was not afraid of smoke; he was brought up in a smoky town, Birmingham, and he liked to see the chimmes pouring out their black volumes. (Hear, hear.) He was very grateful for all the kind things that had been said that night, and he gave his hearty thanks to all who had con- tributed towards the purchase of that bag. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. BROUGH, who also spoke very highly of the services of Mr. McTurk, remarked that he had never been in favour of that rule of their church which required that when a minister had laboured three years in a circuit he was to remove. He thought it was a cruel rule, and he would not care how soon it was altered. Mr. Brough also al- luded in complimentary terms to Mrs. McTurk, and afterwards Mr. Snoddy and several others expressed their high appreciation of Mr. llcTurk's services whilst in that circuit. On Sunday evening the Rev. J. MeTurk preached a closing sermon in Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel to a large congregation. The rev, gentleman took as his text 2 Cor. xiii. 11, dwelling upon the essentials to individual and church progress therein con- tained. After the singing of the last hymn, and immediately before the closing prayer, Mr. McTurk made a few personal remarks, which he had ab- stained from in his discourse. He thanked the friends for the general and uniform kindness they had shown him during his three years' stay amongst them. He had witnessed some substantial progress in the erection of the noble and commo- dious schools in connection with that place of wor- ship, and also in the building of Sankey Bridges Chapel. Ile was also gratified to know that there was a desire in their Warrington societies to plant in other parts of the town two or more centres of Christian work, which were much needed: In con- elusion, he wished, as St. Paul wished for the Corin- thian church, that they might all "fare well.", The ' pronouncing of the Benediction closed the service. As a mark of the esteem in which he is held in this town, a voluntary subscription was entered into, and the stewards of the circuit, on behalf of the contributors, privately presented Mr. McTurk ; with a purse containing over 25 guineas.

THE MOSTON BATTALION AT HEATON PARK.—A. NEW SINGING MACHINE. In the good old days when Lieutenant-Colonel Wigley was still Mayor of Moston and his Mayoral hospitality at the old "Blue Bell," was the topic of week-end gatherings it Major Kay's and Captain Rigby's, there was one of the Moston. Battalion dignified by the title of "Twittering Johnny," from his fine tenor voice, which had often enlivened our meetings with a song—and he could sing too. Lieutenant-Colonel Wigley has, alas, now joined the great majority, and his civic insignia now hangs unappropriated by successor, for none have been since considered worthy, of stepping into the gal- lant officer's mayoral shoes. Captain Rigby has also become a memory •of the past, and the regiment have mourned him—peace be to the ashes of the pair! But Twittering Johnny still remains to gladden the hearts of his fellow warriors, despite the fact that- a rival warbler has joined the corps, Whose forte is in the serio-comic line, and who has almost divided the opinion of the whole battalion as to their respective power and ability in the vocal scale. The rivalship was very strong, and the disputes between the Twitterites" and the " Thumpers " (so-called from the boisterous way in which they always applauded their favourite) culminated one evening in a match being made between them for suppers for the officers' mesti, at Major Kay's hostelry, and "Twitterin' Johnny" and "Pipin' Joe" both went into active training. The hopes :of the Twitterite,s, however, were almost °dashed to the ground, and converted into sighs of de- spondency by the intelligence sthat Johnny, had, in an evil hour, betaken himself with a friend to the Liverpool Exhibition, on a rough, wet day, and rashly undertaken a voyage to the Great Eastern, thereby rendering him- self as hoarse, as he himself expressed it, "as a strikin' coal cart." Major Kay, who was his principal backer, was in despair ! The date fixed for this important musical event yas the 26th July, and in answer to the gallant Mayor's anxious enquiries, Johnny said :- • Ne'er mind me, Major—Pst be o rest when I've had a good sweat at th' Yetton Park feight. Icon byet Pipin' Joe wi' a tooth or two eaut." "I'm deawn on it !" replied the Major. "Nalt tyn' see," said Johnny. " Eaur Ell's lant me summat ut 'ud mak Jenny Lind brast eaut singin' again." . ".Whatis that?" "1 canno tell yo'. It's summat betwixt a suction pipe, an' a trombone. It's a saycret, mind yo', an' if yo' goo tellin' o'th' regiment abeaut it, Joe winno sing." "But what's it.coed 1)". "1 canno' tell what. caur Eli coed it. Th' name's abeaut as big as a milestone. But he says ut Sims Reeves an' Madame Patty use'n it, an' Sam Hague's minstrels, an' oth' rest oth' big singin' folk, an' Glad- stone taks an extra whiff on it afore he maks a big speech, an' th' Prineesst of Wales nevenco'es th' childer eaut. o' bed in a mornin' beaut havin' a spell at it." "I should like t' see it," said Major Kay. " Yo'st see it after th' singin' do," said Johnny. Despite Johnny's precautions, however, it soon became whispered among the denizens of Moston and Barnes Green that Twitterin Johnny had " gan up singin' an' wor larnin' t' play,th' trombone." But even Johnny's trombone became only a secondary subject of conversa- tion as the day ippproached for the grand Heaton Park Review,where the Mostori Battalion was to play a promi- nent figure. The day came, and Twitterin' Johnny managed, some- how, to take with him to Heaton Park the so-called "Trombone." Many of the good Moston folk betook themselves that day to the gentle slopes and wooded shades of the park, in order to see their boasted battalion acquit themselves in the field. Jack Fause made the "The Arrow" into a post of observation fully an hour before the time appointed for the troops to.assemble. Our old friend Jeweller Ben walked leisurely through the ' sylvan windings of the "Crab" to the side gate in Mid- dleton Oki Road, and various other Mostonians were seen winding their way towards one common centre, as Colonel Smethurst at the head of his staff rode in front ' of the splendid Moston Battalion, headed by the Blackley brass band, towards the scene of opprations. .As they passed the spot where Jack Fause stood, he Shouted out to Twitterin' Johnny. • "Hey, Johnny, why arelt' no among th' band' wr thy new trombone F' Johnny smiled, and tried to look wise, but said nothing. As Jack Fause approached the entrance gate, he ob- served people handing cards to the man on duty there, and passing in without payment, but when he came to the gate the demand was—sixpence I " Heaw's that?" "Cant pass without." '` Thoose folk han paid nowt." "They've got cards." "So have I," said Jack, "a whole pack, nobbo' th' Jack o' Spades ut geet lost last New Yer's neet." "Don't obstruct the gate, there," said a policeman who stood by; "either produce card, or pay." Growling at what he considered an infringement on the rights of a free born Briton, Jack paid his sixpence and entered the park. When the firing began, Jack looked for a good place to see the review, and seeing several persons ensconsed in a large tree, he scrambled up to one Of the branches,. and found to his surprise Jeweller Ben and one or two other acquaintances there before him. -.They had not long been on their post of advantage when they observed the Moston Battalion running in among the trees, as if pursued by an imaginary foe. At the foot of the tree on which Jack and his companions were so comfortably seated, Twitterin' Johnny stopped suddenly and faced the foe, and drawing out from some mysterious packet a long queer instrument, he laid hold of both ends and loudly exclaimed : " Stand back. or I'll blow Yo' every one into smithe- reens !" And he clipped the instrument to his mouth. At the sight of this " infern%l machine," Corporal Stretcher and Pipin' Joe, who were close to him, darted round the tree in opposite directions, their heads coming together at the back side of the tree with a crash. It is hard to say whether Stretcher's head was the thickest, or whether it was due to the fact that-he was the heavier man, but he stood his ground, though he dropped his rifle, and looked "dazed." But as for poor Joe, away he went flying backwards about half-a-dozen yards, and his rifle flew still further, as he fell on his back as if shot. If one of the large field guns had not been fired ' at that instant,. Pipin' Joe's yell would have brought an ambulance tram to the spot immediately-7-and it was soreTY needed too, for before the echo of that gun had died away there was another crash, and doWn, came Jack Fause, Jeweller Ben, and two others, branch and all, on the top of Stretcher, who had no time to get away! Jeweller Ben's coat caught a projecting bough as he came down, and was as cleanly split up the back, right to the collar, as if cut by a tailor's shears, and Jack Fause alighted with a soft part of his anatomy upon the spike of Corporal Stretcher's helmet, which had fallen off at his encountbr with Pipin' Joe's head Whilst they were still suffering from the effects of their sudden mishap, the bugle sounded, and the Moston Battalion, leaving the shelter of the wood, formed in the open ground, leaving Jack Fause to matter blessings upon volunteers' ‘helmet spikes, and Jeweller Ben to quit the park in search

div.head: Xettero to the editor.
div.p: Xettero to the editor.
-THE TREATMENT.OF CANCER..

Sir —I and my friend, Mr. Robert Applegartb, called on William Earl. at his residence, 12, Cromwell-street, Mill- field, Sunderland, on Sunday afternoon' the 9th of May, and on reading to him the contents of the Rev. J. H. Guy's letter that appeared in the "Heecham Courant" on Satur- day', the 20.,:h of March, 1880, he happily and most readily endorsed every word which had been published respecting the cure of his cencered tongue. It was also pleasant to hear from his lips the kindly sen- timents concerning Doctor Turnbull's persevering efforts, and most successful treatment of his most difficult case. Having previnusly heard statements which raay be preju- dieal to the Doctor on account of his high charges for the treatment of cancer, nevertheless it is our pleasure to state here that William Earl spoke to us in the very highest praise of Doctor Turnbull's very generous behaviour towards him; indeed, had it not been so, Mr. Earl said his weekly wages would never have allowed him him to persevere with the treatment, because it took nearly five months to com- plete the cure. We would further remark in passing that this is by no means the only instance we know of in Sunderland, wherein Doctor Turnbull reduced his fees to meet the pressing ne- cessities of poor working people who applied to him for can- cer treatment ; indeed, we understand that Doctor Turnbull has always made a great d!fference In his fees to the suffer- ing poor. Mr. Applegarth and I feel it our bounden duty to attest the truthfulness of the Rev. J. H. Gny' letter, which so ably sets forth the real nature of William Earl's most genuine case and cure. We had the satisfaction of see- ing Mr. Earl's tongue, which has been healed about fits months, and really, it looked to us as if nothing had ever ailed that member at all. William Earl tells us that he feels himself as healthy as ever he was in his life, and that be can attend to his daily employment with perfect pleasure. Being thoroughly satisfied with all we have seen and heard about Williara Earl's cancer cure by Doctor Turnbull we most cheerfully append our joint signatures to this tate timony fur the -eneflt and encouregemeut of those people who may be suffering from cancer. (signed) HUMPHREY SIMPSON, Sen., No. 7, Spark Terrace, Sunderland. ROBERT AP PLEG..A.RT El, 13. Howarth-street South, Millfield, Sunderland. August 14. 1836.

To this we may add .Covent Garden Market, the rental of which the Duke of Bedford—deeceßdant of Reformation John—now receives is £90.000. This fortnnate family own also the Bloomsbury estate, with a rental of £280,000. It was arranged by those interested that the last issue of the "Doomsday Book" should mit include London. It is, therefore difficult to get at such incomes AB the Duke of Westminster's, but from the property in London he calls his own, it is calculated he gets not less than half-a-million. add to this land in four counties with an additional rental of £37,145. So I might go on giving the acreage and ren- tals of Salisbury. Deyenshire, Richmond, and other so- called noble families. This may all have nothing to do with the question I set out to write about, but how can we consider what is uuder the soil without thinking of the sur- face. The noble aud aristocratic landowners are, through their obstructive and selfish actions, chiefly to blame for the enormous amount of capital iavested in railways. Tiaey have, iii the words of Earl Fitzwilliam, looked, upon the minerals beneath the surface "as a bank upon which they and their euccessors could draw at pleasure." I find myself without room to deal further with "Eledge," but what lea likes in the above he is welcome to. CLIFFORD D;

div.head: ROYALTY RENTS AND RAILWAYS.
div.p: ROYALTY RENTS AND RAILWAYS.

Sir,—Ercouraged by much practice, the Spirit of idleness has been upon me. I thought not to allow so great a length of time to elapse ere taking notice of the letter of " Jaques" respecting the now burning question of "Royalty rents." It would be a waste of time and space, besides being an insult to the gathered knowledge of "Jaques," to quote figares showing the amount of money paid to those who, through the accident of having a father or of being the favourites of Dame Fortune, have become possessed of the land and all it contains. Ido not care even now to discuss this gneetion, or the kindred one raised by " Hodge," viz Free Trade and Railways. I have no doubt, friends " Hodge " and "Jaques," are pretty clear of all the disagree- able results arising from the system, which gives to those who toil not so large a share of the agreeable results of labour; and they—l had almost said he—can therefore look on with equanimity ; but allow me to assure them it is far otherwise with those who, like the present writer, are suffer- ing from the vicious system. The question resolves itself into an old and very vulgar, one : (An a man do as he likes with his own? It goes a little further than this and makes one ask : What is there that a men can call his own? I take it that if society was of that homogeneous character that we infer when we boast - of a 199 century civilization, we should see less selfishness and more of the true brotherhood of man.

In the case of Royalties, we have first the landowner who in the strivings of nations iinde himself unable to driw his customary rents from the land, and is forced to make large reductions to tenants having no capital; but lately, in any case, does he make these reductions until the tenant's capital is absorbed into his most capacious maw. Following the tiller of the soil, for convenience sale, we 'may take the collier, the iron stone getter, and the et-marry- man. Before either of these three can commence work a bargain has to be made; this done, the capitalist finds hint- self bound to pay a stipulated SUM for the right to gal a something that the forces of nature have been hard at werk creating ever sinee the primeval forests begen to diseppoer. A strange thing this, that nature should have laid up in the bowels of the earth her rich stores of bottled sunshine with the view of enabling a few individuals to enire life I Stranger still that it should have been said that " the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereot. Lean imagine" Jaques" with the full force of his indi- vidualism giving me a bit of goo S (?) advice on this point, and suggesting the possibility of cere and thrift making the present writer into a capitalist. Ah, well ; unfortunately I always see through the capitalist, and find his creator either toiling and moiling from dawn to disk, or moaning. "we've got no work to do." More than this, it seems to me that advice can only be good when its applicability can be made general. In this case we menet all be capitalists ; but I think it is possible for us all to be workers. I think it is also possible fcr the workers to cease making what is not wanted. I beg "Jaques" not to be hard on me for what I say about capitalists, because I quite recognise, that under present circumstances, we shall have to put up with them; but I hope to have his sympathy when I draw a distinction bet:ye-al these gentry. We have the man who, by attention to every-day affairs, knows how to make dimes into dollars, and so become an etrpleyer. As an employer, we see him making use of the thousand and one tricks of trade, to enable him to undersell his fellow manufacturers; not satisfied with foreign compe- tition he labours hard to create a competition that brings his own townsmen, nay, his own flesh and blood, to work at starvation wages. I hope "Jaques" has no symtiathy with thie man, vet it cannot be disputed that he has a right to do as be has a mind with his own. I hope time will remove this man by teaching his successor to have fewer wants and to recognise the wants of others. 'The income of the United Kingdom is said to be £1,200,000,000. Less than half of this goes to the working classes; the larger half goes to, partly the class I have re- ferred to, and to another class, who must he ranked as cloi- talts, hut for whom lam rather wanting in teepee', and of wtom I may give a few examples. Mr. Mulhall, in his dictionary of statistics, gives a list of 20 persons who hold no less than 6,710,000 acres. Also a list of 18 who have a rental of £2,812.000. There are 21 persons who have a rental of £3.552,744; S with £1,442,823. It matters not to pits! up these figures; no one believes that these men have earned these enormous rentals, but "Jaquee" may tell me that they may be inherited, and perhaps bring the aren- resent home and ask—" should I like to be disinherited ?" Well, no; I shouldhat not as things are. As things ought to he, there would be no need for such a course of action. Now for "unearned increment" and my examples. On the 4th of January, 1883, a case was given by a correspon- so dent in "Public Opinion" when, not very torn age. lard which let for £3 per acre now lets for £3.000 ; of greend rents which were £6 per house, are now £BO. Per- inea, readers may remember the Bootle sands, Liverpool. Some years ago the Northern Dock had to be made. A pieco of ground, part of the Bootle ean3e, was required. Nominally this piers of waste belonged to the Earl of Derby. Before the dock could be hilt the Earl claimed £200,000 as compereation. Teo men, v had to he borrowed at 4 per cent., and the people to-day pay £SOOO a year in thashape of interest alone. I call this robbing the poor by adding to the rates. "Jaques" may have some more refined dem/4.i ptirse term. John Russell, Esq., of Dorsetshire, at the time of the
t

div.head: DEATH OF THE VICAR OF RUNCORN.
div.p: DEATH OF THE VICAR OF RUNCORN.

It is our sorrowful duty to record the death of the. 1 Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A., Vicar of Runcorn, which I ' occurred on Wednesday evening after a lingering il and painful illness. The rev, gentleman, who was i . in his 70th year, had held the living of Runcorn for!, the long period of 41 years, and during the whole 1 of that time had filled a prominent position in the 1. regard and estimation of the people of the town. 1: The sad intelligence of his demise quickly circulated I , on Wednesday, and a deep feeling of regret per- . meated all classes. It was about three years ago; that his familiarly robust constitution showed I , signs of failing, and prior to the illness which caused his death he had a prolonged and dangerous attack, during which his life was despaired of. He, however, recovered sufficiently to take some part in the public duties and parochial work to which he was warmly devoted; but it was ' apparent to the numerous persons with whom he was associated that his intellectual faculties had become dulled. He remained in moderately good health until the 15th inst., when he was seized with what proved to be congestion of the liver, which was followed by an attack of jaundice. On Saturday night Dr. McDougall, who had constantly attended the rev, gentleman in his illness, called Dr. Cameron into consultation, and some hopes were entertained of his recovery; but on Tuesday great 1 prostration resultel from failure of the heart's ' action, and he died peacefully on the following evening. The Rev. Canon Barclay was the eldest son of Mr. , Alexander Barclay, of York, and was born on Christ- I mas Day, 1816. When little more than an infant ! he met with a most unfortunate accident. He had been left in the drawing-room with a favourite dog, 1 and upon the return or the nurse the boy was found; lying helplessly on the floor. An examination re- vealed the fact that his leg was fractured, and it is supposed that he had climbed upon the back of ' the animal, and had thus met with an accident, which made him a cripple for life. He received his early education at the Cathedral School of St. Peter's, and as he was unable to take 1 part in the outdoor amusements of his companions, he paid greater attention to his scholastic studies, and succeeded in achieving the distinction of win- ning an exhibition. His inclination leading him to select the church as a profession, he entered at 1 Christ Church, Oxford, and his University career was highly successful. He made himselt acquain- ted with the Greek and Latin poets, and the lead- ing philosophers of antiquity, and obtained a first- t class in /,iteris liumanioribus. At the age of 22, in! the year 1838, he took his B.A. degree, and three years later his M.A. His course of training was . now practically over, but he remained within the precincts of the college as a tutor, and amongst his pupils were men who have figured prominently in po- litical strife. The most distinguished are the present Duke of Westminster, Lord Robert Clinton, Mr. S. Chichester-Fortesque (now Lord Carlingford), Sir Robert Peel, and Sir Francis Scott. The Duke of Westminster even continued to read with his tutor after his appointment to the living of Runcorn. In the year 1840, the deceased was admitted into the ministry of the Church of England, and was ordained deacon by the then Bishop of Oxford. In the following year he was ' ad- mitted as a priest, and four years later he was appointed by the Dean and Chapter of Christ Church to the living of Runcorn, then vacant by the death of the Rev. Frederick Master, M.A. He read him- ! self in as Vicar of Runcorn on St. Thomas's Day, 1845. The scheme for the building of the present . church had just been originated, and the new vicar threw all his energies into the project, with the result that the old church was closed in September, 1846. "Arise, let us 'go hence," was the text of the vicar's last sermon in the venerable fane. With the completion of the present church the vicar intro- duced several improvements in the services, and particularly paid attention to the musical portion. An eloquent preacher, a ready platform speaker, and a polished scholar, he soon made his power felt in the town. Every good object had in him an earnest and able supporter, and he was connected with al- most every public institution in the town. So far as parish work is concerned, it may be mentioned that in addition to the erection of the present church he was instrumental in the building of a commodious structure at New- town, which answers the purpose of school and ! mission room, and recently a new church has risen ' in Greenway-road, at a cost of several thousand pounds; while, from time to. time, the National Schools have been enlarged to meet altered require- ments. He was the chief promoter of the . Penny Savings Bank, the Church Friendly Society, and an auxiliary of the District Visiting Society. In 1865 he was appointed .honorary canon of Chester Cathe- dral by the late Bishop Jacobson, and subsequently he was further honoured with the, office of Rural Dean. This position, he relinquished in January, 1885, on account of his serious illness: His abilities as a preacher were recognised in 1856, when he re- ceived the, appointment of Select Preacher to the University of Oxford. He was allso.a Proctor in Convocation. Canon Barclay was clsolonoured in matters of a secular description. Elected as a Guardian of the poor for Weston in 1860, he was in 1868 appointed vice-chairman of the Board of Guar- dians, and in the following year, on the resignation of Sir Richard Cross, the reverend gentleman was offered and accepted the chairmanship of the Board. He was re-elected from year to year until his resigmstion in 1885. He was also chair- man of the Rural Sanitary Authority. On the formation of the Scbool Board in 1871 he was elec- ted a member, and was subsequently appointed chairman. which position he retained up to the time of his death. The Free Library- Committee, when established in 1882, selected the rev. canon as their head. In the numerous positions of honour and responsibility in which he was placed, the Icanon invariably displayed great business capacity. combined with an urbanity and a friendliness of feeling that won for him the ' respect of all who came in contact with him. In fact, Canon Barclay laboured long and earnestly for the public good. A churchman of the "broad school," his sympathies were wide enough to permit him to do cf,ood with- out reference to difference of creeds; an-cl he will live in the esteem of all classes of the community ' for ,many years to come. On Thursday flags floatea halt-mast from various buildings in the town, and the shops of numerous tradesmen were partially closed. The. funeral, which will be of a public character, will leave the vicarage at I°-30 noon on .Ifonday. Mt. W. 11. Rogerson, Bridge-street, has charge of the arrangements. It may be stated that the living of Runcorn i; valued at £450 per annum with a residence, and is in the gift Of the Dean and Chapter of Christ Church, Oxford.

Thomas Wright, labourer, of Crouton. was Tits ATTEMPTED MIIIME7I OF A GAMIX.F.EPER.— On Thursday, brought up at the Prescot Police Court, before Mr. W. L. Evans, after bAng remanded twice, on a charge of shooting with a gun at Frederick Fryer, with intent to kill and mur- der him. at Tarbock, on the morning of Sunday, the 15th inst. Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared to prosecute ; the prisoner was undefended. The evidence a the prosecutor, Frederick Fryer, who is a gamqkceper in the service of the Earl of Sefton, was first taken ; and as he was in a weak condition, he was accommodated with a chair. The prisoner, it was stated, was cue of a noted gang of Poachers. ;mg on the morning in question was discovered illegally trespassing in search of game in company with another man not in custody, and on being followed threatened twice to shoot. Saving "By God, Fred, I'll !Moot," he cocked his gun, placed it to his shoulder, and tired full at his victim. Clubbing his weapon as the keeper still ran towards him bleeding and staggering from the shock, prosecutor aimed a blow at him with his stick, which slipped out of his bleeding hands. Two desperate struggles then tool: place, in which the gun was broken, the prisoner kicking and attempting to bite the keeper, who was now thoroughly exhausted from loss of blood. Wright got away, but was afterwards apprehended.—Prisoner was committed for trial at the Liverpool Moises.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. AUGUST 38, 1886 THE SCHOOL OF ART, WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. AUGUST 38, 1886 THE SCHOOL OF ART, WARRINGTON.

We give below the results for 1886 of examinations by the science and Art Department. It is satisfsc- tory to know that the School of Art continues to make progress. Jean. Ferrier was arrested at Folkestone on Friday on an extradition warrant for embezzling £4,000 in Paris. A tender of Messrs. Armitage and Hodgson, of Leeds, for the erection of the new town hall at Portsmouth-, at a coat of £lOO,OOO, has been accepted. Margaret M'Cormick, of Sonagh. Swinford, died on Thursday, it is believed, from poisoning. Her mother-in- law and sister-in-law are arrested.

CILICKET.—LucAs and Braun made a good stand on Fri- day against the Australians, the score for Sussex at drawing stumps being 322 for seven wickets. The news from Bayonne respecting Queen Christina's health is of a most disquieting nature. It is reported that she suffered a severe relapse on Thursday. Daring the past quarter, among the deaths registered in Ireland were the following at very advanced ages :—One at 101, one at 102, two at 103, one at 104, and one at 112 yeare respectively. The, interview between M. de Giers and Prince Bismarck was resumed at Franzenstadt on Friday, and, it is believed, resulted in a perfect understanding on the Bulgarian crisis being arrived at. Sin REDVERS BULLER IN InELAND:—On•Friciay morning Major-General Sir Redvers Bailer arrived in Kingston and proceeded immediately to Dublin to make preparations for carrying out his mission far the restoration uf law and order in the seeth-west, particularly in Kerry. • OUTRAGES IN IRELAIITD. -- A. Kingscoart correspondent telegrivAs that a number of ontrages were committed on Thursday night in this part of county Cavan. The gates I of the premises of a man named Malconason, living at Cor- nakell, were stolen ; a valuable cow, the property of a man named Reilly, of Tagart, was stabbed; and John Nelson, of Shercoek, was served with a threatening letter warning him to give up his connection with the emergency men, and to join the National League.

div.p: PRESCOT-

The Rev. H. A. MacnagMon, Vim of Prescot, has, we learn, accepted the living of Tan Bizsley, Yorkshire, offered bin by Earl Fitawilliam. Both Mr. and Mrs. Macnaghton hava taken a great interest in the parish of Prescot, and will, be very mach missed. The living of Prescot is the gift of the Fellows of King's College, Cambridge..

div.head: BREWSTER SE&SIONS.
div.p: BREWSTER SE&SIONS.

The annual Brewster Sessions for the petty sessional divi- mien of Prescot were held on Tuesday, in the police court, Prescot, the magistrates on the bench being Messrs. A. B. Gladstone and W. L. Evans.—Superintendent Barker read a I roper showing the number of licensed victuallers in the Prescot Petty Sessional Division up to the end of July last, from which it appeared that there were 114 licensed victual- lers, 36 beersellers for consumption on premises' 9 beer- sellers. for consumption off premises, and 8 other licenses, making 197, being 4 full licenses, 5 oeersellers, and 1 grocer's licensa- fewer than last year. Tbe population was 44,321, there being one license to every 225. persons. During the year the licensed victuallers and beersellers had conducted their houses well, one licensed victualler only having been conviced. The prasecutions for drznkenness since 1884 had decreased, the numbers being-1884, 1.425; 1885, 1,155-;. 1886, 899. The apprehensions and summonses for all °fences during the five years he had had charge of that division were as follow :-1881, apprehensions and sum- monses, 1,909; 1882, 2.722; 1883, 3;q39 ; 1884,3,814; 1835. 3,3€2`.;. and 1536, 2426. There had thus been a marked decrease in the number of apprehensions and summonses this year as compared with those of 1884. There were no applications for new licenses, and the whole of the old imams were renewe4.

At (71asgow on Thursday, Gavin Loudon, formerly a teller in a braach office of the Bank of Scotland, was sen- tenced to five years' penal servitude for misappropriating £O4O belonging to his employers.

SUICIDE ov Ma. JAMES PEkEIRR.—A. New York corres- pondent gays :—Mr. James Beecher, brother of the Rev. Henry Ward Beecher, has committed suicide at Elmira. The deceased was suffering from ill-health. The eMgy of the Rev. Arthur Robins, Queen's Chaplain, has been burnt at Eton, in an open boat. The rev, gentle- man had created some ill feeling by writing! letters to the uewsnADers on the sanitary condition af Windsor. A WEDDING PAETY PDX-ONED,--Mrs. John Lawson .Botcherly, of Carlisle, who was only married on the 19th inst., died at Edinburgh, on Wednesday, it is believed, from poisoning. The marriage took place at the house of the bride's aunt, Mrs. Lawson, and shortly afterwards twelve of the sixteen guests were seized with symptoms of irritant poisoning, and became very ill. The bride, who had pro- ceeded to Edinburgh for her honeymoon, died there, but the others are recovering. PLACING A SLEEPEI2 OX MZE RAILWAY.—At St. Helens, on Monday, before Alderman J. Harrisen and Mr. J. C. Gamble, a lad named William Vickers, of Earlestawn, was summoned for" unlawfully and maliciously placing a piece of timber upon a certain railway with intent to ob- struct and overthrow certain engines and trucks" on the 25th July. The London and North-Western Railway Co. were represented by Mr. Ferrand, who said that on Sunday, the 25th ult, the lad was seen to place a piece of timber, 3ft din long, 12in wide, And 3in thick, on one of the rails of the line at the east end of the tunnel on the Eecleston branch Ludt He balanced one end of the timber with stones, and if an engine had come it would probal4v have been thrown off and great damage done.—P.C. Clark then de- posed that he saw the lad place the timber on the line.—De- fendant remarked that some lads sent him to place the tim- ber upright so that they could throw stones at it—Railway- detective Perkins said he visited defendant's home and asked him why he had laid the timber on the line, and be ' replied that he found it beside the line, and was fixing it for some lads to throw at it, when they shouted" The bobby's coming." and they ran away. Defendant informed the Bench that he did not place the timber across the line, but it fell in the same place where he got it from.—The Bench ordered him to receive six stzokea with a bitch rod.

A Durban telecram in the second edition of the "Tines" says I—lntelligence received at Manritian states that ar- rangements are proceeding between the Hova Government and the English Btnk Syudioate for the payment of the French indemnity in order to terminate the French occn- pltion of Tamatave. The Hovas are stated to be doing their best to carry out the treaty -despite the French reports to the contrary.

div.head: ADDRESS.
div.p: THE ADDRESS.
The adjourned debate on Mr. Parnell' amendment wail resumed.

Mr. SAXTON said the present Government occupiedt a comfortable position, as they were relieved by casual allies from framing a policy or of defending it in debate. Deal- ing with Mr. Chamberlain's speech, he said the right hon. gentleman, who was absent, showed his confidence in his opinions by running away from a reply. He (Mr. Sexton) denied that Mr. Parnell's amendment was inconclusive, but on the contrary he insisted it was definite, and unmistake- ably clear to withdraw the incentives to disturbance he bad addressed to the Irish landlords or resigns or adopt for a policy of war one of remedial measures. He then pro- ceeded to sharply criticise Mr. Chamberlain's speech. He then took objection to Mr. Chamberlain's opinion regarding land purchase, and was proceeding to refer to the commis- sion the Government proposed to issue, when Mr. C.Litiess rose to order, and objected to his doing so.—The SPELNER ruled that Mr. Sexton was in order; as the last part of the amendment referred to land purchase.—Mr. SBx- TO then at length controverted the statements of Mr. Chamberlain, and strongly urged the ad- visability of revising the judicial rents. ' The policy of Government . was to draw bills on the future which they did not intend to honour, and to urge the land- lords to exact full rents. The Irish party would await the result with feelings of anxiety. They would do all they could to promote fairness and justice, but they would not make themselves traitors to the country. (Cheese.) Sir W. BARTELLOT opposed the amendment and would give the Government his best support to carrying out the wish of the country—the preservation of the legislative union with Ireland. Mr. Sifavv-LErlivriE believed the Government would not be able to carry out the policy they heti shadowed forth, and that they would find their position untenable in the face of 85 Home Rule members for Deland. As regarded the proposed Royal Commission, he suggested that it should commence its sittings at once, and if that was done he be- lieved it quite possible for the report to be made before the winter. _

Mr. McCharrivrr did not believe that the excited language used by some of the Irish members was calculated to ad- vance tbe cause they had at heart, or to improve the posi- tion of the tenant farmer of Ireland. He opposed the amend- ment. Mr. W. ABBAS:UM deprecated the transfer of the losses of Irish landlords to the shoulders of the British taxpayers:

Mr. SETON•KARR opposed the amendment, and doubted the sincerity of Mr. Parnell and his followers, as they strongly objected to the policy of the Government before they knew what it was. Mr. O'DOHERTY insisted that Parliament owed it to the tenants of Ireland to see that they bad the protection which recent legislation was intended to afford them, and contended that steps ought immediately to be taken to pre- vent their undoubted rights being confiscated.
