div.head: ITAYDOCK.
div.p: ITAYDOCK.

A Cirri) RUIT OYER AND KILLED.—On Saturday morn- ing, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Huntsman Inn, near Havdock, touching the death of a child, who met with its death under shocking circumstan- ces on the previous-Thursday. It appeared that deceased, a girl, left home in the morning to attend school, at Black- brook, and took- her dinner with her. At noon she was walk- ing in the road when a horse and lurry, driven lay John Dunn, fruiterer, Earlestown, approached. At that moment another girl was on the opposite side of the road to that on which deceased was walking, and Dann. in turning the sharp corner near the Ship Inn, made an effort to evade the last-named girl, but failed to notice the deceased, who was knocked down. elle of the wheels passed over her and she received injuries which terminated in her death an hour later. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidents./ death," and exonerated Mt driver from all blame in the case.
MYSTERIOUS DROWNIISG CASE.

A mysterious case of drowning was brought to light in St. Helens on Sunday morning, when about nine o'clock the dead body of a farm labourer, named John Kilroy, was dis- covered in the ca.aal owned by the London and liorth-West- ern Railway Company. A short time before the hour men- tioned, a youth named Henry Houghton saw a parcel, attached to a scythe pole, floating in the canal, near the St. Helens station. The parcel was got to the side, and was found to contain clothing. The police authorities were in- formed of the cireumstance, 'and after a few minutes use of the "drags," the deceased's body was brought to the side. From a letter in his pocket it appeared that he was coming to St. Helens to meet his brother, but how be got in the water was a mystery. On Monday afternoon an inquest was held before Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, at the Raven Hotel, on the body of the deceased, who was stated to be 43 years of age, and a labourer in the harvest field.—Michael Kilroy said deceased was his brother, and lived at Charlestown, County Mayo. Witness saw him alive on the previous blonday at Lostock Junction, near Bolton, when witness was coming to work at St. Helens, and deceased was going to work at Lostock. Witness did not know that anyone had a grudge against de- ceased, and he never knew him to be drunk. Witness told his nephew to *write on Friday to the deceased, and the letter produced was the one sent.—The letter was read by the Coroner. It asked the deceased to come over to St. Helens on Sunday, and they would then go on to Lincoln- shire. The letter was posted on the Friday night, and the deceased would receive it on the Saturday morning.—P.S. Pollitt said he saw the bundle and the scythe pole dragged from the canal, and he examined the bundle, which con- tained a shirt, a pair of socks, and a razor. He got the "drags," and about ten minutes afterwards recovered the deceased's body. which was removed to the mortuary. The letter produced was found in one of the pockets, as are' as LI 63 9?:d in silver and copper money. There were no .narks of violenCo on the body. The deceased would not have to pass along the canal to get to the address mentioned in the leiter—Langtree-street. The deceased, in crossing the Raven bridge, might have turned on the canal bank instoad of going along the "opening" further on, which would have been his right road.—The jury returned a ver- dict of " Found drowned," adding that there was no evidence to show how deceased got into the water.

The following were the prize winners Thomas Parr, Wigan, £2; 2, E. Nash Warrington, .£1 lOs 3, F. Clare, Warrington, £1 ; 4,kichard HArt; Warrington, lOs ; 5, G. Burnett, copper .kettle; 6; W. Buckley, ss; and twelve minor prizes. Mr. T.- Rigby officiated as secretary. EXCURSION.—On Saturday, the employs of Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Company had their annual , excursion, Llandudno being the chosen destination. .4 bout 300 persons took advantage of the trip. AI, , start was made from Bank Quay station at about' 6-30 in the morning, and on reaching Llandudno the party dispersed to •visit the many places of *interest in the locality. The weather was not very bright, , and during the day a_ little rain fell, but it was not such as to interfere with the pleasure of the excur- sionists. The return journey was commenced at 17-30, and Warrington was reached soon after-ten o'clock. ST. BAP,NADA.S' CHURCH CHOIR.—The members of this church choir had their annuul trip on Satur- day, Hale being the selected destination. The com- pany started at one o'clock, and after a very plea- sant drive reached the pretty village, where they. ' spent the time at the waterside in games, and visiting the church and other places of interest. At ' six o'clock they all sat down to an excellent knife- -and-fork tea, provided for them by the vicar. Afterwards the Vicar, the Rev. J. D. hlewelly, cu- rate, and others delivered short addresses. The ,party, numbering 51, returned to Warrington at 10-30. The National Anthem was sung before break- ing up. FIRE AT RINTON.—The Warrington Fire Brigade were engaged all day on Monday at a fire which had broken out in a portion of the farm buildings in the occupation of Mr. Richard Lowe, of Ritton Old Hall. The whole bf the hay in a building 130 yards long was destroyed, the damage being esti- mated at £l2O. It is not covered by insurance. The firemen succeeded in saving the building, which was only slightly damaged. The origin of the fire is unknown, but it is by some attributed to overheating. A. narrow escape occurred in connec- tion with the fire. A mounted messenger who brought information to the fire brigade station was returning in front of the engine, and when near the police station the horse he was riding slipped and fell. The messenger was unconscious, and would have been run over by the engine had not the superintendent instantly caught hold of the reins. and diverted the course of the engine. _ _

. - PRESENTATION TO Mn. J. HErwoon.—The i - pre- sentation to Mr. J. Heywood, senr., which we inti- mated two or three weeks ago was about to be made, took place on Saturday night in the vestry lof Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapel. Mr. Heywood.' has for many years conductedthe Society Class held, in Bewsey-rd. Chapel, and having recently removed from Warrington to Weaverham, it was decided by the members of the class to present him with some token of their regard and esteem. This token took-- the form of large-sized portraits of each of the members of the class, suitably mounted, with Mr. Heywood's own likeness as a centre-piece, and', handsomely framed. The presentation has been ; somewhat delayed owing to Mr. Heywood's illness, I but it was ultimately arranged that it should take place on Saturday night as stated. There were about forty persons present, includinc, the three circuit ministers, the Revs. J. McTurk6, G. E. Cut- ting, and J. Howell Jones, and .an excellent tea, provided by Mrs. William Houghton, having been partaken of, the presentation was made in very ap- propriate ternis by the Rev. J. McTurk. The gift was suitably acknowledged- by Mr. Heywood,. and afterwards almost all the members present ex- pressed their high appreciation of his past services and hopes for his future welfare. The portraits, as we previously mentioned; were the workmanship of gr. Webster, Bridge-street, and the framing and. mounting Were done by Mr. D. Owen, Golborne- street, and in each instance the execution was all that could be desired. MAYORAL "AT HOME."—On Thursday afternoon the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Har- rison) held an" At Home " at the Town Hall, from half-past three till seven o'clock. The visitors on their arrival were received by the Mayor and Mayoress in the Council Chamber, which, together with the entrance hall, was handsomely adorned with flowers and ferns supplied from the park by the head gardener,. Mr. Green. The weather being , very fine, most of the guests, after being received, passed through the chamber into the park, which had Wen closed to the general public during the afternoon. Here music was discoursed by the Blue Coat School Band, under the leadershipof Mr. Rose, and the Padgate Industrial School Band: conducted by Mr. Mines. The large lawn being in excellent condition, tennis was also largely indulged in. The appearance of the park, it may be remarked, is at present at its best, and many of the Mayor's visi- tors evidently enjoyed a pleasant saunter along the well-kept paths. In the Councit Chamber light refreshments were provided. There was a good attendance of visitors, and altogether the "At home" passed. oft very pleasantly and successfully. Amongst those present were : Mr. and Mrs Beamont, Mr. C. and Mrs Broadbent, Maser and Mrs Pickmere, Alderman Webster, Mr. P. Monks, Mrs Quekett, the Jim E. C. E. an I Mrs Carleton, the Rev. F. and Mrs Slater, the Rev. Father Fishwick, Councillors Wright, Fleming, J. Pierpoint, Ashton, Captain Nicholson, Lieutenant Buckton, Rev. H. G. Smith, Rev. C. Heath, Mr. Worslei, Rev. C. H. Brown, Rev. M. Stevenson, Rev. G. F. and Mrs Roberts, Mr. and Mrs John Fairhurst, Mrs James Fairclough, Miss Atkinson, Miss Harrison, Mr. Lengton, Miss Dutton, &c. SHOP ROBBERTZS.—At the &Tough Court, Monday, John Jeffries (21), a forge labourer, Ny-2.-12. lives in Foundry-street, was charged with stealing.' on Saturday, a pair of boots, value Gs 9d, from t.hc: shop door of Lewis Fleming, 9, Market-street; with stealing a pair of boots from the shop of Messrs. Stead, Simpson, and Nephews; and with assaulting P.C. Bickley. Prisoner was seen to commit the thefts, and P.C. Bickley, being informed of the matter, apprehended him. Prisoner thereupon be- came violent and bit the officer severely under the right arm. He said that at the time he was alleged to have committed the offences he was drunk arid did not know what he was doing. The Bench sent him to prison for two months for felony, and for fourteen days for the assault.—On Tuesday Mar- garet Mulligan (18), fustian cutter, Morris's-Yard, off Silver-street, was charged at the Borough Court . with stealing a Cardigan jacket, value Es 9d, the ! property of Thomas Henry Poole, draper and hosie.r. .Elorsemarket-street, on Monday afternoon. Ell; deuce was given to the effect that prisoner had pawned the coat, and she stated that it had been given her to pledge by some men. She said that she did not know that it had been stolen. NEW SADDLERY- BUSINESS A.T WARRINGTON.-- Mr. J. Kneen, formerly of Barrow-hi-Furness, _has recently opened the shop 75, Bridge-street, War- rington, as an establishment for the manufacture of all kinds of saddleryand leather goods, from a foot- ball to leather belting.. The shop is already filled with some hundred pounds worth of stock, the 1.11)- per room and cellars being used as workshops, wher the goods are made.. A speciality in Mr. Kneen s establishment is the machine belting, for which ..be has specially constructed machinery, and can com- pete with any of the M'aiichester orLiveroool mann- facturers both as regards quality orprice. In Bar- row-in-Furness Mr. Kneen was the proprietor of a large establishment where a number of hands were employed. Last year he sold it to a company for a considerable sum of money, but not wishing to. be out of business he has opened this shop at Warrington. He is patentee of a.large ball made speclallyr for-seafaring purposes, turbo used in case of a disas- ter at sea for putting money, letters, or • other valu- ables in, in the hope thatpossibly it might be picked up by a passing vessel. He has in his shop tor the inspection of those who may wish to see it, ope which has been thrown in to the sea on three dif- , ferent occasions, and been picked up < several hun.- dred miles away. Although only small in size it is capable of carrying a heavy- weight without Mk"- hag.. It is light, but very durable, and will, n° ' doubt, supersede the use of glass bottles. M. r• Kneen has always a large stock of harness, machine belting, &c., manufactured on his own premis-es- His footballs have received high marks of toM- mend'ation from .numerous football crab captains throughout the country. WHEREAS it appears to us the undersigned, three of Her Majesty's Justices of the Peace for the county of Chester, acting in and for the Division of Runcorn, in the said county, within which division and county the following town- ships, namely:—Aston Grange; Aston-by-Sutton, Clifton, Halton, Norton, Runcorn, Stockham, Sutton, and Weston, are situate, and teing the Local Authority for the said division, as defined by "The Dogs Act, 1871." in Petty Sessions assembled at the usual place of meeting, this 23rd day of August. 1886. at the retty Sessional Court House in Runcorn, in the said divi- sion and county, that there is sense to suspect and reasonable ground for believing that CANINE MADNESS is prevalent within the division of Runcorn aforesaid : Now we, therefore; by virtue and iu pursuance of the stat- utes in this behalf, and of all other powers and authorities thereunto enabling us, hereby order and direct all owners of dogs, or persons having doge, within the said townships, to keep such dogs confined or under proper personal control, and not to suffer the same to be at large, except when securely muzzled. And any dog not being under sugh control or muzzled as aforesaid, or found straying in any street or highway may be, and we hereby authorise the same to be detained, sold, or destroyed, in pursuance of the said Act. And this our order shall take effect and remain in force from the day of the date hereof, until the twenty-third day Of October row next ensuing. Any person acting in contravention of the above order will subject himself to a penalty of Twenty Shillings for each offence. Given under our hands and seals this twenty-third day of August. 1585, in the said Division and. County. JOHN BRUND AL FRED THOMAS 411 JAMES HANDLEY •

THE UNITED STA.TEq.—DISASTROUS FLOODS. NEW YORE. StlNDAY.—Details received here regarding the recent storm in Texas state that it wcis one of the most severe ever experienced on that coast. The towns of Vic- toria and Indianola, as well as many other places, were greatly dattia.ged. Ten persons were killed and others are missing.—lntelligence received here states that a rising has occurred in Mexican territory, adjoining Arizona. It is stated to have been caused by a dispute between the muni- cipal authorities. Great excitement prevails, and bloodshed is apprehended. Geronimoa notorious Apache Indian, who has been for a long time pursued by the American troops, has been surrounded by Mexicans while endeavouring to ne- gotiate with them. He will be handed over to the Ameri- can authorities. INTERNATIONAL POLO MATCH. But, singular as it appears, both these injured Mos- tonians forgot their respective grievances on their way home; they could only think of one thing, and think of that thing in wonder. All that night, even in their dreams, there kept coming again and again to the fore the momentous question "What could that queer thing be ut Twitterin' Johnny poo'd eaut th' review? And the mystery remained unsolved until Monday. After the review there was, of course, a deal of run- ning "chaff expended at Major Kay's on the subject of the past mimic warfare and the coming musical one. Both the contending parties were present', and Pipin' Joe came in for a large share of sympathy, on account of the terrible rap he had received from Stretcher's skull when their heads met behind the tree. "It seaunded as if a railway engine had brasted under th' park tunnel!" said one of the " Twitterites." "Aye, I thowt one o' th' cannons had gone off afore its time," Major Kay said, laughing. "I thowt Johnny's new trombone had blown up an' sent us o to Jericho," Jeweller Ben said. "Does t' no' think it's th' rippin' up o' thy own cooat ut theau yer'd ?" Pipin' Joe retorted. This raised the laugh against Ben, who adroitly turned the subject into another channel by asking— " Hasno' th' knock sent o' th' singin' eaut on thee for Monday neet?" "Not it," said Joe, "if: theau'll only ayt thy share o' th' supper as wed l I'st 'sing for it, there'll be some chance o' thy. meauth bein' shut for an heaur or two. I'st noan be byetten by Johnny theear an' his patent trombone to boot." "It's byetten thee once, chus heaw-," said Johnny, "an' made thee sing too, if theau coes that singin' ut theau did when Stretcher tupped thee." " Theau'd ha' sung eaut too if Stretcher's yed had come again' thy toppin like a steeara hammer! R's every bit as thick as owd Siah's wor when lie split th' mantel-piece at th" Bird in Hand,' at Cheetham Hill," said Jack Fause, laughing. "Hallo, Jack," said Stretcher, "are theau here? I thowt ut theau'd bin carried off to th' hospital for one o' th' wounded. Heaw does t' feel abeaut th' snio' o' thy back? Th' next time theau drops fro' a tree see ut ther's nowt under—theau's twisted th' spike o' my hel- met like a corkscrew !" And so the "firing" was kept up until. Monday night, when the singing contest was to come off, and the par- tisans of both the competitors mustered in great force, the Thumpers boisterously declaring that Johnny had'nt got rid of his hoarseness, and the Twitterites as loudly asserting that Joe was afflicted with " Singin' th' yed," from the effect of his recent rap with Stretcher's cranium. After "tossing up" for the start, which was won by Pipin' Joe, that worthy cleared his throat with a..glass of Major Kay's stout (he had been told that Madame Adelina Patti always indulged in that beverage before singing), lie commenced "A story Pm going to tell ye, Which if you'll attend to you'll hear in a era,ck, It's about a man's hungry belly Conversing along with his back; Says the belly, Here I have been fasting For twenty-four hours or more, And if this fun is to be lasting, Mr. Death will soon enter the door.'" Down came the many hands of the "Thumpers" on the tables, as Pipin' Yoe concluded the first verse of Hudson's old favourite song,with a force that threatened not only to upset all the glasses, but almost to split the tables, and shouts of "Bravo, Piper !" were indulged in by some of the most boisterous, whilst what are called in a larger assembly "counter cheers" were heard from the "opposition." As each following verse of the ballad, which is now rarely heard or seen, terminated, the Kentish fire was renewed, and when Joe came to the end of his performance it was felt, even by Johnny's most ardent admirers, that his reputation as a Moston warbler was at stake. Nothing daunted, however, he stood up when called upon, and Major Kay inquired— "Wilt have a glass o' steaut afore ,theau starts, same as Joe had? Yo'st booath start even, thus heaw." "Not I," said Johnny; "I want noan to swill music an' porter into me eaut of a glass—it's noan a mixture ut suits me." "Well, brast off then." " Howa yo'r hurry a bit," he said, as he quietly walked to the bar, and returned with the identical queer instrument he had made so effective at the review. Stretcher and Piper Joe started to their feet at sight of it.. "Yen no need t' be feeart,": Johnny said; "it's noan beaded wr dynamite same as Kernel Smethurst's soap box wur." And he put it to his lips, and pressed two small buttons at the ends. After inhaling something from it for about a minute, he placed it on the table, and burst into song. He never sang better! The hoarseness on which the " Thumpers " had depended for effecting Twitterin' Johnny's defeat had completely gone, and his clear tenor voice went through the "Death of Nelson" withcipt a fault. Both Twitthrites and Thumpers joined in one tumultuous shout when he concluded, and his rival felt annihilated. Whilst he sang, Major Kay pounced upon the instru- ment which lay upon the table, and holding it up for examination by the light of the gas, he read on one end the word— " AMMONIAPHONR." Twitterin' Johnny's brother had lent him one of those instruments, which he had purchased at the recommen- dation of Doctor Weaklegg as a lung restorer, just to do something towards curing his hoarseness, and the result had been a triumph worthy of Sims Reeves himself! Turning to Major Kay as the applause died out, he said— "Gr me howd o' that thing wr th' queer name. It munno goo eaut o' my sect. I'm noan beaun to let any- body know too mony o' my saycrets—an' neaw, if yo' likeTn, I'll ha' that glass o' steaut." Several "leading hands" about Moston and Blackley have since purchased A namoniaphones, two or three of whom are specially training for the Booth Hall Plate at the coming sports upon these instruments and Stretcher declares that "if th' Blackley Cricket Club 'll get a lot o"rwitterin'.Johnny's Trombones they'll never lose a match this yer."—J.
